title: Where the Trump administration's lawsuits seeking voter data stand
summary: The Justice Department has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia in an effort to force them to hand over their unredacted voter rolls containing voters' sensitive information.
story: Washington — President Trump's administration has mounted efforts in nearly all 50 states to obtain their complete voter rolls containing sensitive information about registered voters in their states.

The Justice Department has argued that the information is needed to ensure states are complying with two federal voting laws, the Help America Vote Act and the National Voter Registration Act, which aim to ensure states have programs in place for maintaining accurate voter rolls.

The administration sent letters to most of the states last year seeking unredacted electronic copies of their statewide voter registration lists, which include voters' birthdates, addresses, partial Social Security numbers and driver's license numbers.

A number of states have turned over publicly available versions of their voter rolls, but have declined to provide their complete lists. In response, the Justice Department has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia in an effort to force them to hand over the voter data.
So far, the Trump administration has lost 27 of those cases. Federal judges have rejected the Justice Department's lawsuits for unredacted voter rolls from:

A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department's initial case against Georgia because it was filed in the wrong court, and government lawyers then refiled it. The Justice Department voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit against Oklahoma after the state agreed to turn over its voter registration list.
The other cases remain pending. Those are in Delaware, Hawaii and Idaho.

The Justice Department has appealed most of the decisions dismissing its cases. So far, one appeals court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, has upheld a lower court decision rejecting the administration's attempt to obtain Michigan's voter rolls.

The Trump administration's bids to gain access to states' unredacted voter registration lists are part of the president's efforts to exert more power over federal elections. Mr. Trump has signed two executive orders aimed at U.S. elections, though both have been blocked by the courts.

The first executive order, signed last year, would require documentary proof of citizenship in order to register to vote. The second, announced in March, tightens the rules for mail-in voting and requires the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Postal Service to compile and maintain lists of U.S. citizens who are eligible to vote.
Mr. Trump is also pushing Congress to enact a package of voting regulations called the SAVE America Act, which would significantly curtail mail-in voting and impose new voter ID requirements.

The president has long taken aim at mail-in voting and claimed it leads to widespread fraud, though he has not put forth evidence in support of those claims. He has also claimed that Democratic states allow noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote.

title: Trump's oil and gas stocks gained millions during Iran war
summary: A report from congressional Democrats found the president purchased millions in oil and gas stocks during the war.
story: Washington —  As President Trump boasts about how much money the U.S. oil and gas industry is making from the war with Iran, the president's personal holdings in oil and gas are now worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million, compared with $12.6 million to $46 million at the end of 2025, according to a new report by Democrats on the Congressional Joint Economic Committee.

The stocks the president holds have increased in value by an average of 43% since the end of 2025, the Democratic minority said, based on data from LSEG Data Analytics. The report also found the president purchased between $4.7 million and $17.5 million in oil and gas stocks between March, after the war began, and the end of August, which is the most recently available data. He also sold between $2 million and $5.4 million in oil and gas stocks in the same timeframe, the minority found.

The report was obtained exclusively by CBS News and is based on the president's financial filings with the Office of Government Ethics. Filers are only required to report transaction ranges, not specific amounts.

But as Americans are paying significantly higher gas prices due to downstream effects from the war, Mr. Trump on Saturday night in Georgia bragged that U.S. oil and gas companies are "making hundreds of billions of dollars."

"And while oil prices are temporarily high and will be falling dramatically in a short period of time, as soon as that war's over, because there's so much oil," he told the crowd. "All in the Hormuz Strait, there are ships waiting to come, we're getting them out so fast. The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars. … Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East."
The president added that his advisers told him not to mention how much money the oil and gas industry is making from the chaos in the Middle East.

The wealthiest person to serve as president, Mr. Trump has a vast stock portfolio with holdings in all sectors of the economy. He has executed thousands of stock and securities trades this year, worth hundreds of millions of dollars, CBS News has previously reported. The White House says Mr. Trump doesn't make trading decisions himself, and his money managers try to replicate major stock indices.

"President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly reelected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle.

Ingle said Mr. Trump's stock and bond portfolio is "independently managed by third-party financial institutions" and all his holdings are "maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes."

"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle added. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest."
In a July 2026 interview with CNBC, Mr. Trump said his son, Eric Trump, also handles his finances.

Energy stocks have surged as the Iran war pushed oil and gasoline prices to their highest levels in years, driving profits for oil companies. The share prices of energy companies that are listed on the S&P 500 jumped more than 50% since the start of the year, easily outpacing the broader S&P 500's roughly 11% jump.

In early February, before the Iran war began at the end of February, nationwide, the average cost of a gallon of regular gas was $2.87, and a gallon of diesel cost $3.68. Now, eight months later, it's $4.29, with diesel at $6.28 per gallon. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, is also hovering above $115 a barrel, compared to less than $75 the day before the war began.

"Trump's Iran War has forced Americans to pay much more at the pump while Big Oil rakes in profits and the president's own stock wealth in the oil and gas industry continues to balloon," said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee. "As Trump — the country's highest ranking public employee — continues to own and trade stocks in companies that stand to benefit from his decisions, his actions raise major concerns about conflicts of interest."
Presidents, vice presidents and members of Congress are allowed to own, buy and sell stocks while in office, although insider trading laws still apply.
The minority said the president's stock purchases or total value may be even higher, since he has not yet reported transactions for September or October.

Among the nine stocks that make up the largest oil and gas holdings in Mr. Trump's portfolio, Chevron and ExxonMobil represent the most significant portion. He owns up to $23.1 million in Chevron stock and up to $18.4 million in ExxonMobil, which saw their stock prices grow nearly 25% and nearly 22% in value, respectively, since Feb. 20.
Democrats on the committee estimated American families have spent an average of $856 more on gas since the war began.
There are occasional reminders that pronouncements the president makes affect policies. In August, Mr. Trump called out ExxonMobil and Chevron by name for making "too much money" on fuel profits.

"They're making too much money, okay?" he said in the Oval Office. "Based on a shortage, they're making too much money. I don't like it. And I should be the last one to say because I'm a big free enterprise guy, nobody bigger."
Energy stock purchases and sales make up a small portion of the president's overall net worth, which Forbes estimated to be roughly $7 billion as of September.

In August, CBS News reviewed the president's oil and gas trades. One notable large transaction was on April 7, the day the president declared a ceasefire in the war. His investment accounts sold between $500,000 and $1 million of ExxonMobil stock, according to a financial disclosure report Mr. Trump filed in late June. The company's share price closed at $163.91 on April 7, before Mr. Trump announced the ceasefire that evening, and it opened down over 6% at $153.52 on April 8.
The cost of living continues to be a top issue for voters.
Last week, Mr. Trump accused Iran of trying to drive up oil prices ahead of next week's U.S. elections.

"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," he wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."

Since Mr. Trump launched the war with Iran on Feb. 28, the conflict has stymied oil exports in the region, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil shipments from the Middle East have climbed since then as exporters look for alternate routes and some traffic in the strait is restored. But the disruptions, constricted supply and uncertainty have pushed up prices, even in the U.S., which is the world's largest exporter of total oil products.

The president has made some efforts to bring down fuel prices, including by making a deal with Russia to purchase Russian diesel fuel and waiving sanctions he had just signed into law. But that fuel from Russia, a controversial move, is a drop in the bucket of the United States' massive demand, and does little to lower diesel prices.
On Thursday, the president announced he would invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production.
Mr. Trump has said gas prices will "drop through the floor" once the war is over, but even if that's the case, it's not clear when the war will end.

The president has not ruled out restarting strikes on Iran after the midterms. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told the Financial Times the war could last another year, although he said he hopes the Iranian leaders "come to the table" before that.
This story published first on CBS News at 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 26, 2026.

title: Violent crime victimization fell 25% in 2025, DOJ survey shows
summary: A new preliminary survey finds that the rate of violent crime victimization in 2025 fell by about 25%, compared with 2024. The DOJ called it the largest decline since 1973.
story: A preliminary survey released on Monday found that the rate of violent crime victimization in 2025 fell by about 25% compared with the prior year, a significant drop that the Justice Department claimed represents the largest decline since 1973.

The National Crime Victimization Survey, conducted by the Census Bureau and released by the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Statistics, found that there were an estimated 669,000 fewer violent crimes, excluding simple assaults, committed in 2025 compared with 2024.
Aggravated assault victimization dropped an estimated 31%, with about 390,000 fewer incidents in 2025, compared with the prior year.

The data for the survey comes from a sample of interviews in U.S. households of people who are 12 or older. The interviewees were asked questions about the frequency, characteristics and consequences of criminal victimization.
The survey for 2025 consisted of 101,980 household interviews. Overall, 53% of eligible households completed interviews, the Bureau of Justice Statistics said.

Other findings from the preliminary results of the survey showed that robbery was down 27% in 2025, property crime victimization was down 19%, burglary and trespassing were down 25% and motor vehicle theft was down 29%.

The preliminary results from the survey bolster findings from earlier this year in the FBI's Uniform Crime Report, which showed that violent crime rates plummeted in 2025 with the country's murder rate reaching a 20-year low.

That report, which compiles crime data from most law enforcement agencies across the nation, also recorded significant year-over-year decreases in multiple categories. Aggravated assaults fell by 7.2%, rapes declined by 7.6% and robbery was down about 18.5%.

President Trump and his allies have sought to capitalize on the decrease in violent crime rates as they have campaigned across the country ahead of the midterms to try to help Republicans retain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

In a break from prior traditions, the White House unveiled the findings from the FBI's Uniform Crime Report ahead of a campaign event on Long Island, New York, that was also attended by Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel.

title: 12 injured in shooting near Florida A&M; 15-year-old arrested
summary: The shooting happened hours after Florida A&M University's homecoming game in Tallahassee.
story: A 15-year-old was arrested in connection with a shooting that injured 12 people, including six children, over the weekend near a football stadium in Tallahassee on homecoming weekend for Florida A&M University, police said Monday.

The Tallahassee Police Department said Anthony Rivers III, 15, is facing 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent. Police said additional arrests were possible and the investigation remains open and active.

Eleven people suffered gunshot wounds in the Saturday night shooting, and another person fleeing the gunfire sustained an ankle injury, police said. Police said Sunday that six of the shooting victims remained hospitalized, and five had been discharged. One of those still hospitalized was being treated for critical injuries.
The department previously said at least three people sustained serious injuries in the shooting, while nine others are reported to be in stable condition.

The preliminary investigation indicates that a fight broke out before the shooting, according to police. It followed a football game in a crowded area. None of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, police said.
The university said on social media that the shooting happened near its campus and that it remained safe.
University President Marva Johnson said in a statement on Sunday that she shares in the "outrage and profound sadness at the senseless and despicable shooting" near the campus.
"To all the victims, please know that we are with you and we are praying for your recovery, in body, mind and spirit," Johnson said in a video.
Quinn Gray, FAMU's head coach, reacted to the shooting, saying in a Facebook post that the "senseless violence has to stop" and that no argument or altercation is worth someone's life.

"Homecoming is about family. It's about coming home to celebrate everything FAMU means to us," he said. "No one should leave our celebration in an ambulance, and no child should ever be caught in gunfire."

title: F-16 uses "headbutt maneuver" to intercept plane near Mar-a-Lago
summary: A fighter jet intercepted a plane over Palm Beach, Florida, on Saturday afternoon, as President Trump cast an early ballot in Florida's midterm election.
story: A fighter jet used a "headbutt maneuver" to intercept a civilian plane that had entered restricted airspace near President Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, on Saturday, U.S. military officials said. Mr. Trump was in West Palm Beach that day to vote in Florida's midterm election.

The interception took place at around 12:20 p.m. ET, when an F-16 deployed by the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, flew closely in front of the plane in order to gain the pilot's attention, NORAD said. That tactic, called the "headbutt maneuver," is considered standard, according to the command.

In this case, the maneuver allowed the military jet to establish communication with the pilot, who proceeded to safely steer the plane out of restricted airspace, in compliance with flight instructions, NORAD said. The plane had violated a Temporary Flight Restriction, or TFR, enacted over the area, which means its pilot could "also be met by federal authorities upon landing and subject to enforcement action," the command said.

The Federal Aviation Administration issues TFRs for a variety of reasons, often linked to large sporting events, extreme weather scenarios, political rallies or any number of other engagements attended by high-profile political figures, especially the president. The FAA transmits the latest information about such restrictions to pilots through Notices to Airmen, or NOTAMs. Pilots are encouraged to keep tabs on those regularly.

Mr. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump were seen at a West Palm Beach polling station on Saturday afternoon, where the president cast an early ballot ahead of next week's midterm elections. Asked whether he voted along party lines, Mr. Trump said: "Very much so." He went on to travel to Georgia for a campaign rally.

His appearances at midterm campaign rallies around the country have triggered various temporary flight restrictions in recent weeks. Earlier this month, NORAD reported that its F-16s intercepted a plane that had entered restricted airspace over Clemson, South Carolina, where Mr. Trump held a rally to support Darline Graham's Senate campaign. Just days before that, the command said a similar interception took place over Cincinnati, Ohio, near the site of another rally that the president attended.

title: Betting companies cap winners while lavishing losers with rewards
summary: As online sports betting companies offer extravagant perks to customers who are losing large sums of money, there are also questions about how they treat their biggest winners.
story: As greater scrutiny is falling on online sports betting companies for the way they offer extravagant perks to customers who are losing large sums of money, there is another question emerging about this fast-growing industry: how the companies treat their biggest winners.
States and state lawmakers have raised questions about a practice called "limiting" — a tactic sports betting platforms use to apply the brakes to gamblers who are having too much success.

"They have to ensure that the house always wins," claims Brianne Doura-Schawohl, the director for the Campaign for Fairer Gambling. "I would argue it's not fair, and what makes it more unfair is all of the pervasive advertising tells us all that we can win."
Last week, a group of U.S. lawmakers wrote to the major gambling platforms to express concerns about the exploitation of vulnerable bettors by granting frequent losers VIP status.

"The dangling of perks — which include access to exclusive events, videos from celebrities and athletes, and tickets to the Super Bowl — distract bettors from their financial losses and encourage betting when they otherwise would not," the letter said.
Big winners, however, sometimes get the opposite treatment — their bets are often capped at under $20, and even under 50 cents at times, effectively cutting them off.

In a 2023 filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, sports gambling company DraftKings explained limiting in fine print: "We follow the industry practice of restricting and managing betting limits at the individual customer level based on individual customer profiles and risk level to the enterprise."
The "sharp" bettor who can hardly bet

When Massachusetts launched sports gambling in 2023, Mike Manning signed up with every sports gambling app available. Manning — a full-time professional bettor, or what they call a "sharp" bettor — doesn't bet on intuition. He uses a mathematical approach with analytical models.

Manning says he was winning on nearly every app. Then, one by one, the platforms began limiting his bets. On DraftKings, he said he was limited to $25 per bet. On BetMGM, he started betting $1,000-$5,000 per game, but soon, he said, he was only able to bet $5.

Limiting caught the attention of the Massachusetts Gaming Commission in 2024. The regulator required gambling companies to answer questions and provide data on how they limit their bettors. After an investigation last year, the Commission found a trend: Winning gamblers have their betting limit decreased while gamblers who lose have their limit increased.
"It's that whole 'ban or bankrupt' model," said Gadoon Kyrollos, a professional sports bettor whose bets are often limited.
Manning called the disparity in treatment predatory and unfair.
"You're exploiting the losing bettor, you're taking advantage of them, and guys like me get shown the door," Manning told CBS News.
BetMGM declined to comment.
The number of accounts the companies limit is small. Massachusetts Gaming Commission found that 0.64% of Massachusetts betting accounts had been restricted.

Matthew Litt, a New Jersey attorney who works on gambling cases, says the practice is legal as long as gambling companies are not discriminating against customers based on protected characteristics such as race or religion.

Massachusetts became the first state to require gambling companies to notify gamblers who had been limited and to stipulate why they were being limited. FanDuel wrote to Manning that he was restricted because of "an assessment of your overall wagering patterns and their impact on our long-term risk position…"
DraftKings told Manning it took action "for internal risk management purposes."
Another bettor, Michael Trevithick of Ann Arbor, Michigan, shared a betting ticket with CBS News that showed the maximum DraftKings would allow him to wager on the NBA Cup was 49 cents.

A DraftKings spokesperson said the company "applies customer-specific wagering limits to less than 0.15% of accounts as an enterprise risk control, generally in response to activity that appears designed to exploit errors or target discrepancies in odds. These decisions are based on customer behaviors, irrespective of whether a customer is winning or losing."
The VIP who was incentivized to bet more

Chris Swett was once a highly paid South Carolina attorney, but these days he is awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to four counts of wire fraud and four counts of money laundering in federal court. Swett stole about $2 million from his law firm to fund his gambling addiction.
"Every bit of it went into FanDuel," Swett said

A young, successful lawyer with a growing family, Swett discovered Daily Fantasy Sports, a game in which contestants could set lineups of athletes and compete against other contestants for money on FanDuel.

By 2019, he was wagering $5,000 to $10,000 a month Then, he says, a FanDuel employee emailed him saying anyone who spent $25,000 a month was eligible to be paired with a VIP host. The host would provide him free tickets to sporting events and complimentary entries to fantasy contests, if Swett wagered enough.
"When they sent me to the first NFL game, I felt like a high roller," he said.
Swett says he was in over his head, but his VIP host kept incentivizing him to bet more.
In one email from 2020, Swett wrote to his VIP host: "I think I'm tapped out this month..." Two days later, the host offered him a 4% bonus on any new bets.

In one two-year span, Swett says he wagered $11 million and lost about $1 million on the site. When he ran out of money, he says he set up a complex illegal scheme, defrauding his law firm and the firm's clients by submitting fake invoices for legal work. He now faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
"I take personal responsibility for everything I did, but it just seems like their system was designed to keep me playing," Swett said.
FanDuel said in a statement:

"Every day, millions of customers use FanDuel responsibly as a form of entertainment and every customer has a robust and easy-to-use suite of tools that support informed and controlled play, including deposit limits, timeouts and the ability to easily self-exclude with a few clicks.

"Since the time [Mr. Swett] was in our VIP program — and as part of our broader effort to foster a culture of responsible gaming and strengthen our customer protection tools — FanDuel has made significant changes to how we operate that program, including additional training for our employees, and new technologies to identify and stop problem gambling.

"FanDuel is an entertainment company — it is not a tool for professional bettors to gain an edge in play or earn a living. In the very rare instances where an individual attempts to deploy sophisticated income generation strategies, it is common for casinos and online sports betting platforms, including FanDuel, to use tools to protect our financial risk. These measures have been reviewed by multiple state regulatory bodies."

If you or a loved one needs help, the National Problem Gambling Helpline offers resources. Call or text 1-800-MY-RESET or get more information on their website. Gamblers Anonymous also has a national hotline at 1-855-222-5542.

title: Dictionary.com announces its 2026 Word of the Year
summary: The viral social media trend "maxxing" has earned its stripes as Dictionary.com's 2026 Word of the Year.
story: From AI chatbots to lifestyle trends, the concept of optimizing one's life came sharply into focus in 2026. That's why Dictionary.com picked "maxxing," a reflection of our increasingly online society, as its latest Word of the Year.

"Maxxing (sometimes -maxxing) is short for 'maximizing,'" says Dictionary.com. "This trendy term can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible."

The word was chosen following an analysis of search data, social media trends and news stories "to capture a society that's deeply online and focused on optimization in all forms," Dictionary.com says.

"Maxxing" rose through the cultural lexicons of Gen Z and Gen Alpha quickly, and now works as a noun, verb, adjective and adverb all at once. Leveling up your workout routine? "Gymmaxxing." Your personal care practices? "Healthmaxxing," an umbrella term that covers numerous subgenres, including "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing."

"Maxxing really stood out this year because not only was it everywhere, in all types of articles, but it crossed a lot of different domains," said Steve Johnson, the director of lexicography for Dictionary Media Group, which runs Dictionary.com.

At work, people talked about "tokenmaxxing," meaning leaning ever harder on AI. In wellness circles, there was "sleepmaxxing." Even leisure received the "maxxing" treatment, with "cozymaxxing," as did politics, when the federal government used "homelandmaxxing" in some of its messaging.
"That's not something that we often get with a lot of slang terms," Johnson told CBS News.
How Dictionary.com picks a Word of the Year

Johnson keeps a running list of words to watch throughout the year, some of which have been rolled over from years prior and tracked for growing usage. To choose an annual winner, Dictionary's lexicographers look at how often a word appears in news articles, on social media and in online searches. They also weigh a word's cultural significance during selection.
"We not only look at the data behind the word usage, but we also are really looking to see what's capturing something distinctive that describes the year," Johnson said.
The latest word choice marks a turn from last year's winner, "67," a term that, despite its virality, left many bewildered over its meaning. "Maxxing" has had the opposite effect, Johnson said.
"'Maxxing' is so accessible," he said. "People do understand it because it's tied to something that people instrinsically get."
What is "maxxing"?

The word itself isn't new. "Maxing out" a credit card, or 100 miles an hour on the highway, are well-established uses that go back decades. But the newer, optimization-focused definition comes from game theory, Johnson said. In the 1940s, academics used "mini-max" to describe a strategy for minimizing their maximum possible losses, an idea that later moved into contemporary games like Dungeons & Dragons. In that context, "min-maxing" referred to building up a character's strengths in one particular area, to the point that its weaknesses no longer mattered.

According to Johnson, words like "looksmaxxing" gave the term its extra "x" and, ultimately, turned it into the trend it has become today. He said "maxxing" started standing out on its own, too, this year, in phrases like, "What are you maxxing?" or "Everyone's maxxing something."

"Looksmaxxing" remains the most popular version of the word by far. Johnson said its use rose more than 1,000% since the start of the year in the media that Dictionary.com analyzed, while "tokenmaxxing" also grew with the proliferation of AI tools.
What "maxxing" says about us
Johnson said the word captures a pressure many people feel, especially online, to constantly do, or be, more.

"Whether it's at work and your career, whether it's in school, in so many aspects of your life, just kind of being more is something that is a pressure that I think a lot of people can feel," he said.
The pressure has also produced its own pushback, as playful versions of the word like "normalmaxxing" reject the drive to optimize everything while still using the same language.
"One of my favorite 'maxxings' is 'nothingmaxxing,' which is just completely paradoxical, right?" Johnson said. "It's going all in an optimizing doing nothing, which also requires a lot of effort."
The flexibility helps explain why the word spread so widely, he said, adding: "It resonates with people."
2026 Word of the Year finalists
Dictionary.com pulled from different corners of internet culture, politics, technology and media to compile a list of finalists. Here are the others that were considered:

Affordability: the quality of being inexpensive, which is an issue at the center of American life and, now, the upcoming midterm elections, as people face increasing costs of housing, groceries, childcare and more.Data center: a building or facility used for processing, storing or transmitting large amounts of computer data, which are cropping up more often around the U.S. with the rise of artificial intelligence.Unc: short for "uncle," Gen Z and Gen Alpha popularized this humorous and lightly pejorative slang term for an older person who's uncool, trying too hard, or just doesn't get it. Odyssey: a long and eventful journey, such as that of Homer's protagonist in his epic poem of the same name, which this summer was adapted into an ensemble blockbuster by director Christopher Nolan.

Data center: a building or facility used for processing, storing or transmitting large amounts of computer data, which are cropping up more often around the U.S. with the rise of artificial intelligence.

title: Trump attacks El-Sayed over his faith, calls him "jihadist"
summary: President Trump is making his case for Republican candidates in Michigan; he spoke at a rally in Port Huron on Sunday ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
story: President Trump is making his case for Republican candidates in Michigan. He spoke at a rally in Port Huron on Sunday ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

During his speech at McMorran Place, the president said Michigan was built by "American patriots who shed their blood, sweat and tears." He praised Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, as "one of the most respected men in Washington" and targeted Rogers' Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed.
"I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator," Mr. Trump said.
CBS News Detroit has reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment on the president's visit and Mr. Trump calling El-Sayed a "jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member," but has yet to hear back.
At a town hall meeting earlier this month in Caro, Michigan, a man asked the U.S. Senate nominee whether he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed said "absolutely."
Rogers and El-Sayed clashed on Wednesday during their second, and final debate in Southfield, Michigan.
Mr. Trump also voiced support for Republican gubernatorial candidate John James, saying he would "fight for jobs" and "lower prices."

In response to the president's visit, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said, in part, "By standing with Donald Trump today, Mike Rogers, John James, and Michigan Republicans made it clear they are fully endorsing and ready to rubber stamp Trump's toxic agenda."
On Saturday, former President Barack Obama was in Detroit to drum up support for El-Sayed, Democratic nominee for Michigan governor Jocelyn Benson and other candidates for state office.
El-Sayed appeared at a rally with Sen. Bernie Sanders at the DeVos Performance Hall in Grand Rapids on Sunday evening.
Sanders said Mr. Trump and his allies were using Islamophobia because they have "nothing to say" about the issues most important to working people, such as health care, housing and income inequality.
"All they can do is foment hatred and divisiveness," Sanders said.
Vice President JD Vance is set to stump for Republicans at CHI Aviation in Howell, Michigan, on Tuesday.

title: Gina Hinojosa says there's "deep disappointment" in both parties
summary: State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running for governor in Texas, said there's "deep disappointment in both political parties" in the Lone Star State.
story: Washington — Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running for governor in Texas, said on Sunday that there's "deep disappointment in both political parties" in the Lone Star State, prompting a new path forward that she argued is "post-partisan in some ways."
"Right now nobody wants politics as usual. Most of us see that it is broken," Hinojosa said on "Face the Nation."

Hinojosa, 52, is taking on Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas. A civil rights and labor lawyer who's represented parts of Austin in the Texas House since 2017, Hinojosa would be the first Democratic governor and the first woman to lead the state in the governor's mansion in three decades. A recent CBS News poll had Abbott leading Hinojosa, 52% to 48%.

But in a state like Texas, which has more registered Republican voters than Democrats, Hinojosa will need support from both sides of the aisle to pull off a victory. She argued that the deep disappointment she described in both parties has made Texans forge "a new way forward."

"There is bipartisan anger about what Greg Abbott has done to our public schools," she said. "Saving Texas public schools is a key part of my agenda, and that's why this campaign has resonated amongst Texans."

Hinojosa said her agenda "is not a Democratic agenda," but rather a populist one aimed at delivering for Texans. She cited healthcare access for children and combating high insurance premiums as key focus areas.

She also pointed to data centers as an issue where Texans can find agreement. She said, "Nobody's pushing back against the data centers harder than MAGA because these data centers are mostly moving into our rural communities that are unincorporated."

"This part of Texas is being taken advantage of by these data centers, and the people of Texas and rural Texas are being taken advantage of," she said. "There are big water concerns, there are big electricity cost concerns, property rights concerns, and so we need to visit all of it and make sure Texans are protected, and first and foremost have a seat at the table."

The comments come as Hinojosa has filed a lawsuit to obtain emails between Abbott and Elon Musk, who's given millions to Abbott's campaign. She said, "We need to know what exactly is going on," pointing to the relationship between Abbott and Musk, the CEO of Texas-based Tesla and SpaceX.

"Governor Abbott is focused on putting Texas on a path to becoming number one in education, codifying his data center guardrails, eliminating sales tax incentives for data centers, and lowering costs for hardworking Texas families," Abbott's press secretary, Eduardo Leal, told CBS News in a statement. "Under Governor Abbott's leadership, Texas public education funding is at an all-time high and average teacher pay has risen by over 30%."
"While Gina Hinojosa continues to run from her disastrous record, Governor Abbott will continue crisscrossing the state to talk directly to voters and to keep Texas, Texas," he added.
Hinojosa expressed optimism about her chances in next week's election, despite Texas being a reliably red state for over 30 years.
"Turnout is high, enthusiasm is high on our side, so we feel really good about where we are," she said.

title: Four Corners region faces more flood threats following days of heavy rain
summary: The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for much of the Four Corners — the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado​, New Mexico and Utah.
story: A rain-soaked swath of the Southwest U.S. braced Sunday for another round of potentially heavy showers and thunderstorms after days of rain forced evacuations and water rescues.

The National Weather Service issued a flood watch for much of the Four Corners — the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. The area has experienced unusually heavy rain since Wednesday that caused rivers to surge, flooding homes and forcing water rescues.

Repeated torrential rain and storms could flood more roads, small streams, narrow canyons and burn scars, according to CBS News meteorologist Andrew Kozak. The rain will expand across the central and northern Plains Sunday night before moving toward the Upper Midwest Monday and Tuesday.

The Colorado Department of Transportation said water flow levels in the San Juan River increased significantly overnight, and the San Juan River Bridge remains closed Sunday. Video shared with CBS Colorado shows a house in Pagosa Springs inundated with floodwaters. All that can be seen is a small piece of the roof and the chimney.

"I'm sorry, buddy. I tried. I really tried. But this one was bigger than the last one," Pagosa Springs resident Chris Mott said in another video of water rushing through a neighborhood. "It moved sandbags and everything."

About 4 feet of water flooded the home of San Juan County, New Mexico, Sheriff Shane Ferrari. He said the area's situation was stable Sunday, but he and other residents were trying to clean up and deal with damage.
San Juan County spokesperson Devin Neeley said the county did not have official numbers on damage to homes or the number of people evacuated, but he was not aware of any loss of life.

Neeley said the floodwaters were receding but left mud and silt, much of which has been contaminated with sewage because of failures at waste plants. There were still power outages affecting multiple areas, and it would likely be a few days until residents got their power back on.
"It's a pretty active disaster zone," he said. "We're not on the downswing by any means."

A tornado touched down in Santa Fe, New Mexico, around 7 p.m. Saturday, and forecasters were trying to confirm whether twisters also struck elsewhere in the state, said meteorologist Scott Overpeck with the weather service in Albuquerque. He did not have damage estimates.

Michelle Vialpando spotted a tornado from her patio in the Aldea de Santa Fe neighborhood, facing north towards Los Alamos. She had just gotten home from work and stepped outside to look at what she called "crazy" storm clouds when she noticed the twister.

"I was pretty surprised at what I was seeing and just started snapping photos," Vialpando wrote Sunday via Facebook. "I was literally in shock. I've lived in Santa Fe my entire life and have never seen anything like that before."
In the Farmington area of New Mexico, local officials said swollen rivers were receding but that many people remained evacuated and hundreds were without power.

The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and areas of New Mexico.
Forecasters said El Niño, the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific, was likely to blame for the latest storm's unusually heavy rainfall.
"It's been more or less three or four days," said Anthony Brown, lead meteorologist at the weather service office in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. "It's pretty unusual."

title: 100 years later, the mystery of Houdini's death endures
summary: Harry Houdini, the greatest escape artist who ever lived, died 100 years ago on Halloween – a fact that has only burnished his image as a daredevil who often cheated death. But was there a cover-up involving the circumstances of his death?
story: Harry Houdini, the greatest escape artist who ever lived, has been the subject of hundreds of books and movies. A pop icon, even today. He died 100 years ago this week, on Halloween – a coincidence that did nothing to diminish his mystique. But we'll get to that.

Erik Weisz was born in Hungary, in 1874. When he was four, the family moved to Wisconsin. As a teenager, he performed magic tricks in sideshows and beer halls. "He was a skinny kid, and he built himself up," said New Yorker staff writer David Denby. "He became this beautiful, incredible body, and he was a handsome man."

But according to Denby, he wanted a catchier name. He turned to his idol, Houdin, the great French magician of the 19th century: "So, he took the name Houdin and added an i and pronounced it as Houdini. But the name always sounded funny. It's vaguely Italian, but it's not. What is it?"

Houdini historian Roger Dreyer owns one of the world's largest collections of Houdini artifacts, such as the Metamorphosis Trunk. He says Houdini's magic tricks didn't exactly bring the house down. "If he was to perform it today, he wouldn't even make it past the second round on 'America's Got Talent,'" Dreyer said. "It wasn't until his Metamorphosis Trunk that Houdini really became bookable; theaters wanted to see his act. People today, over 100 years after Houdini's death, still perform this exact same trick."

After being locked in a trunk, Houdini switched places with his new wife, Bess, instantly. But once he added handcuff escapes to his show, Houdini became a sensation. Denby said, "He would be put in a cell, virtually naked, shackled. He'd come out 20 minutes later holding the handcuffs. The specialists were called out of their corners to produce the most complicated locks for him. He'd lick it every time. There's no record of his failure."
Denby says there was symbolism in his escapes: "He would defeat those police forces all over the world. And so, there was definitely a kind of anti-authoritarian message that people liked."

In time, the act was more than escaping shackles. It became about escaping death. "He always reinvented himself," Dreyer said. "Initially, he got out of a trunk. Then Houdini got out of a straitjacket. Then Houdini would get out of a straitjacket hanging from a crane. Then Houdini would go inside a live jumbo water tank upside down."

Denby said, "Curtain closed, one minute, two minutes … was he drowning? What happened to him? They'd finally open the curtain, and he'd come out and his eyes would be all bloodshot and he would be gasping. He had to risk death."

In 1904, at age 30, Houdini bought a townhouse in Harlem. He moved in with Bess, his mother, and his brother. Today, Vincent Toms lives in that house. He even gives tours. "People, when they come to the house, you know, this is Graceland for them, for all intents and purposes," he said.

After World War I, a new industry sprang up: fake spiritualist mediums. Dreyer said, "Ninety percent of the people that were attending séances back then were women trying to contact their loved ones that might have died in World War I."
In the final act of his life, Houdini became a debunker of fake mediums, exposing the tricks they used once the lights were out.
By the mid-1920s, Houdini was the man who cheated death. But that was one escape he couldn't perform forever. He died at age 52. But how he died is yet another mystery.

The usual account involves college kids visiting him backstage. Dreyer said, "One of them asked Houdini, 'Is it true that you can withstand a blow to your stomach?' Houdini said, 'Yes.' And before Houdini could brace himself, that gentleman threw not one, but a series of punches."
But most experts believe that the punches didn't act alone. Houdini had a precondition of appendicitis. "And the punches in the stomach might have aggravated it," said Dreyer.
But a new book, "Houdini: The Man Who Died Twice" by surgeon and medical researcher Larrian Gillespie, documents a very different telling of the story.
"There's something very wrong with this death certificate," Gillespie said. "I see numbers were copied and then rewritten over. This was a cover-up."

She says that ultimately what killed him was an intestinal blockage and an unreported last-minute surgery. Houdini's team favored the stomach-punch story, in part to get a bigger insurance payment. "Houdini had a double indemnity policy," said Gillespie. "The first policy would pay for his death, but if he died from an accident, it paid an additional – in today's money – $500,000."

According to documents Gillespie found, there's even doubt about when Houdini died. "I can put forth a very strong case that he died on October 30th and not the 31st," she said. "By moving the date over to the next day, every time Halloween came up, you would remember that Houdini coincidentally died that day."
But Gillespie does not believe this version of events would in any way tarnish Houdini's reputation and legacy: "Oh, not at all. Houdini was gifted, and that will never change."

But whatever the details of his death, Houdini never completely ruled out the possibility of an existence beyond. Vincent Toms said, "He did make a pact with Bess that after he died, he would try to communicate with her, if there was any way possible. And so, for the 10 years after he died, they held a séance in this room every year on the anniversary of his death."
Every Halloween since, Houdini's fans have tried to reach him. Toms will try this weekend, hosting a séance in the house at 1:26 p.m.

So many mysteries. How did Houdini do his escapes? How did he really die? Is there an afterlife? But this much, we know for sure: "If Houdini was around today," said Dreyer, "he still would be a household name, because of what he signified: the idea of hope, escape, the power of possibility, the idea of becoming an immigrant going from poverty to stardom to fortune."
And the fact that this charismatic performer, dead 100 years, is still getting new fans is, to Toms, "just mind-boggling."
Denby describes Houdini as "the ultimate symbol of liberation over death, over imprisonment. What a guy! I mean, an amazing man!"

title: Some Florida voters with ties to Venezuela discouraged by Trump's policies
summary: Doral, Florida, has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.
story: Latinos voted in record numbers for President Trump in 2024, but polling shows that voting bloc is up for grabs in the midterms.
And one region that reflects that shift is Florida's Miami-Dade County, where Latinos and Hispanics make up more than 70% of the population.
In January, CBS News met Andrea Ramos and her husband in Doral, Florida, as they were celebrating and closely following the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
Ramos, a naturalized U.S. citizen from Venezuela, told CBS News that she credited President Trump with Maduro's capture. Doral has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.
"I had such big admiration for him," Ramos told CBS News about her sentiments for the president following Maduro's arrest and extradition to the U.S.
But about nine months later, her feelings have changed.
"I feel disappointed," Ramos said. "I feel, in a way, betrayed."
While disappointed with the economy, it is the Trump administration's immigration crackdown that has led Ramos to sour on Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
"Overall, I'm not feeling like the law is being respected," Ramos said.

According to a CBS News Battleground Tracker poll released earlier this month, 60% of Hispanic likely voters said they were likely backing congressional Democrats in the upcoming midterms, compared to 39% who said they were likely backing Republicans.
That marked a considerable shift from 2024 CBS News exit polls, which found that 51% of Hispanics voted for Democrats, compared to 46% who voted for Republicans.
In the same new poll, 59% of Hispanic likely voters found that the Trump administration was trying to deport more people than they had expected, compared to 51% of all likely voters.
Asked in the poll about the Trump administration's focus on deportation, 59% of Hispanic likely voters responded that it was too much, compared to 49% of all likely voters.

Stephanie Caro's family-owned coffee shop in Doral is among many local businesses that have seen a decrease in foot traffic and sales as masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have been photographed on the city's streets.
"I'd say there is a heightened sense of fear," Caro said.
Some local business owners have said they're concerned they'll have to close their doors.
"It really impacts the entire community," Caro said. "People are scared to leave their houses. They're changing their daily routines."
Doral voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, driven by Venezuelan Americans who fled Maduro's socialist regime.

But ICE has increasingly targeted asylum seekers who have pending cases and active work permits, and Mr. Trump's close relationship to Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez has impacted his support in Doral.
When CBS News asked Doral's Republican Mayor Christi Fraga three times if she still supported Mr. Trump, Fraga refused to give a direct answer.
"There is a lot of things that I support, and there's also questions that I've raised," Fraga told CBS News.
Ramos remains undecided on who she will vote for in the upcoming midterms. On that question, Fraga also declined to advise her constituents to vote for Republicans.
Said Fraga, "Vote your conscience."

title: Pope cleared for South America trip after lung cancer surgery
summary: The trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, set for Nov. 6 to 17, is particularly grueling.
story: Only two weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV has been given the medical green light to embark on an ambitious 12-day tour of South America next month.

"Based on his current clinical status, as well as the instrumental and laboratory tests performed, there are no contraindications that would prevent him from undertaking his upcoming apostolic journey to Latin America as planned," the Vatican said in a statement on Monday. "The Pope is following medical recommendations with great care and diligence, and with a deep determination to continue serving the Church."

The trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, set for Nov. 6 to 17, is particularly grueling. The 71-year-old pontiff plans to travel to 10 cities, board 14 flights, and attend many public appearances and religious ceremonies.

The Vatican also confirmed that the trip would proceed "according to the program previously published," which means that a visit to the Peruvian city of Cuzco, Peru, situated at more than 11,000 feet above sea level, remains on the schedule. The thinner air there could pose difficulties for someone recovering from lung surgery.

Doubts about the pope's ability to undergo the South American trip surfaced again last week, when, on the advice of his doctors, Leo canceled a visit by helicopter to Assisi for an international peace gathering to take place Tuesday. Doctors said they advised him to do so preventively, because of the unpressurized air on the helicopter journey.
The upcoming journey carries particular personal significance for the first American-born pope, who spent more than two decades working as a missionary and bishop in Peru.

"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," he said in a statement Monday. "May this journey be an occasion for us to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaiming the Gospel with joy."

Leo was operated on Oct. 13, when doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after discovering a malignant tumor.  The cancer, identified as a lung adenocarcinoma, was discovered accidentally during a routine abdominal examination, his doctors said. The operation was successful, without complications, and Leo was discharged from the hospital on Oct. 17.
Since leaving the hospital, Leo has gradually resumed his public duties, including his weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square and meetings with visiting church leaders.

title: These factors could decide Netanyahu's fate in Israel's election
summary: Israelis are about to vote to choose their next government. The race is wide open, and Benjamin Netanyahu's political fate could hinge on a couple key factors.
story: Tel Aviv — After three years with their country at war on multiple fronts, Israelis will go to the polls Tuesday in a hotly contested election that will shape their next government. Polls show it is an incredibly tight race, and as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to hold onto his job, there's no guarantee of a quick, definitive outcome for him or his political opponents.

Polls vary widely regarding the expected outcome. Right-leaning pollsters give an advantage to the right-wing and religious bloc led by Netanyahu, while left-leaning pollsters show an advantage for the so-called change bloc opposing the incumbent.

Most polls show neither side is likely to win a decisive majority of the 120 seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, which would enable it to unilaterally form a new government. The tight margins mean the voting may end in a stalemate, which could lead to protracted negotiations across ideological lines, the formation of a minority government, or even an election do-over.
"It looks like an indecisive outcome is the most likely outcome," said Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute.

This will be the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis will go to the polls Tuesday with their country still fighting in the subsequent multi-front war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for a third.

Against that backdrop, there are a few key issues that could determine the election outcome, even if it does take days or weeks to shake out. But first, here's a look at the two main factions vying for the votes.
The Netanyahu camp

Netanyahu, Israel's longest serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.

He has two main pitches to voters: First, that only he can form a government without the support of Israel's Arab parties, which he argues would be a danger to the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts.
Netanyahu's second argument to voters is that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon, and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.

President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump said.
Since that endorsement, Netanyahu has argued that only he can work with Mr. Trump to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon, which many Israelis see as an existential threat.
Netanyahu's campaign slogan, which rhymes in Hebrew, is: "Either right wing or Palestine, either right wing or a nuclear bomb."
Over the weekend, Netanyahu posted an AI-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv on social media, with a caption reiterating his insistence that Iran poses an existential threat to Israel.
Netanyahu's supporters see him as a top-tier global leader.
"Bibi can handle the whole world," restaurant owner Benny Abraham told CBS News, using Netanyahu's nickname. "Bibi is charismatic. He has a strong voice. The world loves him."
"He's the king of Israel," Abraham added.
The (anyone but Netanyahu) "change bloc"
Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of Arab, right, left and center parties that have one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.

The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.

Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.
Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.

Eisenkot responded Monday to Netanyahu's rhetoric about Iran posing a nuclear threat by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats — including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv."
"This time, it won't work for him," he said.
Eisenkot's key campaign promises include launching a state inquiry into the intelligence and security failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas —  something Netanyahu has thus far blocked.
Uzi Aharoni, 73, an engineer from Tel Aviv, told CBS News he saw Eisenkot as the only real alternative to Netanyahu.
"Eisenkot is not left, he's not right. He's straight and honest. He's the kind of leader who will take care of us, the people of Israel, and not himself or his corrupt family," Aharoni said.
The Arab vote and the ultra-Orthodox draft
There are a few factors analysts believe could hand a victory to either side.

One thing polls can't predict well in Israel is voter turnout. Past elections have shown voters backing Netanyahu's Likud party, and Arab-Israeli voters, vary the greatest in their enthusiasm to come out on election days, so there could be room for turn-out surprises that significantly change the electoral math in favor of either side.
Arab Israelis, also referred to as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up around 20% of Israel's population.
"The higher the Arab turnout, the less likely that Mr. Netanyahu, within the current coalition, can form another government," said Plesner at the Israel Democracy Institute.

More Arab voters will head to voting booths this year because of their strong desire to prevent Netanyahu from forming another government with far-right allies, who have made life difficult for them over the last four years, Jehad Abomoch, a cafe owner in the predominantly Arab city of Baqa al Gharbiya, told CBS News.
"The last four years were a real catastrophe, both socially and in terms of wars," he said, adding that many Arab Israelis feel that under Netanyahu, they have "no hope, no future."

There are also two new parties entering this election, and polls show each is hovering around the threshold of support required to gain seats in the Knesset. Whether either party ultimately crosses that threshold could also tip the scales —   in either direction —   toward a new coalition government.
Both parties are focused on challenging Netanyahu's alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties by demanding that ultra-Orthodox Jewish citizens be formally included in Israel's mandatory military service.
It's a key issue that cuts right through Netanyahu's traditional support base and coalition partners.
Not all election outcomes are neat and tidy
In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in parliament, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.

One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.

Another possibility is that the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than 50% of the 120 available. Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.
If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.
Plesner told CBS News that, if all the politicians running effectively stick to their campaign promises and refuse to swap sides in the event of a stalemate "we will roll into another election."
"I'm sure that most politicians are not interested in that," he added.

title: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine
summary: Here's what to know about Starlink and Starshield, the technologies Ukraine is relying on in the war against Russia.
story: Over the past month, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.

Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.

The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.

Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.

Musk understands the extent of Ukraine's reliance on his technology and what it would likely mean if he flipped the switch off: "Starlink remains critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now," he wrote on X. "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately." This was not a threat, he said — just a "statement of fact."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials, though the world's richest man has denied it and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also said he's not responsible for slowing the network.

However, CBS News reported on Oct. 20 that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.

Asked by reporters whether he asked Musk to turn Ukraine's service back on, Mr. Trump said on Thursday, Oct. 22: "I don't want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether somebody else called. Doesn't make any difference."
"The bottom line: He put it back," the U.S. president said.
On Oct. 24, Musk admitted he had throttled Starlink, stating that the Ukrainian military had "violated Starlink terms of service."

For days, there was conflicting information about whether full access to the networks had been restored, but on the same day Musk admitted he was behind the slowdown, Zelenskyy said in an X video post, "Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored to the speeds we had before the restrictions."

"The speeds are now where they need to be. The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient," Zelenskyy said. "This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered 'shaheds.'"
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
What happened in Ukraine?

On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News.

Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.

Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said on Oct. 17 that the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
What are Starshield and Starlink?

Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.

The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.

There is no working alternative to Starlink, no direct competitor that approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.

Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.

Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.

During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Oct. 21 that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.

On Oct. 22, more than a week after the speed limits were first imposed, a Ukrainian government official told CBS News that some military units have been able to operate at higher speeds, but only at sea. Other units said restrictions remain in place, causing disruptions at speeds of 160 to 200 km/hr.
Is Ukraine using Starshield or Starlink?
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters.
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.

Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
Musk and throttling Ukraine's access to Starshield

CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.

Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, sources said. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.

The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.

The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Can Elon Musk stop the use of Starlink and Starshield?
Musk has now admitted he's behind the Starlink disruption experienced by Ukrainian forces, though he has said he has not restricted its use of Starshield.

"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X. He added that Starlink is a "commercial service" and that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."

His admission that he had throttled Starlink came in an X post on Oct. 24: "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Oct. 21, "The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk." But then he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used. Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
Intelligence-sharing
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.
Ukraine relies on a mixture of American sensors, aircraft, surveillance and human intelligence to map Russian positions and launch sites.

The early warning system, which is distinct from the SpaceX products, notifies Ukraine when Russia has launched a ballistic missile in its direction. It failed in at least two instances, on Oct. 13 and Oct. 18.

On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage. That overnight attack targeted energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.

Ukrainian sources said U.S. officials said the warning system had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials expressed doubt about that explanation and accused the U.S. of "playing" with the system. By 3 a.m., that system seemed to have been restored.
Then on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been hit by another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again, there was no warning from partners."

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
By Wednesday, however, the warning system appeared to have been restored: "Now intelligence works. Thank you so much. That was crucial for us," Zelenskyy said on Fox News.
Rising pressure to end the war
Deliveries of key Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine have also slowed, Ukraine has said.

Rubio on Tuesday called interceptors the "most in-demand product right now in the defense field," and said that "when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too."
"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," he said. "It's simply a balance between our obligations."

Mr. Trump has grown impatient with the more than four-year-long war. He has sought to portray the ongoing Ukraine war as the reason for high energy prices and has vented his frustration with Zelenskyy more frequently in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to end it.

He waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.

Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.
Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday that Russia keeps "grinding away" and is more capable of sustaining casualties than Ukraine, arguing "it's time" for Zelenskyy to make a deal.
