title: Prince Harry making 'big mistake' that could destroy chance of royal reconciliation: expert
summary: Prince Harry told GQ he wants peace with his family, but royal experts say his public interviews are thwarting any chance of reconciliation.
story: Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham-Turner argues King Charles must take action to bring Prince Harry and Meghan Markle back into the royal fold amid family tensions.
Several royal experts believe Prince Harry is making a "big mistake" that could ruin his chances of reconciling with his family.

In his first major interview since returning to the U.K. with his family, the Duke of Sussex told GQ he wants to make peace with his father and brother. However, royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital that Harry's willingness to publicly discuss his strained family relationships only makes the royals more reluctant to extend an olive branch.

"The peace offering is already undermined as it is public," said Fitzwilliams. "That continues to be his big mistake. He cannot be trusted. [The Sussexes] had already launched brutal attacks on the royal family [with their tell-alls]. Family disputes are bitter. But numerous interventions from 'friends' and interviews like Harry's in GQ make this highly unlikely."
PRINCE HARRY SAYS ‘MOST IMPORTANT THING IS TO RECONCILE’ WITH ROYAL FAMILY

Prince Harry sat down with GQ for an interview recorded in New York in late September 2026 and published Oct. 20. The Duke of Sussex spoke about grief, the death of his mother, Princess Diana, fatherhood, his family's return to the U.K. and his desire to reconcile with his father, King Charles III, and brother, Prince William. (2026 Max Mumby/Indigo)

Speaking about the family rift, Harry told GQ: "Some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile — that's the key point."

"Scars stick around forever," Harry continued. "But what your perception is, and what your mindset is to those things that have happened, letting go of the past. That’s something that I would encourage everybody to do: If there’s certain things from the past that are still affecting you every day, that’s harder to let go of. But, for me, there’s enough drama in the world and enough drama in people’s lives to continue with issues with family."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrives for a visit to the Community Recording Studio in St. Ann's on Sept. 9, 2025, in Nottingham, England. (Getty Images)
Harry also told GQ that he has been "really criticized" for sharing his side of the story.
WATCH HERE: KING CHARLES URGED TO BRING PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE BACK INTO FOLD: EXPERT
"I find it fascinating because everybody else is allowed to tell their version of my story, but God forbid I should be able to tell the other side of it."

Royal broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that although Harry may yearn for reconciliation after years of the Sussexes publicly airing their grievances, "the palace doesn't trust Harry and Meghan." Chard said Harry's decision to speak publicly "proves Prince William's fear — anything said in private will end up in print."
Prince Harry's book "Spare" seen displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)
"Vindication on Megxit and absolution without apology do not equate to reconciliation," Chard added.
Prince Harry told the BBC in 2025 that he's ready for reconciliation. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back from their roles as senior royals in 2020, citing intense media scrutiny and a lack of support from the palace. After moving to California that year, the couple discussed their struggles in interviews and documentaries. Harry's 2023 memoir, "Spare," further strained his relationship with the royals. Several experts told Fox News Digital that Harry and William are still not on speaking terms.
Office workers in London watch the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's "Harry & Meghan" docuseries on Netflix on Dec. 8, 2022. (Jonathan Brady/PA Images via Getty Images)

On Oct. 15, the Sussexes attended a series of charity events in Nottingham, marking their first major joint outing since their reported return to the U.K. The appearances drew attention from royal experts, many of whom compared them to official royal engagements.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during a visit with Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

In January 2020, Queen Elizabeth II made clear following the Sandringham Summit that there would be no "half in, half out" role for the Sussexes. They couldn't remain working members of the royal family while pursuing independent, income-generating ventures.

"Following conversations with the duke, the queen has written confirming that in stepping away from the work of the royal family it is not possible to continue with the responsibilities and duties that come with a life of public service," Buckingham Palace said in a statement on Feb. 19, 2021.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle returned to the U.K. six years after leaving for California. (Getty Images)
In response, the couple issued a statement of their own, saying: "We can all live a life of service. Service is universal."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, poses for a selfie with well-wishers after a visit to Community Recording Studio in Nottingham, central England, on Sept. 9, 2025. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Shortly after the couple returned to the U.K., Buckingham Palace released a letter from the Lord Chamberlain, written on behalf of King Charles III, stressing that there was "no change" to their status. The letter stated that Harry and Meghan are "no longer working members of the royal family" and that their charitable work "is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity."
"In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests," the letter added.
Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, arrive at the Endeavour Fund Awards at Mansion House in London on March 5, 2020. Soon after, the couple moved to California. (Justin Tallis/AFP)
A source close to the Sussexes then pushed back against the description of the couple as "private citizens."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Prince Harry is seen here during a visit to Himmah Hub during the couple's visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
"They are public figures," the source told People magazine. "Members of the public know who they are. The idea that they can live a normal, 'private' life is sadly not realistic."
Another friend of the couple told The Times that Harry and Meghan "hate" the phrase "working members of the royal family."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen greeting members of the public at the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia on April 17, 2026, in Sydney, Australia. (Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

"'Working members of the royal family' is a really lazy phrase," the friend told The Times. "He hates it, she hates it. They are not 'working' for the institution, but they are members of the royal family, and they work."

From left: Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex watch a flypast marking the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace in London, on July 10, 2018. (Getty Images)
The friend said the Sussexes also dislike the term "former royals."

"Things like Nottingham aren't done in the name of the institution or the crown, but Harry is the son of the king, he is still a member of the royal family, he's just not a member of the institution. It's misleading to call them 'former royals.' It has an impact on how they're perceived and the way people talk about them."

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle meet well-wishers during a visit to Reprezent 107.3FM in London on Jan. 9, 2018. The "Suits" alum became the Duchess of Sussex when she married the British prince later that year. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)
A friend of the Sussexes told Hello! magazine that Harry and Meghan never agreed to the late queen's decision to prohibit a "half in, half out" arrangement.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, leave a service of thanksgiving for the reign of Queen Elizabeth II at St. Paul's Cathedral in London on June 3, 2022, during Platinum Jubilee celebrations marking the monarch's 70 years of service. (Matt Dunham - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
"It doesn't trouble them," the friend said. "They never agreed they wouldn't be half in, half out. That was what was decided and foisted upon them."
"They’re just living their lives and they can, because they’re financially independent," the friend added.
Meghan Markle attended a special screening of the documentary "Cookie Queens" in Los Angeles. (Eric Charbonneau/Roadside Attractions via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Archewell for comment.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex during a visit to Himmah Hub during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026 in Nottingham, England. The Sussexes are still non-working royals who are financially independent. (Annabel Lee-Ellis - Pool/Getty Images)
British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital that former palace courtiers were appalled by the unidentified friend's remarks.
"Harry publicly declared he'd accepted the agreement with his grandmother, the queen," Fordwich said.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting Queen Elizabeth II's coffin to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that the royal family, often referred to as "The Firm," made "a mistake" by not allowing the Sussexes to resume their royal duties and support the king.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
King Charles III delivers a speech during the ceremonial opening of the seventh Senedd in Cardiff, Wales, on Oct. 15, 2026. (The Welsh Parliament via Getty Images)
"Harry and Meghan are not private citizens — this was decreed by King Charles in the letter created by the Lord Chamberlain which, in my view, was humiliating for the couple," Turner said.

"What that means is that Harry and Meghan can do whatever they want right now. … It just goes to show at the moment that whoever is advising the royal family [is] constantly making mistakes. Because if they really wanted to control Harry and Meghan, they would invite them back so that they can be part of the royal family and could actually control what's going on."
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex visit Epic Partners during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Joe Giddens - Pool/Getty Images)

"Yet the same accusations are levied against Meghan and Harry when they apparently have decided to do an event for themselves in Nottingham," Turner said. "What is the difference? I ask. Because, in reality, they are allowed to do whatever they want to do now to actually promote their charities and good causes."

King Charles III meets guests during a reception to celebrate the Commonwealth Diaspora ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda at St. James's Palace in London on Oct. 14, 2026. (Getty Images)
Fordwich also suggested there was a "divide" between King Charles III and Prince William over how to handle Harry's return to the U.K.

"The divide is as follows: The king craves family united, keeping the door open and aiming to facilitate some sort of way back, while he is though completely united with Prince William that the Sussexes will never again represent the royal family," Fordwich explained.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, visit The Commons, a project transforming a church into a self-sustaining community centre, during their visit to Northern Ireland on Oct. 9, 2026, in Belfast, Northern Ireland. (WireImage)

"Obviously, from both his actions and words, Harry is rather desperate for reconciliation," she said. "But with every public statement and action, rather ironically, he's actually thwarting any remote chance now of even a familial thawing."
PRINCE HARRY RISKS 'LOBBING A GRENADE' AT PRINCE WILLIAM AS CHANCE TO HEAL YEARSLONG FEUD EMERGES: EXPERT

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Prince William, Duke of Cambridge, watch a flypast to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London, England. (Getty Images)
Fordwich doesn't believe Harry will reconcile with his family anytime soon.

"Writers of 'The Crown' must be sitting with pens poised at this now ridiculous situation escalating," Fordwich said. "Although Harry and Meghan wish to build proper bridges, the king apparently refuses to even discuss the subject."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Donna Mills, 85, draws the line at unexpected OnlyFans request: ‘I’m not going to’
summary: "Knots Landing" star Donna Mills revealed the one surprising everyday activity she refuses to film for her OnlyFans subscribers.
story: Donna Mills tells Fox News Digital what changed her mind about joining the platform — and why she says there's no pressure to bare it all.
"Knots Landing" star Donna Mills is revealing the one unexpected request she refuses to fulfill for her OnlyFans subscribers.

During a Friday appearance on ABC's "Nightline," the 85-year-old actress told correspondent Kayna Whitworth that her content largely consists of glimpses into her daily life but asserted that there is one routine she won’t perform for the camera.

"I do the Peloton," Mills said. "Just, you know, they’re the things of everyday life: having a cup of coffee, you know. They say they like it when you brush your teeth…I’m not going to brush my teeth."
Donna Mills revealed the one OnlyFans request that she won't fulfill. (Disney via Getty Images)
DONNA MILLS DOES 100 SIT-UPS A DAY, PLAYS TENNIS FIVE TIMES A WEEK AT 85 BUT WON'T QUIT DORITOS
When asked if she believes that most of the OnlyFans users who are engaging with her are men, Mills said, "I think so. Yeah. Sometimes you don’t know."

While Mills drew the line at brushing her teeth on camera, she appeared more open to sharing racier content with her subscribers. However, she explained that she does not believe full nudity is necessary to be sexy, pointing to one of her past Playboy shoots as an example.
PLAYBOY'S CELEBRITY-DRIVEN RELAUNCH FACES CREDIBILITY TEST IN ONLYFANS ERA, EXPERT SAYS
The "Knots Landing" star said she plans to sell never-before-seen "Playboy" photos. (2005 CBS WORLDWIDE INC.)
"I think it’s sexier to be not just totally naked, you know," she said. "And have a little imagination about it."
"One of the pictures in ‘Playboy,’ which I think is one of the sexiest things, is me in the shower, in a dress," Mills added.
CRYSTAL HEFNER FELT 'ABSOLUTELY BRAINWASHED' DURING HUGH HEFNER MARRIAGE, REVEALS STRICT PLAYBOY MANSION RULES
The "Play Misty for Me" star said she believed that the never-before-seen "Playboy" outtakes could be particularly enticing for her OnlyFans subscribers.
"I think the probably the most appealing would be the ones that weren't in the magazine, right?" she said. "Because they're from the shoot, the same shoot, but they weren't in the magazine."
'HARRY POTTER' ACTOR SAYS ONLYFANS VIDEOS EARNED HER MORE THAN HER ENTIRE ACTING CAREER
After Whitworth asked how much she might charge subscribers for one of the previously unseen photos, Mills floated a potential price.
Mills launched her OnlyFans page in July. (2024 Getty Images)
"Boy, I'm not sure," she said. "Maybe I'm not sure — $100."
"$100?" Whitworth replied.
"More?" Mills asked.
DREA DE MATTEO SAYS ONLYFANS BECAME ‘POLITICAL STATEMENT’ AFTER FINANCIAL STRUGGLES THREATENED HER HOME
"We're thinking you could go up a little higher," Whiteworth told her.
Mills surprised her fans when she announced that she had launched an OnlyFans account in July.
WHY WWE LEGEND DAWN MARIE IS HEADING TO ONLYFANS AT 55

The actress, who became a television sensation playing the glamorous and ruthless Abby Cunningham on "Knots Landing" from 1980 to 1989, said the platform would give her a chance to connect with fans in a more personal way.
Mills said fans were hungry for a behind-the-scenes look at her life, which she noted wasn't possible during her TV heyday.
Mills said she shared a glimpse at her daily life with her subscribers.  (Photo by Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)
'KNOTS LANDING' STAR DONNA MILLS ISSUES URGENT WARNING ABOUT AGING

"They want to know me," she told Variety at the time. "They want to know what I do during the day when I’m home. They want to see my home. They want to know much more about my personal life than we ever experienced back in the ’80s and the ’90s that, you know, the fans were cut off from."

"I've always appreciated the incredible support and encouragement I've received from my fans over the years," Mills said. "Social media has been a wonderful way to stay connected, but I'm excited to join OnlyFans because it offers the opportunity for a more personal and direct connection,"
However, Mills emphasized that she planned to approach OnlyFans on her own terms.
"It’s simply another platform to spend quality time with the people who’ve supported me throughout my career while staying true to who I am," she said.
Andy Bachman, CEO of Creators, Inc., the talent agency that manages Mills' OnlyFans account, noted that the Hollywood veteran isn't switching up her image.

"This is not about changing who she is. It is about giving her longtime fans more access to the personality, style and behind-the-scenes moments they already love," Andy Bachman, CEO of the talent agency Creators Inc., said.
The actress is reportedly making "many six figures." (© 2025 Disney. All rights reserved.)

"Donna has always been fearless and ahead of her time," Bachman added. "She told me, 'YOLO — let's do it,' and that perfectly captures her attitude. She is approaching OnlyFans on her own terms and creating a space that feels authentic, personal and completely true to her."
During an appearance on "TMZ Live" shortly after launching her account, Mills said that she wasn't planning to pose nude but didn't entirely rule out the possibility.
"Who knows? My first answer would be, oh, no, I won’t do that," she said. "But then my second answer is, I don’t know."
"I don’t want to do anything that’s salacious, you know what I mean?" Mills added. "That isn’t my personality. That isn’t what I feel good doing. But if it’s cute and sexy … we’ll see."
In August, Mills appeared on "Creators Inc. Podcast," less than a month after launching her account. At the time, Bachman, who hosts the podcast, shared an update on her page's performance.
"I can say that you are doing incredibly well," he said. "Many six figures, and it’s been early."
Bachman noted that Mills had already received some unusual requests, including "foot kink people" who asked to see the actress "stomping on grapes" with her bare feet in her vineyard.

title: Brandi Glanville says doctors are 'taking my face off' in exploratory surgery after years of health issues
summary: Brandi Glanville details the $5,000 exploratory surgery to remove what she believes is something alive moving beneath the skin on her face.
story: Reality star Brandi Glanville explains why her recent financial strain made turning down opportunities more difficult and pushed her to prove she could perform again on FOX's "Special Forces."
Brandi Glanville is taking a major step in her ongoing health battle by going under the knife.

During an episode of her "Brandi Glanville Unfiltered" podcast, shared on Thursday, Oct. 22, the 53-year-old reality star went into detail about the "exploratory surgery" she is scheduled to have on Friday.

"Dr. Carlo Honrado is taking my face off on Friday and going to do an exploratory surgery to kind of do a power wash under my skin," she said. "And then he knows where there's two definite spots, like either fungal balls or something alive. I think it's alive personally cause it moves when it wants."

She explained that after four years of dealing with the issue, she is "super excited" but also "scared to death" because she has "never had facial surgery" and has heard the procedure is "more intensive than a facelift."
Glanville shared that she is undergoing "exploratory surgery." (Paul Archuleta/Getty Images)
FORMER REALITY STAR OPENS UP ABOUT NEW DIAGNOSIS AFTER YEARS-LONG HEALTH ORDEAL

While she is nervous, Glanville is hopeful the surgery will be a success, as facial plastic and reconstructive surgeon, Dr. Honrado, "comes highly recommended." She noted that she is "okay" with the $5,000 price tag, telling herself, "what if he actually does take it out and it's done?"
"It started in my face, my cheek and my jawbone, and then it went over my head back in my neck. Now it's down my spine," she explained.
She went on to say that the doctor told her if he is able to "cut that head off the beast", getting rid of the rest of it will be more manageable.
Glanville previously shared that she believed she picked up a parasite after visiting Morocco in 2023. She suffered from facial paralysis and was initially diagnosed with stress-induced angioedema.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" alum revealed she agreed to compete on the current season of "Special Forces" because she needed the money after years of spending on medical treatments.

title: Country star Cody Johnson says Nashville wanted to change him before success
summary: Cody Johnson walked away from a Nashville record deal after executives told him to ditch his cowboy hat, then spent a decade proving them wrong.
story: Cody Johnson talked to Fox News Digital on the iHeartRadio Music Awards carpet, and admitted his pre-show ritual is "pretty simple."
Nashville wanted Cody Johnson to ditch his cowboy hat before giving him a shot at country music stardom.

The Texas-born country star said he walked away from a record deal after executives suggested he swap his signature cowboy look for a baseball cap — a move he viewed as a demand to change who he was before he could make it in the music business.

"They wanted a baseball cap, which I have nothing against, but it was the approach. It was the 'you're great, but once we change you, you'll make it.' And it pissed me off," he said in an interview with "CBS Mornings." "I tipped my hat and said, 'Thank you for your time.'"
CARRIE UNDERWOOD SAYS HER FAMILY COULD BE 'SELF-SUSTAINED' ON TENNESSEE FARM AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD SPOTLIGHT
Cody Johnson performs onstage during the 61st Academy of Country Music Awards at MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, on May 17, 2026. (John Shearer/Getty Images for ACM)
It was a gamble that could have cost him his shot at stardom.
Instead, Johnson spent the next 10 years building a career on his own terms, playing bars and honky-tonks before becoming one of country music's biggest stars.
During his interview, Johnson spoke candidly about his rise to fame and the years of work behind his success.
COUNTRY SINGER CODY JOHNSON FORCED TO STOP 'GOD BLESS AMERICA' PERFORMANCE AS VIOLENT BRAWL BREAKS OUT
Long before arena crowds and industry recognition, the singer was a small-town Texas kid who dreamed of becoming a rodeo star.

Country music star Cody Johnson revealed he walked away from a Nashville record-label opportunity after executives pushed him to trade his signature cowboy hat for a baseball cap. (Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
He eventually traded bull riding for music after years of injuries and setbacks and selling CDs in rodeo parking lots as he tried to build a following.
The country star also struggled to believe his ambitions were within reach.
THOMAS RHETT REVEALS WHY HE AND WIFE LAUREN REJECT CELEBRITY PERKS FOR COUNTRY LIFE
"Truthfully, in my core, I didn't feel I was capable of attaining a goal that big, you know, to be a huge country music star, to own a cattle ranch," Johnson said.
Cody Johnson refused to compromise his cowboy image to satisfy Nashville executives, choosing to build his country music career on his own terms. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
After turning down the label opportunity, he spent years playing small venues, struggling financially and spending long stretches away from his family to keep his career alive.

"The pressure of knowing that you don't know how to pay your water bill, and you've just been on the road for a month and haven't seen your wife or your child, and you have nothing to show for it. That's that's tough to look in the mirror."

Country singer Cody Johnson spent a decade performing in bars and honky-tonks before achieving mainstream success without abandoning his traditional cowboy style. (Christopher Polk/Dick Clark Productions via Getty Images)
He continued, "I think that I just had decided at that point that no matter what, no matter how hard, no matter how high the mountain, I will not back down. I will not quit."

After a decade of grinding it out as an independent artist, Johnson saw record labels return with another opportunity — this time, he said, without the same demand to change his image.
"I just get to be myself and be authentic," he said.

title: Rob Lowe gets candid about his best on-screen kiss as other major stars dish on their worst
summary: Rob Lowe called Nastassja Kinski his best on-screen kiss, while Nicole Kidman roasted Alexander Skarsgard over a falafel-fueled smooch scene.
story: During an appearance on "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia," the "Seinfeld" star recalls filming romantic scenes with Carol Burnett, revealing the actress's playful joke. He also reflects on other unforgettable TV legends.
Celebrities are getting real about their best and worst on-screen smooches.
Rob Lowe recently praised one of his former co-stars as the best on-screen kiss of his career, while Nicole Kidman previously roasted one of her former screen partners as her worst.
Whether it was the circumstances surrounding the shoot, the chemistry between the actors or a co-star's choices at lunch, these star's share what can make or break a romantic scene for them.
Here are some stars who have disclosed their best and worst on-screen kisses.

Lowe said Nastassja Kinski was his best on-screen kiss. (Clark Clifford/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)
Rob Lowe dished on the actress he considers to be his best on-screen kiss.

During a recent appearance on "Watch What Happens Live," the "The Outsiders" star told host Andy Cohen while playing "Plead the Fifth" that his best kiss was with co-star, Nastassja Kinski, while filming "The Hotel New Hampshire."
"Have a look at her," he said when asked what made her the best. "At that moment in time, she was probably the most beautiful woman I’d certainly ever seen."
While she was his favorite co-star to kiss, he also mentioned he felt "very, very scared" to kiss her.
Sharon Stone
Robert De Niro and Sharon Stone having a tender moment as they lay on a bed in a scene from the film 'Casino', 1995. (Photo by Universal Pictures/Getty Images) (Universal Pictures/Getty Images)
Sharon Stone has only one co-star in mind when it comes to her best kiss.

During an interview on  SiriusXM’s "Radio Andy" in April, the actress called Robert De Niro, "the best kisser in the business," and said the kiss they shared while filming the 1995 movie, "Chicago," "really just knocked me out."

"We did this scene where I have to go to the bathroom, and because I play this hustler, I get him to give me money to go," Stone explained. "He gives me this money and I look at him like, ‘Really? I think a little more than $50 for the bathroom.' And he … reaches in, and he gives me, like, $100, and then I lean over, and I kiss him."
ROBERT DE NIRO GETS EMOTIONAL AS AMY POEHLER PRAISES HIM FOR SPEAKING 'TRUTH TO POWER' AS REGULAR TRUMP CRITIC

The kiss was enjoyed by both her and De Niro, with Stone telling Andy Cohen that when director, Martin Scorsese, asked if they wanted to film the scene again, "We both looked at him and went, 'Yeah, I think maybe we need one more.'"
Sylvester Stallone
Stallone said his kiss with Talia Shire was the worst in his career. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
Although fans love the kiss between Rocky Balboa and Adrian in "Rocky," Sylvester Stallone doesn't have fond memories from filming the scene.
In a recent interview with Page Six Hollywood, Stallone referred to his kiss with actress Talia Shire as "the kiss from hell," but it was no fault of the actress.

"Then I go in to kiss her — pull the hat off, the glasses — and… her nose is running. Badly," he said. "So we go in for the kiss and she goes [bad coughing noise]. And I go, ‘Oh my God!’And I have to keep moving forward. There is no reverse. So I knew exactly as soon as I kissed her that within an hour I had the flu."
He then recalled that shortly after filming the romantic scene, he found himself in bed with a runny nose.
Nicole Kidman
Kidman said Skarsgard is her worst on-screen kiss because he ate falafel before filming the scene. (Dan MacMedan/Getty Images)
Nicole Kidman did not hold back when it came to describing her worst on-screen kiss.

During an appearance on the "Las Culturistas" podcast in March, the "Practical Magic" star revealed she "cannot stand bad breath," calling it a "dealbreaker" for her when it comes to men. She noted, "You want me to lean in? Smell good."
She then called out her former "Big Little Lies" co-star, Alexander Skarsgard, for eating a falafel shortly before they were going to film a romantic scene.

"I'm like, 'No, no, no, Alex. I'm meant to be kissing you and into you. Put away the falafel now. Because the bad breath does not turn me on,'" she recalled. "I said, 'No more falafel. Nope. Not before you kiss. Not before you make love. No more falafel. Put the falafel away.'"

story: Julie Andrews, 91, was spotted in a rare outing in the Hamptons. The "Sound of Music" star recently said she won't return for the third "Princess Diaries" movie. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

PAT SAJAK MAKES RARE PUBLIC APPEARANCE AFTER STEPPING AWAY FROM 'WHEEL OF FORTUNE'

title: 'Baywatch' star David Chokachi credits 3 am wake-ups, twice-daily workouts for unbelievable physique at 58
summary: David Chokachi reveals the Andrew Huberman-inspired ice plunge and 3:30 a.m. routine that got him camera-ready for his return to "Baywatch."
story: David Chokachi, 58, told Fox News Digital that the new "Baywatch" cast couldn't believe his insane figure.
David Chokachi is in the best shape of his life thanks, in part, to an unconventional routine.
Chokachi, 58, wanted to "make a statement" when he returned to the "Baywatch" set nearly 30 years after he first appeared on-screen as beloved lifeguard Cody Madison.

After climbing out of a dark place following an arduous recovery process due to Achilles tendon ruptures, Chokachi said that he "found a higher operating system" within, and became hyper-focused on optimizing his brain chemistry to benefit both mental and physical health.
'BAYWATCH' STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SHARES FITNESS SECRETS AT 57, SAYS SHE'S 'NOT READY TO HANG UP MY BIKINI YET'
David Chokachi admitted he's more fit now than when he worked on the original "Baywatch." (Getty Images; Clint Brewer/Backgrid)

"I'm up at 3.30 in the morning every day and ready to go. My body's like, 'It's time to go,' and everybody thinks I'm insane, but it's my dream window of time, I love it," Chokachi told Fox News Digital.
He cited neuroscientist Andrew Huberman's approach to health as an influence on his own routine and noted that former Navy SEAL DJ Shipley also helped shape his mindset.
WATCH: 'BAYWATCH' STAR DAVID CHOKACHI CREDITS EARLY-MORNINGS, TWO-A-DAY WORKOUTS FOR PEAK FITNESS
Shipley "found this program of stacking micro wins, which are the little things you do, but you do them every day, and you recognize them, like, 'OK, that was a win,'" Chokachi said.
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE

"The easiest win you can do in a day is get up early, like, really early – I mean it doesn't have to be 3:30, but if you're getting up before other people are, and you're being productive, subconsciously you start to — your brain starts going, your body starts going, 'I am a badass,' you know? And it works, I'm telling you," Chokachi said.
David Chokachi, 58, showed off his washboard abs on the beach in Malibu earlier this year. (Clint Brewer/Backgrid)
In the pursuit of personal challenges, Chokachi doubled down with prepping to be on-screen once again playing a role that made him a global superstar.

"With 'Baywatch,' I realized, on the original, the more fit I was, the more stories they'd write for me, the more episodes I'd be in ... not that money is everything, but you want your character to take off," he said. "I've always been into fitness because I grew up playing sports my whole life.
"So I did the same thing on this, but I like doubled down because I was the original coming into this new cast and I wanted to make a statement and I made a statement."
CARMEN ELECTRA SAYS 'BAYWATCH' PUSHED BOUNDARIES WITHOUT CROSSING THE LINE: 'IT WASN'T PORN'
Chokachi said he trained twice a day for six months before stepping on set.

"And I showed up on set and when it was time to take my shirt off ... we were shooting a rescue and people were just like, 'Oh my God. Dude, what have you ... how old are you?'" he recalled. "They just, they can't believe it."

"I have an ice plunge and a sauna, and that's usually how I start my day," Chokachi said. "That alone burns a lot of ... brown fat, which is the fat we want to get rid of at the fastest rate by being cold, and ice plunge is really good ... it's a positive stressor on your brain."
He added, "So I do that routine, and by the time I've already done that, I'm like, I'm off to the races, like, and I just go."

According to the National Institutes of Health, brown fat actually helps the body generate heat by burning calories when exposed to cold temperatures, though research has not established cold plunges as an effective weight-loss method.
Chokachi and David Hasselhoff have remained friends years after "Baywatch" ended. (Getty Images)

"Baywatch" first aired in 1989 and ran for a decade before its last episode in 1999, followed by two seasons of "Baywatch: Hawaii." The show became the most widely viewed TV series in the world, with an estimated weekly audience of more than 1.1 billion viewers across 142 countries in 1996, according to Guinness World Records.
While Chokachi may have felt he was at his physical peak back then, he said he's "way more fit" now than ever before.

"I have a leaner fitness," he said. "I used to just bang weights and run back then, so I was a little beefier. And now I live like ... I don't go out, I don't party ... I'm not obsessed about diet, but I don't drink or do anything."

He added, "I'm not that diligent, but I do do everything in a day that has gotten me to where I'm at now. And the crazy thing is, it not only helped my fitness level, I feel like I'm doing the best work as an actor I've ever done in 30 years of being an actor, which is wild."

title: 'Vertigo' star Kim Novak plans to become compost after death
summary: Kim Novak, 93, reveals she's arranged to have her body composted after death so loved ones can plant trees, calling it "a beautiful expression."
story: Laurence Leamer has written a new book about the muses of the late director, "Hitchcock's Blondes: The Unforgettable Women Behind the Legendary Director's Dark Obsession."
Kim Novak's final act comes with a twist even Alfred Hitchcock couldn't have scripted.

The "Vertigo" star has arranged to have her body turned into compost after her death so friends and loved ones can use the resulting soil to plant trees. The 93-year-old, who is the subject of "Kim Novak's Vertigo," a documentary about her life and career, first confirmed her plans to People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA).
Novak, who lives on a ranch in Oregon, told Fox News Digital she made the arrangements "a few years ago."
'CRIMINAL MINDS' STAR MANDY PATINKIN SHARES UNCONVENTIONAL PLAN FOR AFTER HIS DEATH

Kim Novak is seen here in this undated photo. The actress confirmed to Fox News Digital she's arranged to have her body turned into compost, so friends can plant trees in her honor. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

"The idea is that I get to live after I'm gone through trees," Novak said. "It's an exciting adventure because this is what I want after I pass. I want to keep living. And one thing that I've always been short on is patience. And a tree has to have patience. I will get to continue to express myself and be an observer of life. To me, it's a beautiful thought. It's given me great peace of mind because I'm going to keep growing. So I'm excited about that."
"It sounds funny perhaps, but it isn't really," she said. "I can't imagine being turned into ashes or being put under the ground. Both of those concepts are not too attractive to me."
Kim Novak arrives at Hotel Excelsior during the 82nd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 1, 2025, in Venice, Italy. (Getty Images)
Novak isn't afraid of death, even if her plans may strike some as unconventional. The lifelong nature lover said her connection to the environment has given her peace about what comes next.
WATCH: ALFRED HITCHCOCKS BLONDES HAD A GREAT DEAL OF SEX, AUTHOR CLAIMS

"Some people may not even be aware that's a choice," Novak said. "And I know some people don't like to talk about death, or think they're going to be turned into ashes or be underground. It sounds awful. But you have a choice. You can decide what comes next."
Frank Sinatra and Kim Novak are seen here in a scene from the film "The Man With The Golden Arm," circa 1955. (United Artists/Getty Images)

"For me, this was a beautiful concept, the idea of becoming one with the soil," Novak continued. "And with compost, of course, everything grows so much better than if you didn't have it. It helps with growth. You become part of the process. It's natural, it's real, it's honest, it's pure. And I even get to choose the kind of flowers that are going to be part of my compost — forget-me-nots."

American actress Kim Novak poses with the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement trophy at a ceremony during the 82nd Venice Film Festival in Venice, Italy, Sept. 1, 2025. ( Li Jing/Xinhua via Getty Images)

Although human composting is legal in Oregon, Novak has arranged for her remains to be transported to an Earth Funeral facility in Washington state to undergo the process, known as natural organic reduction.
"I’m in Oregon, so it's not that big a deal," Novak said.
Kim Novak poses after receiving an Icon Award for her career during the 51st Deauville American Film Festival on Sept. 6, 2025, in Deauville, France. (WireImage)
"However, they’re going to have to pack me in ice in order to make it all the way to this place," she said with a laugh.

Kim Novak bites a pearl necklace in a 1950s publicity portrait. (Getty Images)
Novak acknowledged that additional options may now be available since she made her arrangements years ago.

"I'm having all of my compost, once it's done, delivered to friends and family, a bit of it," she said. "I have instructions for all of them to plant a tree or a shrub, but preferably a tree, because I look forward to keeping growing. That's what it's all about for me. I want to keep growing. This is a beautiful expression of life continuing after death."
American actress Kim Novak with British director and producer Alfred Hitchcock on the set of his movie "Vertigo." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
When Novak began planning her final sendoff, she knew she didn't want to be buried or cremated. She began exploring other options.

Kim Novak delivers a speech prior to receiving an Icon Award for her career during the 51st edition of the Deauville American film festival, in Deauville, northwestern France, on Sept. 6, 2025. (Loic Venance/AFP via Getty Images)
"Here in Oregon, there was one place where I could have had a tree planted over me," she said. "However, it was only one tree. I'd like to be many trees."

According to The Associated Press, Novak was the world's top box-office star from 1958 to 1960. The outlet reported that she stepped away from Hollywood in 1966 to pursue a private life devoted to painting.
Kim Novak poses with her painting at a photocall during the Febiofest Prague International Film Festival on March 20, 2015, in Prague, Czech Republic. (Getty Images)

"Leaving Hollywood taught me that how I live my life matters," she said. "When I left, what mattered the most was being out in nature. I’ve always wanted to be close to nature and live a natural life. Painting has allowed me to continue expressing myself while out in nature. And every day of my life, I’m painting. I can’t wait to wake up each day and start working on a new painting. Sometimes, I’ll stick with a painting for months just because I haven’t fully figured out what I want to express. It’s been a wonderful way to live a life of expression."

James Stewart and Kim Novak on the set of "Vertigo," directed and produced by Alfred Hitchcock. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"Films were wonderful too," she said. "It’s just all the other stuff that went with it that wasn’t very appealing. But playing a character, becoming one with another person, that always gave me joy. When I look back at my life, I remember all the wonderful opportunities I was given to become a different, beautiful character. But even then, I was drawing too. I used to always draw the characters I was playing in my script. Every time I’d find some new feeling about my character, I would draw it and paint it."

Novak's film credits include Otto Preminger's "The Man with the Golden Arm," Joshua Logan's "Picnic," "Pal Joey" and "Bell, Book and Candle." Today, she continues to pursue painting away from Hollywood. But Novak believes her story won't end with her death.
Kim Novak attends the "Hommage A Kim Novak" photocall during the 66th annual Cannes Film Festival on May 25, 2013, in Cannes, France. (Getty Images)

"I made my decision because I want to do something good for the environment, and others can too," she said. "After we're gone, the Earth is still here, and we need to protect it. Life goes on when we're no longer here. And in some ways, this doesn't make you feel like you're dying. You're continuing to live on becoming part of the environment. It's something beautiful to look forward to, not dread."

title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ star Sarah Drew met husband leading worship at Christian youth camp
summary: Sarah Drew reveals how meeting husband Pete Lanfer at a Christian youth camp nearly 30 years ago gave her a grounding force against Hollywood's chaos.
story: The "Grey's Anatomy" alum is starring in Lifetime's "When I Said I Do," inspired by Clint Black and Lisa Hartman Black's hit duet.
"Grey's Anatomy" star Sarah Drew found lasting love long before she found Hollywood fame.

Drew opened up about meeting her husband while leading worship at a Christian youth camp nearly three decades ago. The actress, who has been married to Peter Lanfer for 24 years, credited their shared faith and strong partnership with helping her navigate the highs and lows of Hollywood. Drew and Lanfer married in 2002 and have two children.
"He's been my steady rock really and safe haven – since way before I had any success in this industry," Drew told Fox News Digital while promoting her upcoming movie, "Jimmy."
‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY
Sarah Drew and her husband, Pete Lanfer, have been married for 24 years. The couple met nearly three decades ago while Drew was leading worship at a Christian youth camp. (Paul Archuleta/FilmMagic)

"And we have been real partners in parenting and in being humans in this world together," she added. "And I think anytime one of us is feeling shaky, the other one is always able to provide a safe harbor and some real like rock-solid strength for the other. So, I do think probably he's my greatest grounding force."

Drew described the entertainment industry as an unpredictable business that can celebrate an actor one moment and discard that person the next, explaining why she refuses to let Hollywood determine her self-worth.

"I think that it's very easy for Hollywood to tell you who you are. And what I mean by that is, they love you one second, they've forgotten you the next. You're gorgeous one second. They're tearing you to pieces the next. You're working all the time one second, all of a sudden, you're not working anymore, and you don't know what's going on. You never know when you're gonna work again. There is no stability anywhere."
Drew said the industry's constant uncertainty makes it difficult for actors to find a sense of stability in their careers.

Sarah Drew credited her husband and Christian faith with keeping her grounded in Hollywood. She described Peter Lanfer as her "steady rock" and said her identity as a child of God matters more than her success as an actress. (Tiffany Rose/Getty Images)

"There is no place to be grounded in Hollywood. It just doesn't exist," she explained. "We are players to the whims of whoever is making the thing at the certain time and whoever's decided who's interesting or not, and I can't do anything about that."

"If I were not sure that my identity was firmly rooted first as a child of God, whose total identity is so much bigger than just who I am as an actress, if I wasn't rooted in that truth — and I know that truth to my cellular level and in my bones — I could so easily get caught up in the highs and think I'm God's gift to the Earth and then fall so miserably into I am absolutely worthless based on how Hollywood has decided to value me at any given time," she added.

Drew said her faith has helped her maintain a strong sense of identity beyond her career, reminding her that being a child of God, a wife, a mother and a friend matters more than her success as an actress.
Scene from Frank Capra's 1946 classic, "It's a Wonderful Life," starring Donna Reed and Jimmy Stewart.  (AP)

Drew stars in "Jimmy," a biographical drama scheduled for nationwide theatrical release Nov. 6. The film follows actor James Stewart's military service, his struggles upon returning to Hollywood and his eventual comeback in the 1946 Christmas classic "It's a Wonderful Life," directed by Frank Capra.
Drew stars as Hedda Hopper, one of Hollywood's most influential and feared gossip columnists.

"18 months before we started shooting, Aaron Burns …reached out to me and told me that he'd gotten the rights and had a script for this movie, ‘Jimmy,’ that he was gonna make about this incredibly important time in Jimmy's life. And I've always been a huge fan of Jimmy Stewart," she said.

Drew said Burns told her he wanted her to play Hedda Hopper, but she didn't know much about the gossip columnist. Burns told her about "this formidable and complicated person." Drew said she doesn't "generally get the opportunity to play roles like this, so I said yes before I got off the phone, before I read the script."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sarah Drew has turned down acting opportunities because of their messages. The "Grey's Anatomy" star said she prioritizes projects that offer hope, redemption or meaningful connections over money, prestige or network affiliation. (Eric McCandless/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

The "Supernatural" star's Christian faith has also influenced her decision to turn down acting opportunities. While Drew isn't opposed to exploring difficult subjects onscreen, she said she has rejected projects that she believed lacked a meaningful message.
"I have turned down jobs because I'm like, I don't know what we're supposed to walk away from this feeling," Drew explained. "I don't see any hope. I only see cynicism. Then I'm not interested."
Drew said she has always been drawn to stories that offer something meaningful rather than leaving audiences feeling hopeless.

"I just don't understand choosing something that is only going to make people feel darker or more devastated or more hopeless, like those kinds of things," she said. "And I think that that does very much stem from my faith and from my sense of the story that sort of bubbles through my life and has all through my upbringing. And through my adult life and as a parent and as a friend and all of these things, is that I want there to be hope associated with everything that I touch or am a part of – something that you can really like look toward as a beacon of goodness in some ways."

That philosophy also plays a central role in how Drew evaluates potential projects, a process she said often involves conversations with her husband. Rather than focusing on the prestige or financial rewards of a project, Drew said the couple first considers whether the story is one she wants to tell.

Sarah Drew stars as influential Hollywood gossip columnist Hedda Hopper in the upcoming biographical drama "Jimmy." The film follows James Stewart's military service, his struggles returning to Hollywood and his comeback in "It's a Wonderful Life." It is scheduled for a nationwide theatrical release Nov. 6. (Gilbert Flores/Variety/Penske Media)

"It almost never is about what I might get paid, how fancy the project is, what network it's going to be on," she explained. "Those things are absolutely secondary to the first question, which is, 'Do you want to tell the story? Is this story that you think is going to resonate with people?'"

"I find that the stories that I'm drawn to are the ones that help people feel less alone and where someone can see themselves in a story," Drew said. "They can pick a redemption arc or a restoration arc and feel a little less alone. And they might laugh and cry and think on their way through the story of it, but at the end of it, they're like, 'Me too. I've also been through something like that. title: Sacha Baron Cohen says 'Ali G: Who Iz I?' is his last in this style of comedy, calling them too risky
summary: Sacha Baron Cohen reveals why "Ali G: Who Iz I?" will be his last over-the-top comedy, citing dangerous stunts and severe dehydration on set.
story: Comedian Adam Carolla says he was troubled by what he saw during COVID, when some performers appeared less willing to question authority or push against conventional thinking.
Sacha Baron Cohen is done starring in over-the-top comedies.

In a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, the 55-year-old actor confirmed that his new movie, "Ali G: Who Iz I?," will be his last in the risky, character-driven comedic style that made him famous.

"I want to do stuff that challenges me," he told the outlet. "So again, I’m not doing 'Borat 3,' which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more."

The actor has said he was done with this style of comedy in the past, but decided to make this movie because he is "terrified of where our society is headed" and thinks of his comedy as a way to comment on it.
Cohen says he is not going to make any more comedies like "Borat." (Taylor Hill/FilmMagic)
SACHA BARON COHEN’S RIPPED NEW LOOK FOR MARVEL ROLE HAS FANS DOING A TAKE

He explained that through his films, he can "show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence." He added that at the end of the day, he also "wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made."

"These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI," he said. "If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble, and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy."
Cohen's early breakthrough came in 2000, with "Da Ali G Show," and he later gained international recognition with the release of "Borat" in 2006.
He followed that up with "Bruno," "The Dictator," "Who is America" and "Borat Subsequent Moviefilm," as well as some dramatic roles in "The Trial of the Chicago 7," "Les Misérables" and "Disclaimer."

Cohen made a name for himself playing characters such as Borat and Bruno. (Steve Granitz/WireImage)

Throughout the interview, Cohen explained that these comedies "are dangerous to make" and are "incredibly demanding" on the body, but that he and his crew "try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe."
He described the final scene of his latest project as "an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations" with a lot of different elements, filmed as "a continual shot."

"There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert," he said. "On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, 'You will go to hospital if you make this movie,' because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, 'You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.'"

The "Balls Up" star explained that he hired "an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France" to be next to him throughout filming and that, despite the precautions, "a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration."

"I was about to do a scene [in 'Borat 1'] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, 'Why is your gun on your thigh?' He goes, 'Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.' I said, 'Well, how close are you to me?' And he said, 'I’ll be with you within three minutes.' I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene."

title: David Spade and Dana Carvey call out Hollywood for focusing too much on race and gender
summary: David Spade and Dana Carvey urge Hollywood to stop labeling actors and directors by race and gender at award shows on their popular podcast.
story: David Spade, Dana Carvey, and Tim Dillon spoke about how the entertainment industry in LA has been in crisis for years, to the point that people and projects are fleeing to other states. ("Fly on the Wall" podcast, April 8, 2026)
David Spade and Dana Carvey call out Hollywood's focus on race and gender.

In a recent episode of their "Fly on the Wall" podcast, the two comedians questioned Hollywood's emphasis on race and gender, with Spade arguing that the industry should "stop separating us like that" by highlighting those distinctions.

"On race, let me just say at any of these award shows, I saw a clip the other day saying, 'And this gentleman won, and he's the first Black director to win for this documentary,' I wish they would quit saying that because I think everyone we can't all be equal to you," Spade said. "'Oh, the first in 30 years to have a Black actor win this.' If you just say we're all actors . . .now this is my point of view, that it just makes it more even and not, we're all just the same. We're all acting."
Carvey then joked that when he won his Emmy Award, they announced that he was the "198th straight white male that has won this award."
Spade called out the focus on race and gender in Hollywood during a recent podcast episode. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Netflix)
ISSA RAE SAYS DEI HAS BECOME A 'BAD WORD' IN HOLLYWOOD AS EXECUTIVES OF COLOR 'TIPTOE' TO KEEP JOBS
Spade also pointed out that while he was working on the hit NBC show, "Just Shoot Me," from 1997 to 2003, they would inform him anytime they would be working with a female director that week.

"There’s an art to sex scenes in films. It’s not easy to do things like shadowing people when you’re on top and this and that," Douglas said.

"But the big thing with sex scenes is trust," he continued. "And as long as the lady is trusting me — obviously I trust her — it’s like a dance. You’re taking the lead."

BILLY BALDWIN ADMITS HE REFUSED TO KISS CO-STAR AFTER WEEKS OF TENSION ON SET

"You just talk it out slowly. ‘Kiss, kiss, bite. Looking at you. Is it all right to touch your breasts?’ ‘Yes.’ ’All right, I'm touching your breasts. Kiss. Kiss,'" he said. "You do it, and it’s just like choreographing a fight scene."

title: Jason Alexander admits ‘Seinfeld’ fame sent him to therapy
summary: Jason Alexander revealed on a podcast that he was in therapy while "Seinfeld" was still airing and explained why the fame was so overwhelming.
story: Comedian Tim Young tells Fox News Digital that anti-Israel protesters are interrupting the comedian's stand-up performances in hopes of getting a reaction that will spread across social media.
For Jason Alexander, fame wasn't all it was cracked up to be.

The "Seinfeld" star was a guest on Daniel Lubetzky's "Build or Break" podcast and discussed the iconic sitcom that helped shape his career. Alexander told Lubetzky that therapy was the only way he was able to cope with how much the show changed his life.
"You literally went to therapy?" the host asked.
JOHN GOODMAN ADMITS HE FELT 'FRIGHTENED' AFTER THE SUDDEN FAME HE EXPERIENCED FROM 'ROSEANNE'
Jason Alexander said he needed therapy to deal with the way "Seinfeld" fame affected him. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Netflix)
"You bet," Alexander replied. "I was in therapy while it was happening."
When Alexander was asked why, he explained that the transition from the fame that "Seinfeld" brought him would be hard for anyone.
Michael Richards, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jerry Seinfeld and Jason Alexander all starred in NBC’s "Seinfeld." (Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images)

"The transition from successful at your job to international celebrity, let me just tell you, I don't care how well you've been raised or who you are, you're going to need some therapy," Alexander said.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Alexander went on to explain that he had one vision for himself when he was young, one dream to accomplish, and that was to make it to Broadway.
Jason Alexander leaned on therapy after "Seinfeld" ended in 1998. (Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images)
"My fantasy of a successful life for myself as an actor growing up in New Jersey was getting across the river and working on those Broadway stages. That was the pinnacle for me," he began.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

He continued, "I didn't think about television. I didn't think about film. I dreamt about a life in the theater. God gave me that starting at age 21. By the time I was 30, I'd won a Tony Award. And now they throw in my path 'Pretty Woman,' some of the other films, 'Seinfeld.' And I now live a life as an actor that I never dreamt of, never. I never thought I would have this kind of money, that I could keep my family the way I keep them, that I would have these opportunities, that I would work with the people I've met."
Comedian Jerry Seinfeld is credited as a star and co-creator of "Seinfeld." (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images)
Alexander said that when "Seinfeld" ended, his first thought wasn't to try and replace that level of success, rather he was in awe that he was able to get there in the first place.

"So, if you hit that and then that goes away, I would never go, 'Why couldn't I keep that?' I go, 'I can't believe I ever got that.' That's not what I was thinking. So for me, life gave me more than I ever dreamed of," he said. "I didn't expect that to last. I objectively could sit back. And one of the reasons that we were so adamant at the end about making money on 'Seinfeld' is because I grew up at a time when if you had a hit series on television, you never worked again. I mean, that was it."

"Seinfeld" is an American sitcom created by comedian Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David. The series premiered in 1989 and followed a fictionalized version of Seinfeld as he navigated everyday life, relationships and friendships in New York City.
Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jerry Seinfeld and Jason Alexander are seen on the set of the last episode of "Seinfeld" on April 3, 1998. (Getty Images)
The main cast included Alexander as George Costanza, Seinfeld as Jerry Seinfeld, Julia Louis-Dreyfus as Elaine Benes and Michael Richards as Cosmo Kramer.

Often described as a "show about nothing," the series focused on ordinary situations that spiraled into comedic chaos. It ran for nine seasons and 180 episodes before ending in 1998. "Seinfeld" is widely regarded as one of television’s most influential and successful sitcoms.

title: Larry the Cable Guy knocks 'hypocrisy' in corporate America, jokes about missed endorsements
summary: Daniel Whitney, known as Larry the Cable Guy, calls out corporate hypocrisy during a podcast appearance, comparing his treatment to other popular rapper's deals.
story: Larry the Cable Guy and Nebraska legend Eric Crouch join the ‘Big Noon Kickoff’ to preview Nebraska-Indiana, discuss the Cornhuskers' ceiling, Crouch's 2001 Heisman season and more.
Larry the Cable Guy says corporate America has a double standard when it comes to choosing which entertainers are too controversial for advertising campaigns.

The comedian spoke about DirecTV, suggesting the satellite TV provider missed an obvious advertising opportunity with the slogan — "Larry the Cable Guy has switched to DirecTV." He later clarified on X that it was a "light-hearted conversation," adding that his "career has been amazing and I’m not unhappy about anything."

During an appearance on "The MeatEater Podcast," Larry recalled seeing a DirecTV commercial with an actor "back in the day" and said, "The first thing I thought was, 'Why don't they get me? Larry the Cable Guy is switching to DirecTV.’"
JEFF FOXWORTHY REVEALS HOW 'REDNECK' INSULT INSPIRED DECADES OF COMEDY

Larry the Cable Guy criticized what he sees as a double standard in corporate advertising, arguing that brands embrace entertainers he considers more controversial than himself. (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images)
A podcast host agreed with the idea, saying, "Oh, dude, that would have been genius."
The comedian agreed, saying, "It would have been huge!"
Larry said he believed there was concern that his Southern accent and edgy humor might appeal to only one slice of America and make him too controversial for a national advertising campaign.

"At the time, ‘Well, Larry the Cable Guy is only really for one part of the country, you know, ’cause of the Southern accent, sometimes he says things that are a little controversial,'" he explained of the general sentiment then.

He singled out Snoop Dogg, who has appeared in major advertising campaigns, including Super Bowl commercials. Larry emphasized that he did not fault the rapper for accepting those opportunities.

Snoop Dogg has appeared in major advertising campaigns, including Super Bowl commercials, but Larry the Cable Guy questioned why corporations embrace entertainers he considers more controversial than himself. (James Wiltshire/AFL Photos via Getty Images)
"I got nothing against Snoop Dogg," he said. "God bless Snoop Dogg.
"There's a lot of hypocrisy in corporate, who they get and who they don't get. Look, I've had a good career. I ain't worried about it. But I'm just saying that DirecTV pissed me off."

title: Kate Gosselin says her kids know who she ‘truly’ is as son Collin levels abuse allegations
summary: Kate Gosselin responded to a fan on TikTok, saying her kids know who she "truly" is after Collin Gosselin's abuse allegations and memoir release.
story: ‘In the Shadow of Eight’ author tells Fox News Digital he's willing to hear from estranged mom Kate Gosselin but insists she must own up to her alleged treatment of him during his childhood.
Kate Gosselin says her children know who she "truly" is amid abuse allegations made by her son Collin.
The 51-year-old former reality star took to TikTok Thursday to celebrate her boyfriend Steve Neild’s birthday and got support from her fans in the comments section.

"Happy Birthday Steve ! Strength isn’t just about enduring—it’s about loving deeply enough to do what is right even when it costs you," one TikTok user wrote in the comments section. "Look at the beautiful life and happily ever after You have found now that You made sacrifices that no Mama should have had to make alone.
"When people attack You, it might sting for a moment, but it can never shake who You are. It only confirms that You stood your ground and remained true through it all. God is guiding You two."
‘JON & KATE PLUS 8’ STAR COLLIN GOSSELIN ACCUSES MOM OF TRYING TO ‘BURY’ HIM TO ‘PROTECT HER REPUTATION’
Kate received support from fans in the comments section of her latest TikTok. (David Buchan/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images)
KATE GOSSELIN DEFENDS HERSELF AGAINST SON COLLIN AS HE PREPARES TO RELEASE SHOCKING NEW MEMOIR

Kate responded to the comment by thanking the fan, adding, "I needed this encouragement, and you are right," before adding that "I know who I am and my kids know who I truly am and to me, that’s all that matters."

The exchange came shortly after Collin alleged on "The View" that his sister Hannah felt compelled to say the two of them had not spoken in a year as a form of "damage control" for having participated in an upcoming Netflix documentary alongside Collin and their father.
Kate thanked her fans for their support, writing that she and her kids know who she is and "that's all that matters." (Kate Gosselin TikTok)

In a statement, Hannah wrote that she has a relationship with her mother and other siblings but has not "lived with my dad for over a year" and hasn't "spoken to Collin in close to a year." She added that she will not be making any more statements about "Collin's behavior growing up" or her experiences with him as a kid.

"All families are very complicated, and that statement sounded like a lot of the words of my mother, especially the last part. What I do believe has happened is that Hannah’s caught in the middle, and nobody deserves that," Collin said on "The View."

"I know what it feels like to have to fight to have a relationship with your siblings. I don’t have one with my siblings, and I know how much that hurts. Not only is she caught in the middle, but I do believe my mom is either leveraging finances or Hannah’s relationship with our siblings over Hannah."

title: ‘80s pop star Taylor Dayne celebrates 4 years cancer-free after frightening diagnosis with no symptoms
summary: Taylor Dayne opens up about her colon cancer journey, urging women to advocate for colonoscopies earlier as she prepares for her Las Vegas residency.
story: ‘Tell It to My Heart’ singer Taylor Dayne says she's been cancer-free for four years after battling Stage 2 colon cancer. Dayne is gearing up for her first Las Vegas residency. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Taylor Dayne has plenty of reasons to celebrate.
The pop star, known for the '80s hit "Tell It to My Heart," has been keeping busy gearing up for her first Las Vegas residency at Harrah's Las Vegas.
The Grammy-nominated artist, who announced in 2022 that she'd privately battled Stage 2 colon cancer, said she's been given the all-clear and is ready to party with her fans.
TAYLOR DAYNE RECALLS FINDING FAME WITH ‘80S HIT ‘TELL IT TO MY HEART’: ‘I WAS PRAYING TO GET SIGNED'
Taylor Dayne is launching a Las Vegas residency beginning Nov. 24, 2026, at Harrah's Las Vegas titled "Tell It to My Heart" after her hit song. (Sequoia Emmanuelle Photography)

"I've been cancer-free for four years now," she told Fox News Digital with a smile. "I've been on the path of being very ardent about taking care of my health and being on top of my colonoscopies. There are no guarantees in life, but especially as women, we need to advocate for our health and be on top of our checkups.

"I was already on top of my colonoscopies when I was told I had a lot of polyps," the singer said. "It was through a routine checkup that they found a very aggressive polyp. This is how quickly these things can escalate and really take a turn. But my mindset was, 'What do I do right now?' I was very much in action mode."

Taylor Dayne performs onstage during the 2026 Songwriters Hall of Fame induction ceremony at the New York Marriott Marquis June 11, 2026, in New York City. Dayne was diagnosed with colon cancer four years ago and survived it. (Getty Images for Songwriters Hall Of Fame)
Dayne, who didn't experience any symptoms before her diagnosis, stressed that routine screenings are essential.

Taylor Dayne attends the 28th annual Angel Ball at Cipriani Wall Street on Oct. 19, 2026, in New York. The pop star is "all clean" four years after her colon cancer diagnosis. (Variety via Getty Images)

"I was 50 years old, and they said, 'Now's the time to go in for this,'" Dayne, 64, said. "It's not like that anymore, because of our food, our diets, what we're exposed to daily. You really have to think about your timeline earlier than we've ever done. And we have such high-paced lifestyles. Most people are busy working, busy being parents, busy just being out there juggling. We can't put our health on the sidelines."

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends that adults at average risk begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45, down from the previous recommendation of 50. People at increased risk, including some with a family history of colorectal cancer, may need to begin screening earlier.
Taylor Dayne circa 1990 (Getty Images)

"I thought it was a male-dominated disease, like prostate cancer," she said. "I was like, 'Colon?' It wasn't really resonating with me, and it certainly wasn't resonating with anyone in my family. I learned from my experience: Be your own warrior, be your champion. And that's what I did. It started with me asking, 'Why do I keep developing polyps?' You have to be your own champion, your own voice in getting the information you need, the plan you need."
Taylor Dayne is embarking on her first Las Vegas residency in her career. (Sequoia Emmanuelle Photography)
Dayne said her experience also taught her the importance of speaking up early. She noted that advocating for oneself can be harder when seriously ill.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Taylor Dayne told Fox News Digital she didn't experience any symptoms before her diagnosis four years ago. (Getty Images)

"When you're that ill, there's very little that the person can do," she explained. "Your advocate is usually your partner, your spouse, your best friend. But, oftentimes, it's just yourself. It made me realize a lot of things. And I'm so grateful, ever grateful. For me, it turned on a lightbulb, a desire to live, a desire to really push through things. And it's brought a lot of love to my heart because I've met so many people I otherwise wouldn't have met because we have so much in common now. Survivors."
Singer Taylor Dayne and her children attend the premiere of Battlefield America at AMC Universal City Walk in Universal City, Calif., May 23, 2012. (Getty Images)
Dayne's renewed focus on her health is also tied to her desire to be present for her children.

"Your kids don't think of you as having a career," she said. "They don't think about your fame, your awards, the guest house. All they want is for their needs to be met. You're just mom to them. I became a very different touring artist then. And touring was the largest component of my career. But I was a single parent. I raised them. I was then the mother bird who needed to always come back to her nest."
Taylor Dayne and son Levi Dayne attend the Big Game Kick-Off event hosted by Merging Vets and Players at Academy LA in Los Angeles Feb. 9, 2022. (Getty Images)
Dayne follows a no-nonsense health regimen that helps her look and feel her best as she prepares for her Las Vegas residency.
Taylor Dayne performs onstage at the 28th annual Angel Ball held at Cipriani Wall Street Oct. 19, 2026, in New York. (Variety via Getty Images)

"I'm very religious with my morning ritual, whatever my morning looks like, because my morning could be one o'clock in the afternoon, and it could be five in the morning," she said. "I do my peptides. I do my collagen. I do my bone broth. I do copper for my skin. I want to be optimal. That takes stretching, Pilates, yoga, daily exercise. You have to take care of yourself spiritually, emotionally, mentally.

Taylor Dayne and Kelly Clarkson appear on "The Kelly Clarkson Show." Dayne told Fox News Digital she follows a no-nonsense health regiment to help her look and feel her best. (Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

"It's a real juggle," Dayne continued. "But the first moment you have in the morning, the first two minutes you have, should be centering yourself. And then I do my tinctures. I also like to have a big ol' smoothie. I usually have just liquids in the morning. I also love soursop, especially when I travel. I have to have a healthy lifestyle to meet the demands of what it takes to be physically on stage every night."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Taylor Dayne attends the Songwriters Hall of Fame 55th Annual Induction and Awards Gala at the Marriott Marquis Hotel in New York City on June 11, 2026. (WireImage)
Long before her health battle, Dayne experienced another life-changing moment of realizing just how quickly "Tell It to My Heart" had made her a star.

"I was in Munich preparing to make an appearance and I said, 'What are all these people doing outside? Why is their hair crimped? Why do they have red lips? Oh my God, they look like me,'" Dayne recalled.
Taylor Dayne performs on BR German TV show "200th Formel Eins" in Munich, Germany, in March 1988. (Redferns)

"It's not overnight stardom because I spent 15, 16, 17 in every club conceivable in New York in the '80s," she said. "But when you have a single like that, the next thing you know, you're on 'Top of the Pops.' I just knew my life would never be the same. I had no idea people would love my music so much, that they would want to look like me. Here we are, 39 years later.
Taylor Dayne (left) and Debbie Gibson (right) attend the 16th annual American Music Awards in Los Angeles. (FilmMagic, Inc)
"I never said, 'This is going to last forever,'" she said, reflecting on her fame. "How could you ever know? It was a moment. I was young, I was 22, 23. You just want to catch the wind."
Nearly four decades into her career, Dayne sees her upcoming Las Vegas residency as a victory lap.

Taylor Dayne poses for portraits on the red carpet during the 68th Grammy Awards pre-Grammy gala at the Beverly Hilton on Jan. 31, 2026, in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

"This is the cherry on top and recognizing that after three decades in this business, my music is still the soundtrack of so many people's lives," she said. "I am honored. My health, my wellness, my family, I am grateful for it all."

Taylor Dayne is celebrating her health and family on stage. (Sequoia Emmanuelle Photography)
