title: Major school district's pledge with teachers' union sparks racial discrimination complaint
summary: Defending Education filed a civil rights complaint alleging Cherry Creek Schools in Colorado discriminates by race in its teacher hiring policies.
story: White House senior policy strategist May Mailman discusses the University of Pennsylvania allegedly violating Title IX on 'The Will Cain Show.'

FIRST ON FOX: One of Colorado's largest school districts is facing a new federal civil rights complaint over a pledge it made with its teachers' union to recruit, retain and advance educators of color.

Defending Education filed a federal civil rights complaint Monday, which was first obtained by Fox News Digital, with the U.S. Department of Education alleging that CCSD is discriminating on the basis of race in employment. CCSD is notably Colorado’s fourth-largest school district, and serves 52,000 students and more than 300,000 residents in the southeast Denver metropolitan area, according to the district’s website.

At the heart of the complaint is the district's June 2023 "Educators of Color Declaration," which commits Cherry Creek School District and its teacher’s union to recruiting, retaining and advancing educators of color, even as a separate provision in the same agreement calls for recruitment, hiring and advancement to be based on qualifications without regard to race.

"Cherry Creek Schools has written racial preferences directly into its teachers’ contract. The district’s ‘Educators of Color Declaration’ commits it to recruiting, retaining, and promoting teachers based on the color of their skin — which means other equally qualified teachers are passed over for the same reason," Sarah Parshall Perry, Vice President and Senior Legal Fellow at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital.
Hundreds protest outside a rally held by President Donald Trump at Macomb County Community College in Warren, MI, on April 29, 2025. (Getty Images/Dominic Gwinn)

"That's not diversity; it's discrimination, and it is precisely what Title VI and the Fourteenth Amendment forbid. The Supreme Court could not have been clearer in Students for Fair Admissions: the law is colorblind, and a school district cannot cure a race-based hiring policy with generic 'equal opportunity' language."

Title VI prohibits race discrimination in federally funded programs under specified conditions, while Title VII more directly governs employment discrimination, leaving the legality of Cherry Creek's teacher recruitment and advancement commitments dependent on how those policies are implemented.
OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE CLEARS WAY FOR WHITE EMPLOYEE TO CHALLENGE SEATTLE'S DEI POLICIES

The "Educators of Color Declaration" also commits the district and its teachers' union to intentionally recruiting highly qualified educators of color while making a concerted effort to retain those already employed by the district and help them advance into leadership positions, according to the district's negotiated agreement.
A Department of Education sign is displayed outside of their federal student aid office on May 18, 2025, in Washington, DC. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images))
JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY

Additionally, the policy says that "to fulfill these goals, all policies in this agreement shall reflect Cherry Creek School District core values by grounding the work of negotiations in diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI)," according to the school district's 2026-2027 Negotiated Agreement.
A Department of Education sign is displayed outside of their federal student aid office on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY HIT WITH FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS INVESTIGATION OVER RACE, SEX-BASED SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAMS

"Cherry Creek is under no obligation to accept federal funding, but because it has, it cannot run a racial balancing scheme for its own workforce and still adhere to federal law," Perry continued. "We are asking the Office for Civil Rights to open an investigation and put an end to it."

Defending Education's latest complaint comes after the Department of Education announced a separate investigation on June 8, into allegations that Cherry Creek School District sponsored racially discriminatory programs involving students, teachers and parents.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"These allegations of racially discriminatory conduct in this District seem to permeate almost every aspect of the school community, affecting students, teachers, and parents alike," Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey said in a statement at the time. "Federal law prohibits racial discrimination, which means that race cannot be a factor in how the school educates its students or trains its teachers."

The Trump administration has been cracking down on DEI efforts across the nation's education system, including proposing new regulations in September that would revoke the tax-exempt status of private schools and colleges that consider race in admissions, scholarships or other school-administered programs.
CCSD did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment on Monday.
When reached for comment, a Department of Education spokesperson told Fox News Digital that "the Department does not confirm complaints."

title: Inside House GOP's far-reaching push to monitor midterm elections and prepare for legal fights
summary: House Republicans are sending dozens of congressional observers to monitor ballot counting in close midterm races and prepare for legal challenges.
story: Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil spoke with Fox News Digital about the election observer program seeing federal employees deployed across the country for Nov. 3.

House Republicans are deploying "dozens and dozens" of staff across the country next Tuesday to ensure the midterm elections are being run cleanly and fairly as both parties fight tooth and nail for control of Congress.

The Committee on House Administration, which has jurisdiction over federal elections, runs an annual election watcher program aimed at adding oversight in districts where races are anticipated to be particularly close, and in some cases, paving the way for legal challenges if improprieties are found.
Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., the panel's chairman, told Fox News Digital that this year's program will be "the most robust program the House has ever done."

"We're building on the success that we had last cycle and recognizing that a large number of House races are likely to be close," Steil said. "The balance of power in the United States House of Representatives is at stake, and we wanna make sure that we have eyes and ears on the ground in close races across the country."
BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS VOTER-FRAUD PROBES IN BATTLEGROUND STATES JUST DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS

Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil spoke with Fox News Digital about Republicans' nationwide election observer program. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images; Allison Joyce/AFP via Getty Images)
How that plays out will vary from state to state depending on varying election laws, he explained. But many of those observers are potentially in for lengthy shifts.
SENATE REPUBLICANS PUSH ELECTION DAY DEADLINE FOR CALIFORNIA'S MARATHON BALLOT COUNTS

"Some jurisdictions that run their elections well, like Florida, their shift may end early in the evening. States that have kind of poor election policies, like California, those shifts go on for days on end until the counting is done," Steil said.

"Two years ago, I went to Los Angeles County — about 10 million people — counts all their ballots at one location. And of course, we know California has bad election policy. They allow ballots to arrive after the polls have closed. And so I went to Central Count, met with our election observers as we watched ballots arrive days after the election. We want eyes and ears on the ground, recording what is occurring, and documenting what's happening, and making sure that the rules are followed."
Steil also recalled an instance in Milwaukee where an issue arose during tabulation "where ultimately thousands of ballots would have to be recounted."
People vote early at the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's office on Oct. 19, 2026. (Jason Armond/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
But those poll watchers, trained under the jurisdiction of Congress, will often stay the entire time votes are being cast on Election Day. In some cases, they observe votes being counted as well.
MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY

"These are long days. I mean, polling locations are often open for a full 12 hours. They're arriving, they're staying often until the early evening or late evening, in some cases as the ballots are actually tabulated, but they play an absolutely essential role in verifying... our elections are run freely and fairly," he said.
It is all part of a process to build a case in the event the results need to be re-examined. Their documentation could potentially lead to recounts in close races or even lawsuits.
Residents vote in the state's primary election on Aug. 11, 2026, in Madison, Wis. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

"Not only are they documenting what they're seeing, but they're in direct contact with myself and the committee on Election Day, so that we're in a position to deploy additional resources, if necessary, to make any court challenges if that was required," Steil explained. "They are the first step in identifying if there is a problem, and then they notify our team and we get to work immediately."

Election observers' jobs are federally protected under the Confirmation of Congressional Observer Access Act, which was enacted by Congress in 2024. The program is open to any staffer of the House of Representatives, save for interns.

Democrats are free to run their own program under the law, but they do not do so in coordination with Republicans.

title: Mamdani message to residents on how to deal with ICE results in viral internet backlash: 'Treason'
summary: Zohran Mamdani's Spanish-language video on handling ICE encounters drew over 7 million views and fierce backlash from conservative lawmakers.
story: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused ICE of terrorizing New Yorkers after an agent shot a man whose 5-year-old son was in the vehicle.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faced viral backlash on Friday after posting instructions in Spanish on how residents should handle interactions with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
"If you encounter ICE, here's what every New Yorker should know," the socialist mayor of the nation’s largest city posted on X on Friday in a message that quickly racked up over 7 million views.

Mamdani explained "what every New Yorker should know" if they "encounter ICE," adding that ICE "cannot enter private spaces like your home, school, hospitals or private areas of a workplace without a judicial warrant signed by a judge."
Mamdani reminded New Yorkers they have the right to remain silent and gives tips on best practices for interacting with ICE, saying that "these are very frightening times for many people."
MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION'
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks at a press conference at Deno's Wonder Wheel on Coney Island in the New York City borough of Brooklyn on Feb. 15, 2026. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu/Getty Images)

Mamdani’s post was quickly criticized by conservatives on social media, with many characterizing the video as the mayor encouraging obstruction of federal law enforcement and encouraging illegal immigration.

"It should be insulting to every American that the mayor of our largest city is a guy who became a citizen less than a decade ago and now spends his time coaching illegal aliens in a foreign language on how they can avoid being lawfully deported," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, posted on X.
MULLIN CALLS MAMDANI'S ANTI-ICE RHETORIC 'DANGEROUS' FOLLOWING NEW YORK SHOOTING
"Unless you're here illegally, you have no reason to fear ICE," actor Dean Cain posted on X. "This wanker is dangerous."

"At no point in this video is anyone urged to abide by the laws of the United States," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, posted on X. "Because it was not made for the benefit of the people of the United States."
"If you're here illegally, you're not a New Yorker," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., posted on X. "Period."
"Treason," Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, posted on X.

"Here we are in 2026 with foreign born Democrats instructing illegals how to evade the law and remain in our country to suck off our system and best case scenario free load off our hard work," Fox News commentator Tomi Lahren posted on X.
"Dangerous incitement full of disturbing falsehoods by communist terrorist supporter @NYCMayor," Judicial Watch President Tom Fitton posted on X. "This statement could put lives in danger."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at the site where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during an operation in the Bronx on Oct. 8, 2026, in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s office for comment.

Mamdani has repeatedly positioned himself against ICE and the Trump administration’s immigration-enforcement agenda. During his campaign and after taking office, he called for abolishing ICE and said the NYPD would not assist the agency with civil immigration enforcement. He has also described ICE operations as harmful to immigrant communities.

As mayor, Mamdani signed an executive order strengthening New York City’s sanctuary policies. The order directs city agencies to limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, protect personal information and establish protocols for handling ICE requests to access city property or records. It also called for expanded "know your rights" materials and training for city employees.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Alaska Dem Senate candidate suffers minor injuries in car crash, forcing her to skip campaign events
summary: Democratic Senate-nominee Mary Peltola and her family sustained minor injuries in an Anchorage crash, delaying her campaign tour in the Alaska Senate race.
story: Speaking before departing for Michigan, President Donald Trump argued his campaign blitz has "turned the whole thing around," for the GOP.

Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola and members of her family were involved in a two-vehicle collision in Anchorage on Saturday night, prompting her campaign to adjust upcoming schedule commitments in the final stretch of the midterm race.

The crash occurred Saturday in the vicinity of the Alaska Federation of Natives (AFN) convention, where candidate events and campaign appearances had been underway over the weekend. It happened when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, the campaign said. The family was on their way to the Alaska Federation of Natives Annual Banquet.

"Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits," campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement. "Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover."

"Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families," Bruce added.
TODD BLANCHE CHALLENGES DANA BASH FOR ONLY CITING PART OF CONSTITUTION DURING HEATED ELECTION CLASH

Former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, a U.S. Senate candidate, missed Sunday's campaign tour events and will be resting Monday before returning to the trail Tuesday for the final week before one of the most consequential Senate races on the midterm map. (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The pause comes at a pivotal moment in Alaska’s high-stakes Senate contest between Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, as both campaigns scramble across the state to mobilize voters and secure turnout ahead of the November midterm vote.
DEMOCRAT'S DEBATE 'CUE CARDS' STEAL SPOTLIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE CLASH

Peltola, an Alaska Native and former congresswoman, is hoping to become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate. Both she and Sullivan have tried to rally support from Alaska Native voters, a key constituency in the high-stakes race that has become one of the most watched in the nation.
ALASKA HAS A VOTING SYSTEM LIKE NO OTHER STATE; REPUBLICANS WORRY IT COULD COST THEM IN NOVEMBER

President Donald Trump — who held a rally in support of Sullivan earlier this month — said Friday he told his administration to sue to block certification of the race if the incumbent loses. The lawsuit cites potential confusion with another candidate who is listed on the ranked choice ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

Alaska allows voters to rank their top picks rather than choosing a single candidate. Voters will have four choices, including Sullivan, Peltola and the other Dan Sullivan, a candidate Republicans have called a decoy in what they believe is a Democratic effort to confuse voters.
COURT KEEPS ‘DECOY DAN’ ON ALASKA BALLOT AS EXPERT WARNS RANKED-CHOICE SYSTEM CREATES VOTER ‘TRAPS’

"I revealed what everyone knows, that the Ranked Choice Voting Ballot is a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before, named Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.," Trump wrote early Sunday morning on Truth Social. "He is only there because the Democrats want to steal the Election."
It is a reason to vote out ranked-choice voting, Trump added.

"The Democrats are trying to steal this important Republican Seat and, if that happens, everything we’ve done for Alaska will come to an immediate hault [sic]," Trump concluded. "VOTE 'YES' AGAINST RANKED CHOICE VOTING, on Ballot Measure 2. SAVE ALASKA!"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Peltola has outraised Sullivan through October, $33 million to nearly $14 million, but Sullivan reported having more campaign cash, $5.1 million to Peltola's $3.2 million. Republicans have outspent Democrats in the race, $42 million to $38 million.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Dem Senate hopeful rejects Schumer but benefits from millions in spending by his allies
summary: Adam Hamilton distances himself from Chuck Schumer even as Senate Majority PAC pours millions into the Kansas Senate race against Roger Marshall.
story: Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., told Fox News Digital that if Adam Hamilton really meant he would not support Chuck Schumer to lead Democrats, he would reject the millions flowing into Kansas from Schumer and national Democrats.

WICHITA, Kan. — National Democrats are pouring millions of dollars into Kansas to bolster Adam Hamilton, who has spent much of his campaign arguing that he would not be beholden to the top Democratic leaders in Washington, D.C.

Tens of millions are flowing into Kansas to boost Hamilton, with a sizable chunk coming from Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC closely aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., whom Hamilton has repeatedly said he would not support as the Democratic leader should he win in November.
But his opponent, Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., questioned how he could benefit from "$30 to $40 million from Chuck Schumer and not be beholden to him in some way?"
THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES

Democrat senatorial candidate Adam Hamilton answers questions from the media after a televised debate with Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., at WDAF studios in Kansas City, Mo., on Oct. 21, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

"Regardless of what he says, if we lose this seat, then it's going to give the Senate control to the Democrats," Marshall told Fox News Digital during an interview on the campaign trail. "Chuck Schumer would be the leader of the Senate."
"Look, if he's going to denounce Chuck Schumer, let's denounce him with his money as well," he continued, "Look, we're going to be outspent five to one, and we knew that."

Candidates, notably, can’t directly accept outside funding from independent groups like the Senate Majority PAC, given the guardrails are established by federal election law, according to the Federal Election Commission.
SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL

The Schumer-aligned group teed up $5 million in advertising spending in Kansas earlier this month, a sign that Democrats are bullish about flipping the seat in a contest that has gotten closer than Republicans expected.

Hamilton's campaign pushed back on Marshall, arguing that the first-term senator has been given a lifeboat by national Republicans. Hamilton has vastly outraised Marshall, scoring nearly $14 million compared to Marshall’s almost $6 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

"Adam has said repeatedly he believes it’s time for fresh leadership in Washington," Tyson Brody, a Hamilton campaign spokesperson, told Fox News Digital. "Adam will always put Kansas first. Meanwhile, Roger Marshall is totally dependent on Washington money to save his campaign because he has abandoned Kansas to support D.C. corruption, endless war and high prices."
KANSAS DEMOCRAT BEGS KAMALA HARRIS NOT TO CAMPAIGN WITH HIM, ‘PLEASE DO NOT COME TO MY STATE’

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., departs after a weekly Senate Democratic Policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images)

In all, national Democrats and their affiliated groups — combined with spending from Hamilton’s campaign — are slated to dump $38 million into the race, according to AdImpact. National Republicans, along with Marshall’s campaign, are putting $32 million into the contest.
Marshall has sought to tie Hamilton, who is running as a moderate in ruby-red Kansas, directly to Schumer, a point he made several times during their final debate before Election Day this week.

Hamilton pushed back, arguing that Marshall had mentioned Schumer "maybe 20 times so far."
"I’ve already said I wouldn't support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats took control of the Senate," Hamilton said.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: $800-a-day penalty threatens to bleed reporter dry as explosive legal fight heads to Supreme Court
summary: Catherine Herridge's Supreme Court petition challenges how courts weigh reporter's privilege when confidential national security sources are at stake.
story: Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn discusses the Department of Justice filing complaints against Minnesota judges speaking to the media about ongoing case on 'America Reports.'

Former Fox News investigative reporter Catherine Herridge is asking the Supreme Court to protect her confidential sources after a federal court ordered her to identify who helped expose a woman's alleged ties to China's military.
The outcome of the case could dramatically reshape the legal protections afforded to journalists working in the U.S. under the First Amendment.

Herridge was held in contempt and ordered to pay $800 per day for refusing to reveal sources behind her 2017 reporting on Yanping Chen, a Chinese American businesswoman who operated a university attended by U.S. military personnel. Her reporting raised questions about Chen's alleged past as a colonel for the People's Liberation Army (PLA) of China and the potential exposure of sensitive information about American service members.

The Department of War subsequently cut off military tuition assistance funding to Chen's university following a national security review, according to a filing by Herridge's legal team. The school had been receiving approximately $200,000 a month in taxpayer-funded tuition assistance.
NEW YORK TIMES BLASTS ‘ABUSIVE’ TRUMP SUBPOENAS TARGETING REPORTERS’ SOURCES
Catherine Herridge, right, formerly of Fox News and CBS, is asking the Supreme Court to protect her confidential sources. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Now Chen, who was investigated by federal authorities but never charged with a crime, is pursuing a lawsuit against the federal government, alleging that officials improperly disclosed her private records to Herridge in violation of the Privacy Act. She has sought to compel Herridge to identify her sources as part of that litigation.

The dispute has reached the Supreme Court, where Herridge's attorneys are asking the justices to reconsider the legal standard used to force journalists to disclose confidential sources in civil cases.

Her legal team argues that the lower courts failed to adequately weigh the broader circumstances of Chen's lawsuit, including the Pentagon's national security findings and whether Chen can ultimately prevail in her claims against the government.

The case also exposes a longstanding disagreement among federal appeals courts over the scope of the reporter's privilege, an issue the Supreme Court has not comprehensively addressed in more than five decades.

Herridge's original investigation, published while she was working at Fox News in 2017, examined Chen's background and her operation of the University of Management and Technology in Arlington, Virginia, which enrolled U.S. military personnel using Defense Department tuition assistance.
The U.S. Supreme Court during a rainstorm in Washington, D.C., on Friday, Feb. 20, 2026. (Annabelle Gordon/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The reporting included photographs appearing to show Chen in a Chinese military uniform and examined allegations that she had concealed her previous military service when applying for U.S. immigration benefits.

It also raised concerns about the university's collection of information on American service members, including details about their military training and professional backgrounds. A whistleblower interviewed for the investigation alleged that information stored on the school's computers could be accessed remotely from China.
WASHINGTON POST BOASTS IT STARED DOWN ‘UNWARRANTED’ JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUBPOENA

Federal authorities had previously investigated Chen over potential immigration violations and counterintelligence concerns, but prosecutors in the Eastern District of Virginia declined to bring charges.
Following Herridge's reporting, the Pentagon completed a review of Chen's university and terminated its eligibility for military tuition assistance funding, according to her filing.

Chen subsequently filed suit against the federal government, alleging that confidential information from government records had been improperly disclosed to Herridge. She contends that identifying the officials responsible for the alleged disclosures is necessary to establish her Privacy Act claims.
Herridge refused to identify her sources, arguing that compelling disclosure would undermine the ability of journalists to obtain sensitive information from government officials and whistleblowers.

A federal judge ultimately ordered Herridge to disclose the sources and held her in civil contempt when she refused. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the order, prompting her appeal to the Supreme Court.
Fox News Media has continued to support Herridge's legal fight, including covering her legal fees, despite her departure from the network in 2019.

Former Fox News investigative reporter Catherine Herridge is asking the Supreme Court to review a ruling compelling her to reveal confidential sources behind her reporting on a woman with alleged ties to China's military. (Shedrick Pelt/Getty Images)

At the center of Herridge's petition is a disagreement among federal appeals courts over how judges should evaluate a journalist's claim of privilege when confidential sources are sought in civil litigation.

The filing argues that the D.C. Circuit applied a narrow test focused primarily on whether Chen needed the information to pursue her lawsuit and whether she had exhausted alternative means of obtaining it.

They contend that courts should also consider the strength of the underlying lawsuit and the consequences of compelling disclosure, particularly when confidential national security sources may be involved.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The distinction could prove significant for journalists reporting on sensitive government matters. Under the standard challenged by Herridge, a plaintiff could obtain a reporter's confidential sources even if other deficiencies in the lawsuit would ultimately prevent the plaintiff from recovering damages, according to the petition.

title: Candy prices surge beyond inflation, but Americans still plan to spend billions on Halloween staples
summary: Candy prices rose 7.7% over the past year, but Halloween shoppers are expected to spend $4.1 billion on sweets using coupons and sales strategies.
story: 'The Five' co-hosts discuss whether equity is ruining Halloween after a homeowner association requested residents stop handing out full-size candy bars. Dana Perino shares her thoughts on the neighborhood pressure, while Greg Gutfeld suggests giving out old tube socks instead.
Trick-or-treating, like most expenses recently, will come with a bigger price tag this Halloween.

The increase is hitting as families prepare for a holiday built around candy. Shoppers, however, still plan to spend billions on Halloween treats, even as rising prices make affordability part of the seasonal calculation.

Candy prices rose 7.7% over the year through September, more than twice the overall inflation rate of 3.7%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The figure tracks candy and chewing gum broadly, rather than Halloween-specific products.
But higher prices haven’t pushed candy out of the Halloween budget.

The National Retail Federation expects Americans to spend $4.1 billion on candy this year as part of a record $13.5 billion in overall Halloween spending. Its survey found that 96% of Halloween shoppers plan to buy sweets.

"Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind," NRF Vice President of Industry and Consumer Insights Allison Zeller said.
THE FAMILY BEHIND AN ICONIC AMERICAN FAIR FOOD REVEALS THE SECRET TO ITS STAYING POWER
Americans are expected to spend $4.1 billion on Halloween candy this year, even as prices rise faster than overall inflation. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The NRF found that 31% of shoppers plan to comparison shop if prices are higher than expected, while 26% will look for coupons or sales. Retailers are offering products across a range of price points to help shoppers celebrate within their budgets, Zeller said.
NIQ said rising costs for housing, transportation and everyday essentials are shaping spending decisions, but Halloween remains an occasion consumers are willing to protect.

That resilience showed up in last year’s sales. Halloween confectionery sales rose 7.6% in 2025 even as unit sales fell 2.5%, suggesting shoppers spent more while taking home fewer items. Chocolate had the largest average unit-price increase among the confectionery categories NIQ tracked, at 11.5%.
YOUR SUMMER BBQ IS ABOUT TO COST MORE – HERE’S THE SURPRISING REASON WHY
The National Retail Federation found that 31% of shoppers plan to compare prices if Halloween candy costs more than expected. (Sarah L. Voisin/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

"Consumers continue to make room for Halloween. What’s changing is how they participate," said Chris Costagli, NIQ’s vice president of food and beverage thought leadership. Shoppers are starting earlier, spreading purchases across more trips and evaluating items more carefully, he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The National Confectioners Association said candy makers and retailers offer seasonal promotions and different package sizes to give shoppers options at various price points.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Trump's fingerprints seen on Latin America's rightward shift while Brazil throws up roadblock
summary: Trump's political influence is fueling right-leaning shifts across Latin American countries, with Javier Milei leading Argentina's charge.
story: Marcelo Sandrin, who has lived in the US for three decades, points to Argentina's Javier Milei and changing politics across South America as signs of Trump's growing influence.

President Donald Trump's political influence is reaching far beyond America's borders as several Latin American countries shift toward right-leaning leadership, though that momentum hit a roadblock Sunday when Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated conservative challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the country's presidential runoff.
For Argentina-born Trump rally attendee Marcelo Sandrin, who has lived in the U.S. for roughly three decades, the shift is unmistakable — and Trump deserves substantial credit.

Speaking to Fox News Digital outside the T. Ed Garrison Arena near Clemson before Brazil's election results were known, Sandrin pointed to Argentine President Javier Milei and the possibility of another conservative victory in Brazil as evidence of what he sees as Trump's growing influence. Lula's subsequent victory complicated that outlook, even as the Trump administration has asserted U.S. power more directly across the region, most dramatically through the capture of Venezuelan socialist leader Nicolás Maduro.

"[Trump deserves] a lot of credit," Sandrin told Fox News Digital, adding that Milei is a very forceful libertarian, right-wing/small-government figure, and that during the Trump era, South America has moved "more and more to the right."
CONSERVATIVE WAVE HITS ROADBLOCK IN BRAZIL AS LULA HOLDS OFF BOLSONARO CHALLENGE
President Donald Trump greets Argentine President Javier Milei at the White House in Washington, D.C., October 14, 2025. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)

In Argentina, Milei has emerged as one of Trump's most prominent ideological allies in the hemisphere, pursuing sweeping economic reforms and challenging the left-wing political establishment that dominated much of the country's recent history.

"Brazil is almost going to be [moving] to the right again. It's only Mexico and Uruguay for now [on the left]. The problem in my country is one side or the other, they have to steal, stop stealing. That's the number one thing."

Brazil instead delivered a setback to the region's conservative momentum, with Lula winning 51.8% of the vote to Bolsonaro's 48.2%, according to the country's electoral court. The result secured Lula a fourth, nonconsecutive presidential term and demonstrated that the rightward shift Sandrin described has not extended uniformly across Latin America.

The Trump administration's impact on the region has also extended beyond electoral politics. Venezuela underwent a dramatic change following the U.S. capture of longtime socialist leader Nicolás Maduro, an operation that Venezuela native and Manhattan Institute researcher Santiago Vidal Calvo argued reinforced Washington's influence across the hemisphere and weakened the political order Maduro represented.
COAST GUARD FIREFIGHT PUTS US, MEXICO AT ODDS DESPITE COORDINATED BORDER OPERATIONS

President Donald Trump, center, Dominican Republic President Luis Abinader, second from left, Argentina's President Javier Milei, El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, Guyana's President Mohamed Irfaan Ali, Costa Rica's President Rodrigo Chaves Robles, Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz and Chile's President-elect Jose Antonio Kast pose for a family photo during the Shield of the Americas Summit in Doral, Fla., on Saturday, March 7, 2026. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
"I have no doubt that President Trump has had a good, influential policy towards making governments more right-leaning in Latin America," Calvo said.

"I think that got exacerbated with the capture of Maduro," he added. "A lot of people saw that the United States was again an influential force in the continent, that China was being kicked out in many fronts."

Calvo argued that Trump, Milei and Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele have helped inspire right-leaning movements across the region, with implications extending beyond elections to immigration, trade, Chinese influence and national security.

He also pointed to China, arguing that Beijing expanded its influence in Latin America through loan agreements that differ from conventional North American banking transactions and can give it leverage in countries' domestic affairs.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The regional shift is far from uniform. Mexico remains governed by the left-wing Morena movement, while Uruguay also remains under left-wing leadership. Lula's reelection in Brazil adds another major counterpoint to the conservative gains elsewhere in the hemisphere, underscoring the limits of a regionwide political realignment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Calvo also singled out Secretary of State Marco Rubio for praise, arguing that the administration's Latin America strategy has been an underappreciated foreign-policy achievement.
"I think one of the highlights of this Trump administration has been a good example of foreign policy in Latin America, especially at the hand of [Marco] Rubio," Calvo told Fox News Digital.
Fox News Digital's Reagan Schroeder contributed to this report.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Nicki Minaj pledges to support Donald Trump again during Michigan Republican campaign rally
summary: Nicki Minaj told President Donald Trump she would support him forever at a Michigan rally backing Mike Rogers and John James in the midterms.
story: Rapper Nicki Minaj joins President Donald Trump onstage at a Michigan rally in the final stretch before the 2026 midterm elections.

Rapper Nicki Minaj doubled down on her support for President Donald Trump during a Republican campaign rally in Michigan on Sunday, telling the president she would back him again if he ever sought another term.
Minaj was invited onstage at the Port Huron rally by Trump, who was campaigning for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers and gubernatorial candidate John James.
"President Trump, it is an honor to stand with you every single time," Minaj said. "And I will continue to support you forever and ever. If you run again, I will support you again."
Trump, who is serving his second term, is barred by the 22nd Amendment from being elected president to a third term.
TRUMP BRUSHES OFF REPORTER QUESTION ABOUT RUNNING FOR THIRD TERM IN 2028: 'THE LAW IS VERY STRONG'
Rapper Nicki Minaj joined President Donald Trump onstage during a Republican campaign rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday. (2026 Getty Images)

The Grammy-nominated hip-hop star has increasingly voiced support for the president and recently served as a celebrity judge for the Small Business Administration on the Small Business Administration's Million Dollar Pitch Competition, serving as one of the celebrity judges.

"I am so honored to be working with this president. He represents resilience," Minaj told the crowd. "Since he's come back, he's changed the energy of our country. And he's given us a future to look forward to, a brighter future for us and our children."
She added, "I love him so much."

Minaj also urged support for Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections, as the party seeks victories in two major Michigan races. She described the upcoming vote as a "major turning point for our country."
NICKI MINAJ OFFERS CAREER ADVICE TO YOUNG AMERICANS, DELIVERS BLUNT RESPONSE TO TRUMP CRITICS

Nicki Minaj pledged her continued support for President Donald Trump during a Michigan campaign rally, telling the president she would back him again if he sought another term. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)
"We really need all of these great people to be elected," Minaj said.
Minaj also addressed transgender-related issues involving children.
"We don't want our children to be bombarded with sex changes, right?" Minaj said. "We don't want that for our children. We want people to leave the children alone. Leave them out of it."
Trump introduced Minaj as the "queen of rap" before joking that he did not like someone stealing the spotlight.
"I don't like being overshadowed," Trump quipped. "And this woman overshadows me, and I'm angry about it."
NICKI MINAJ BLASTS GAVIN NEWSOM'S SILENCE, JAY-Z'S ALLEGED SABOTAGE IN SCORCHED-EARTH BREAK FROM DEMOCRATS
Rapper Nicki Minaj exits Air Force One after traveling aboard the presidential aircraft with President Donald Trump for a Republican campaign rally in Michigan. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)
As the crowd cheered her on, the president observed, "They're going crazy over her."
After Minaj wrapped up her remarks, Trump praised her again, saying, "You see why everybody likes Nicki."
"She is a very, very special person. She gets it."

Minaj's appearance on the campaign trail comes after the "Super Bass" and "Starships" singer recently said in a Fox News interview with Lara Trump that young Americans should participate in the midterms and urged them to "vote red now."
White House communications director Steven Cheung also weighed in on Minaj's growing political involvement, the next White House press secretary in a post on X.

President Donald Trump joked that Nicki Minaj was stealing the spotlight during their appearance together at a Republican campaign rally in Michigan. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
"Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House press secretary! @NICKIMINAJ," he posted on X.

title: Bruce Blakeman calls Kathy Hochul Zohran Mamdani's 'puppet' during New York campaign rally
summary: Bruce Blakeman called Kathy Hochul a "puppet" of Zohran Mamdani at a campaign rally, accusing both of failing on crime and illegal immigration.
story: Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman called Gov. Kathy Hochul a "puppet" of NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a Sunday rally, accusing her of embracing his agenda while neglecting immigration and crime.
Republican New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman blasted Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul as a "puppet" of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a campaign rally Sunday.

Speaking at the event in Yorktown Heights, New York, Blakeman, the current Nassau County executive, accused his opponent of embracing the democratic socialist mayor's agenda while failing to crack down on illegal immigration and crime.
"Kathy Hochul, she was out campaigning with Mamdani this week," Blakeman said, according to the New York Post. "And I say that’s great."

"Please take him everywhere you go, Kathy, because I want to remind people that this un-American, antisemite, anti-Christian mayor is running the Democratic Party and Kathy Hochul is nothing more than his puppet," he continued.
HOCHUL DEFLECTS WHEN PRESSED ON TIES TO 'ANTI-CHRISTIAN' MAMDANI IN FIERY DEBATE MOMENT: 'SHAME ON YOU'

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman sparred over her support for NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a contentious debate last week. (Anna Connors - Pool/Getty Images ; John Nacion/Getty Images for Empire State Realty Trust)
Hochul has been campaigning alongside Mamdani, including at a recent rally in Brooklyn.
The political alliance between the mayor and the governor, who is seeking reelection to a second full term, comes as democratic socialists have gained greater influence in New York politics.

Along with Mamdani's victory in last year's mayoral election, candidates aligned with Mamdani and New York's democratic socialist movement scored major victories in congressional primaries this year, including the defeats of two Democratic incumbents.
Blakeman has previously targeted Hochul and Mamdani over public safety, accusing both Democrats of failing to address crime in New York City.
FAR-LEFT SURGE: MAMDANI-BACKED CANDIDATES OUST DEM ESTABLISHMENT INCUMBENTS
Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, left, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images/Getty Images; Alexander MacDougall/Albany Times Union via Getty Images)
During a campaign appearance on the city's subway system earlier this month, Blakeman described Hochul as the "most pro-criminal governor" and accused both leaders of failing to keep commuters safe.
Mamdani has also publicly criticized Blakeman, accusing the Republican gubernatorial candidate of engaging in "bigotry and racism" following a debate between Blakeman and Hochul earlier this month.

"I think the governor did a good job," Mamdani told reporters when asked about Hochul's response to Blakeman's criticism. "And I'll never fault someone for not being able to catch all of it because that is a fool's errand when it comes to Bruce Blakeman."
Hochul and Mamdani have emphasized affordability and child care while campaigning together, arguing their policies are aimed at lowering costs for working families.
Fox News Digital has reached out to Hochul's and Mamdani's offices for comment.

title: Ninth Circuit questions Trump DOJ's emergency request to set aside 20,000 California mail ballots
summary: A Ninth Circuit panel grilled Justice Department lawyers over forcing California to set aside mail-in ballots tied to suspected noncitizens.
story: A three-judge federal appeals panel questioned the Trump administration's emergency bid to set aside roughly 20,000 California mail ballots tied to suspected noncitizens ahead of the midterms, with a ruling pending.

A federal appeals court on Sunday scrutinized the Trump administration's emergency effort to force California to set aside thousands of mail-in ballots tied to people the Justice Department suspects are noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections.

The three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit raised questions about both the government's legal arguments and whether the court has jurisdiction to intervene during a hearing in which attorneys representing the Trump administration and California argued for nearly two hours, Fox News' Matt Finn reported.
The federal government asked the panel to rule immediately, arguing that hundreds of thousands of California ballots could be tabulated each day while the dispute remains unresolved.
The hearing comes after the Trump administration filed an emergency request involving roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots sent to people it suspects are noncitizens.
CALIFORNIA MUST RESPOND TO DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST OVER BALLOTS MAILED TO ALLEGED NONCITIZENS, COURT RULES

In this photo, an official vote by mail ballot, mailed to a Southern California resident ahead of the general election is seen on Oct. 17, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. (Jay L Clendenin/Getty Images)

The DOJ wants California election officials to set aside ballots associated with individuals on its list while their eligibility is reviewed, rather than allowing the ballots to be processed alongside other votes.

Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the administration's requested injunction could be reconciled with the Constitution's Elections Clause, which gives state legislatures authority over the times, places and manner of congressional elections, subject to congressional regulation.

"It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause," he told Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly.
BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO

Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during an event about new savings for California car buyers and a major milestone in the state's clean energy future at the Bridge Yard Facility in Oakland, California, on Aug. 7, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
"How can we do that?"
The panel also questioned whether the Ninth Circuit has jurisdiction to intervene at this stage.

Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, questioned why the Ninth Circuit should weigh in when the district court has yet to rule on the DOJ's request and a hearing before U.S. District Judge David Carter remains scheduled for Tuesday.

Judge Patrick Bumatay, another Trump appointee, focused more heavily on the government's concerns about potential noncitizen voting and questioned California's handling of challenges involving suspected ineligible voters.
The Justice Department sought emergency relief from the appeals court after Carter did not rule by a deadline previously requested by the department.
California, meanwhile, has argued that the Ninth Circuit should not intervene before the lower court has ruled.
The Justice Department initially filed the suit Oct. 15, roughly two weeks after California began mailing ballots.
TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit questioned the Trump administration's emergency request to set aside thousands of California mail ballots ahead of the midterm elections. (Getty Images)
Before oral arguments, the Trump administration accused California of having a history of "mishandling voter rolls."

California has disputed the federal government's underlying data while emphasizing that it has robust safeguards against noncitizen voting. Los Angeles County officials have said a preliminary review of a portion of the federal government's list identified apparent discrepancies, including people who were born in the United States or were not registered to vote. In a filing this weekend, California argued that the federal government's theory would "turn the Constitution on its head."

"When it comes to rules of elections administration, the federal government has no power to interfere with the States unless Congress passes a law governing the time, place, or manner of elections," the state contended.
More than 3 million people have already cast ballots statewide, including more than 500,000 in Los Angeles County, according to figures cited during the litigation.

The Justice Department has emphasized the urgency of its request, arguing that each day without a ruling risks allowing additional ballots to be processed before the citizenship dispute can be resolved.
Bennett said the three-judge panel would try to issue a ruling as quickly as possible.

title: MAPPED: The states Trump and top Democrats are targeting before Election Day
summary: With Election Day less than two weeks away, Trump rallied in Florida, Georgia and Michigan as both parties deploy top surrogates to battlegrounds.
story: Voters at the State Fair discuss whether Talarico can defeat Ken Paxton, turn Texas blue and end Democrats’ decadeslong statewide losing streak.
With just eight days until Election Day, both parties are making a final push to shape the fight for control of Congress.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are rallying Republicans across the country, while former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris are campaigning for Democrats.
The map traces their campaign stops so far this month, with states visited by both sides shaded gray.

Trump has been on the campaign trail nearly every day this month, with stops from Texas and Oklahoma to Ohio, Georgia, Florida and Michigan. He said in early October he planned to hold five to seven rallies a week, and this past weekend he campaigned in Florida on Friday, Georgia on Saturday and Michigan on Sunday.His schedule continues this week, with rallies planned in Mississippi and Texas.
HIGH PRICES PUT TRUMP’S ECONOMY IN THE SPOTLIGHT AS THE GOP FIGHTS TO HOLD CONGRESS
U.S. President Donald Trump arrives for a campaign rally at Laughlin/Bullhead International Airport on October 14, 2026, in Bullhead City, Arizona. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
The map includes both reliably Republican states and states with competitive races. Oklahoma and Alabama, for example, are deep-red states where rallies can help energize the GOP base.
Ohio, Texas and Iowa have competitive Senate contests; recent Cook Political Report polling showed Democratic candidates narrowly ahead in all three. Michigan is also a key Senate battleground.
REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE.
The 2026 midterms will determine control of the House and Senate, shaping President Donald Trump's legislative agenda during the final two years of his term. (Al Drago/Getty Images)
The stops by Obama and Harris show Democrats are also leaning on well-known figures in states with consequential races.
Obama campaigned in Ohio and Michigan, while Harris’s recent appearances included Nevada, Mississippi and New Hampshire.

The map tracks campaign travel, not a formal ranking of battlegrounds. However, it offers a snapshot of where the parties are trying to rally voters in the final stretch before Nov. 3.

title: Trump immigration win could strengthen admin's hand in looming Supreme Court fight
summary: The Fifth Circuit Friday ruled illegal immigrants never formally admitted to the U.S. have no constitutional right to individualized bond hearings.
story: Supreme Court justices will begin hearing oral arguments Monday on a wide range of cases this term involving gun rights, religious freedom, immigration detention and the limits of government power.

The Trump administration scored a major full-panel victory at the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals Friday, which ruled that detained illegal immigrants who were never formally admitted into the U. S. are not constitutionally entitled to bond hearings while awaiting deportation.

The ruling comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha this term, a closely related fight over whether the federal mandatory-detention statute applies at all to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country — setting up the possibility that the justices could either undercut Friday’s ruling or strengthen the government's hand.

The Fifth Circuit answered the constitutional question in Ignacio Sosnava Rodriguez v. Sylvester M. Ortega, finding that three immigrant men detained under the mandatory-detention statute are not entitled to bond hearings under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The court held that their years or even decades of residence in the United States, along with ties to the country and their communities, do not create a constitutional right to a bond hearing.
"The Constitution does not entitle them to a bond hearing," the court wrote.
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT

Dozens of immigrants are detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents inside the Federal Plaza courthouse in New York City on Thursday, June 26, 2025, following their legal proceedings.  (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court will consider Rhoney, a case out of the Second Circuit, to determine whether the mandatory-detention law applies to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country in the first place.

At the center of the issue is a 9-2 circuit split over which federal detention law applies to immigrants who entered the country illegally, were never formally admitted and were later arrested by immigration authorities after living in the U.S. for years — sometimes decades after crossing the border.

The Fifth and Eighth Circuits have held that those immigrants remain "applicants for admission" under Section 1225 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, subjecting them to mandatory detention without an ordinary bond hearing while their removal proceedings play out. Nine other federal appeals courts have ruled that Section 1226 applies instead, which provides a path for them to seek release on bond.

The Supreme Court will essentially decide whether immigrants who entered illegally and have lived in the U.S. for years can be subjected to the same mandatory-detention provision that applies to certain immigrants seeking admission into the country.

If the Supreme Court sides with the Second Circuit, Barbosa da Cunha — a Brazilian national who entered the country illegally roughly two decades ago and was detained in 2025 — would have a path to seek release on bond. Such a ruling would likely apply to the three longtime immigrants at the center of Rodriguez as well, substantially undercutting the significance of Friday’s ruling by eliminating the need to answer the constitutional question of whether due process requires a bond hearing.
SUPREME COURT TAKES UP FIGHT OVER TRUMP’S THIRD-COUNTRY ILLEGAL ALIEN DEPORTATION POLICY
The US Supreme Court in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 4, 2025. (Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Judge Leslie Southwick pointed directly to the looming Supreme Court fight in her dissent.

Should the Supreme Court eventually determine that this court was wrong as to the statute, then the constitutional issue we address here will have far less significance. It certainly has significance at the moment," Southwick wrote.

But conservative legal experts say Rodriguez could also strengthen the administration’s hand in Rhoney by undercutting one argument against the government’s interpretation of Section 1225: that applying the mandatory-detention provision to longtime residents would raise serious constitutional concerns.

Michael Morley, a constitutional law professor at Florida State University, said Friday’s ruling could influence how the justices approach that question because courts often consider whether a particular reading of federal law would create constitutional problems.
FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA

U.S. federal agents working for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detain immigrants and asylum seekers reporting for immigration court proceedings at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building's U.S. Immigration Court in New York, New York, Thursday, July 24, 2025. (Getty Images)

"The Fifth Circuit’s en banc ruling in Rodriguez today takes the next step by holding that such detention would not violate the U.S. Constitution’s Due Process Clause," Morley said. "This holding may impact the Supreme Court’s reasoning, because an important consideration in disputes over federal laws is whether a particular interpretation would be unconstitutional."
"If the Court agrees with the Fifth Circuit’s analysis that the Due Process Clause allows such detention, it may be more likely to conclude that federal law permits it, as well, Morley continued.
Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, argued that the decision could bolster the administration as the justices prepare to resolve the circuit split.

"I actually think this ruling will help the government in the Rhoney case," von Spakovsky said, pointing to the Fifth Circuit’s position that the applicable immigration statute does not require bond hearings for immigrants who were never admitted to the United States.

"There was already a split in the circuit courts on this issue but the Fifth Circuit has consistently held that the applicable immigration statute does not require bond hearings for aliens who were never admitted to the United States," he said. "I will be surprised if a majority of the Supreme Court disagrees when they ultimately issue a decision in the Rhoney case."

title: Data brokers don't just collect facts. They guess about you
summary: Data brokers assign labels predicting your health, finances and religion based on browsing and purchases, then sell those profiles to businesses.
story: Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson explains how algorithms track browsing history and location to estimate what shoppers are willing to spend on ‘Fox & Friends.’

They know where you live. They may know your phone number, your relatives' names and roughly what your house is worth. By now, most people have at least a vague sense that data brokers collect personal information. What many don't realize is what happens next.

Data brokers also analyze that information. They use algorithms, compare records from different sources and sort people into categories that predict their interests, circumstances and behavior. Those predictions can involve your health, finances, religious beliefs and potential vulnerabilities.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Data brokers analyze personal information to identify patterns and predict your finances, health and behavior. (Neil Godwin/Future via Getty Images)

Some may be wrong. Others could reveal sensitive details you never intended to share. And depending on the company and the type of information involved, those profiles may be sold or shared with businesses you have never heard of. Here's a closer look at the labels data brokers assign to you, how they come up with them and what you can do to protect your personal information.

Here's what data brokers' labels actually look like

Data brokers do far more than maintain databases of addresses and phone numbers. Some build detailed profiles designed to help advertisers identify specific audiences. The Federal Trade Commission documented this practice years ago. Its investigation found that brokers combined information from multiple sources to infer sensitive characteristics, including income, religion, political views and health conditions.

Acxiom, a major data company, developed a segmentation system called PersonicX that grouped households into lifestyle categories. One documented historical category was called "Rural Everlasting." According to the FTC, it described older adults with relatively low income and educational attainment. Other categories included "Urban Scramble" and "Mobile Mixers."

These were classifications built from data, not personal descriptions written by the people involved. The FTC also documented how companies used location information to create even more specific advertising audiences. For example, InMarket offered audience categories such as "Christian church goers," "parents of preschoolers," and "wealthy and not healthy." The FTC subsequently restricted InMarket's use and sale of sensitive location data.

Then there was Oracle's BlueKai advertising business, which helped advertisers use extensive consumer data for targeting. Oracle shut down its advertising products in September 2024. Still, its history illustrates how sophisticated this industry became. The important point is that a label doesn't have to be accurate to influence how a company views you.

The categories data brokers can put you in
Some of these classifications sound harmless. Others are surprisingly personal. Here are examples of the information brokers have historically inferred or used to create consumer segments.
Data broker research and enforcement cases have documented categories involving:
Diabetes and related health interestsPregnancyHigh cholesterolHealth and wellness behaviorFinancial status combined with health-related assumptions
Diabetes and related health interests
Pregnancy
High cholesterol
Health and wellness behavior
Financial status combined with health-related assumptions

A major concern is that these classifications can originate outside the medical system. HIPAA protects health information handled by covered healthcare organizations and their business associates. However, health-related information independently gathered or inferred by other businesses may fall outside HIPAA's protections.

For example, searching for information about diabetes doesn't mean you have diabetes. You could be researching the condition for a family member. Yet advertising systems may still use that activity as one of several signals when building a profile. Other federal and state privacy laws may apply, but they don't necessarily provide the same protections as HIPAA.
AMAZON ABOUT YOU MAY KNOW YOU A LITTLE TOO WELL
Your online activity can help data brokers build detailed profiles, even when you're simply browsing the internet. (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

Data companies have also offered categories based on estimated income, spending behavior and financial circumstances. These can include people classified as affluent, price-sensitive or likely to respond to certain financial offers. One particularly troubling example comes from the Justice Department's case against Epsilon Data Management. According to federal prosecutors, Epsilon used sophisticated modeling to identify consumers likely to respond to solicitations. The company sold information about more than 30 million Americans to operators of fraudulent schemes, including fake sweepstakes promotions. Epsilon agreed to pay $150 million as part of its deferred prosecution agreement. This is a documented example of consumer data being used to help fraudsters identify potential victims.

Data brokers have also inferred people's religious interests and political leanings. These predictions may draw on information such as location patterns, purchases, public records and other available data. For example, the FTC documented the use of a "Christian church goers" advertising segment. A person visiting a church doesn't necessarily belong to that faith. Similarly, someone researching a political candidate doesn't automatically support that candidate. Nevertheless, profiling systems can use these signals to group people into audiences.

Another category focuses on what may be happening in your personal life. Data companies have developed segments involving parents with young children, empty nesters and households at different stages of life. These classifications can help businesses decide what products or services to advertise. However, they can also reveal potential pressure points. Someone approaching retirement may receive different financial offers than a young parent. A household believed to be managing health expenses may attract another type of marketing. And when those assumptions are wrong, the resulting profile may still influence what someone sees.
How data brokers make guesses about you

Consider what you've done online recently. Maybe you searched for joint pain relief. Perhaps you compared retirement plans or looked up treatment options for a relative. Individually, these activities might reveal very little. However, companies can combine information from websites, apps, purchase histories, public records and commercial databases.

Then predictive models look for patterns. For example, a company may consider your age range, estimated income and browsing activity when deciding whether you fit a particular advertising category. These classifications are often called modeled attributes or inferences. They represent predictions rather than verified personal facts. And here's the problem: a company buying access to an audience segment may use the prediction without knowing how accurately it describes each person.
How scammers use personal data to make attacks more convincing

Basic information helps a scammer contact you. More detailed personal information can help make the approach believable. For example, someone who knows your name and address could send a convincing-looking financial notice. Now suppose that same person also has information suggesting you're approaching retirement or researching medical expenses. A criminal could use those clues to tailor a fraudulent Medicare offer, investment pitch or fake medical service.

This doesn't mean every scammer buys sophisticated consumer profiles. However, the Justice Department's case against Epsilon Data Management shows how targeted consumer information can end up in the hands of fraudsters. The company sold consumer data to operators of fraudulent schemes, helping them identify people more likely to respond.

Meanwhile, the FBI reported that Americans age 60 and older lost approximately $7.7 billion to internet crime in 2025, up from $4.9 billion in 2024. While those losses weren't all connected to data brokers, the documented sale of targeted consumer lists shows how personal information can help criminals identify potential victims and make their scams more convincing.
Can you see what data brokers have predicted about you?

Finding every profile attached to your name can be difficult. Unlike a credit report, there isn't one centralized system where you can review all the marketing predictions companies have generated about you. However, some state privacy laws give residents rights to access, correct or delete personal information, including certain inferences.

California provides one important example. Under the California Consumer Privacy Act, eligible residents can request information held by covered businesses, subject to legal exceptions. California also launched its Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, known as DROP at privacy.ca.gov/DROP/, in January 2026.

It allows eligible California residents to submit one deletion request covering registered data brokers. Those companies began processing requests in August 2026. Matching records, including inferences, generally must be deleted unless an exception applies. Other states have different privacy protections, so your options depend on where you live.
IS YOUR PERSONAL DATA CHANGING WHAT YOU PAY ONLINE?
Scammers can use personal information to create targeted attacks that appear more convincing and trustworthy. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)
How to reduce what data brokers know about you
You may not be able to eliminate every prediction about yourself. However, you can take practical steps to reduce how much personal information remains available.
Here's where to start:

Kurt's key takeaways

I've warned you before about data brokers collecting your personal information, but I find the predictions they make about us even more troubling. Think about it. You could search for a medical condition on behalf of someone you love and end up in a category suggesting you have that condition yourself. Someone buying access to that profile may have no idea the assumption is wrong. And when personal information gets into the wrong hands, it can help scammers make their pitches sound much more convincing. What concerns me is how little most of us know about the profiles being built around our names. You may never see every label a company assigns to you, but you can start reducing the information available to build those profiles. I recommend checking what appears when you search for yourself and taking advantage of the privacy protections available in your state. A reputable data removal service can also help by automatically sending removal requests to data brokers and continuing to check when your information reappears. You won't disappear from the internet, but you can make it harder for strangers to assemble a detailed profile of your life.

title: Elon Musk vows to give every US child SpaceX stock
summary: Elon Musk says he'll give one SpaceX share to every kid in America in 2027, but key details about eligibility and distribution remain unclear.
story: Elon Musk announces a plan to give one share of SpaceX stock to every child in America. The 'Big Money Show' debates the business and charitable aspects of this multi-billion dollar giveaway, contrasting it with Anthropic's decision to commit five percent of its equity to a public benefit fund. Panelists discuss the motivations behind these high-profile corporate charity initiatives.

You probably don't expect Elon Musk to show up in your child's investment portfolio. But that's exactly what could happen next year. The billionaire behind SpaceX has made a remarkable promise. He says he'll give one share of his space company to every kid in America.

We're talking about a potential giveaway worth more than $10 billion. Free SpaceX stock for kids sounds appealing, especially when you're thinking about your child's financial future. But before you start looking for a way to sign up, there are some pretty important details Musk has yet to explain.

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. No technical experience is needed.
