title: Data center group jumps into the Kansas governor’s race to boost Republicans
summary: Building the Future is an offshoot of the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, arguably the leading super PAC promoting industry interests in the midterm elections.
story: Building the Future, a new pro-data center super PAC, is spending more than $1.5 million to back Kansas state Sen. Ty Masterson, a Republican, in the state’s battle for governor, a person familiar with the spending said Monday in details first shared with NBC News.
Building the Future is an offshoot of the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, backed by AI heavyweights and arguably the leading super PAC promoting industry interests in the midterm elections.
Earlier Monday, The New York Times reported that Building the Future is also set to spend about $1.5 million in advertising to boost GOP Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race.

In August, Build American AI, a nonprofit that is also in the Leading the Future network, announced a multimillion-dollar ad campaign in Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin seeking to boost preferred policies to govern data center growth. At the time, it announced the formation of the political group, Building the Future.

The group said in August it would back candidates who support “responsible policies that strengthen and protect communities, preserve water resources, and prevent rate hikes on electricity bills, while ensuring American leadership in AI and creating good-paying jobs for American workers.”
The new spending followed months of opposition to data center development intensifying, with the sprawling structures needed to power the AI boom becoming a key issue for voters across the country.

Kansas is one of the only Democratic-controlled governorships that Republicans have a shot at flipping this fall. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report lists that race as leaning Republican. The state also features a competitive Senate contest between Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton.
In a statement Monday, Holscher called Masterson a “stooge for Big Tech” who wants “to put a data center on every corner and in every cornfield.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“It’s also why he’s going to give them tax breaks while everyday Kansans’ costs go up,” she added. “These billionaire CEOs know that I won’t do their bidding, and that’s why they’re spending millions to beat me. But I’ll keep fighting for guardrails on data centers, and I’ll always put Kansans first.”
Masterson did not immediately provide comment for this article.
Data centers have been a hot issue in both Kansas and South Carolina, as well as other states across the country.

In Kansas, Masterson has opposed moratoriums and has defended a 2025 law he voted for that provided sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher voted for that law too but has since called for a statewide moratorium on the developments.

In South Carolina, Graham has framed the investments as necessary for national security while expressing support for local control over their construction. Annie Andrews, Graham’s Democratic opponent, has called for a moratorium on new projects and labeled Graham as “Data Center Darline.”

title: WNBA championship may be decided on a Thursday morning because an NBA game took priority
summary: The WNBA scheduled its potential championship-clinching game between the Golden State Valkyries and the Atlanta Dream for 12:30 p.m. ET on Thursday.
story: The WNBA scheduled its potential championship-clinching game for 12:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, the league announced, settling a logistical nightmare that appeared to have few satisfactory solutions.

The Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream’s Game 6 had always been set for Thursday night in Georgia with its location and exact tipoff time listed as TBD due to an unfortunate series of scheduling conflicts.
The Dream’s playoff home, State Farm Arena, has an Atlanta Hawks game scheduled for Thursday night.

“We thank the NBA, Dream, Valkyries, Hawks, State Farm Arena and USA Network for the collaboration and flexibility that made this move possible,” retiring WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert said in a statement on Monday afternoon.

The Dream played most of its 2026 season at the 3,500-seat Gateway Center Arena at College Park, the league’s smallest building. But the team had been able to move major regular seasons games and all playoff contests to State Farm Arena, the 17,000-seat home of the NBA’s Atlanta Hawks.
But with Game 6 set for Thursday, the same day as a 7 p.m. Cleveland Cavaliers-Hawks game at State Farm, that big venue was not available for a prime time women’s game.
For Subscribers

If the Valkyries win Monday’s Game 5 in San Francisco, that means their West Coast fans would have to get to a TV by 9:30 a.m. PT on Thursday and possibly pop champagne bottles before noon should Golden State wrap it up in Atlanta.
For Subscribers
In the WNBA’s prepared statement, Engellbert did not address the odd start time, but instead chose to focus on the league playing in front a larger crowd.

“The sellout crowds and extraordinary atmosphere of State Farm Arena for Games 3 and 4 were a tremendous success and we’re excited to give thousands more fans the opportunity to experience Game 6 with a championship on the line,” Engellbert  said.

title: Texas redistricting left these Latino voters confused, but will it impact midterm vote?
summary: The electoral map that Texas redrew at President Donald Trump’s request left many voters in Houston and southern Texas facing unfamiliar candidates.
story: HOUSTON — When José Cantú checked his voter registration information one morning in early October, he discovered that his house was no longer in Texas’s 29th Congressional District, which Democratic Congresswoman Sylvia García represents.
Two years ago, when he voted for the first time, Cantú cast a ballot for García, whom he says he’s known since he was “a little boy.”

Now, “I texted my mom and said, ‘Mom, we’re now part of District 9. What am I going to do?’” said Cantú, a medical student at the University of Houston, referring to the fact that he didn’t recognize anyone listed on the ballot and had to figure out who the candidates were.

Although Cantú, 20, didn’t move, the map of his district had changed. His friend, Jessica Campos, 44, a mother of three, was also unaware of the changes and believed she still voted in District 29, not District 9.
“I didn’t know until a few days ago who our candidate was,” she said. “Even though I’m very interested in politics, I didn’t know who was representing me.”

Cantú and Campos are not isolated cases. In 2025, at the request of President Donald Trump, the Texas Legislature redrew its electoral map with the aim of taking away five congressional seats from Democrats who represented a Latino- or Black majority-district. Texas thus opened a redistricting race that extended to a dozen states, from California to Florida.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Districts 9 and 34 show what this change means for many Latino voters.

In Houston’s newly created District 9, 97 out of every 100 residents were in a different district in the 2024 election; in the case of District 34, in the southern part of the state, the map swapped areas near McAllen with Corpus Christi. Both districts have a Hispanic majority and, according to experts, both were drawn to favor a Republican candidate.

According to analysts, the Republican strategy for the new electoral map rests on two assumptions: that many Latinos don’t vote and that those who voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 will vote Republican again.

On Nov. 3, with control of the House of Representatives at stake, it will become clear whether this was a sound gamble. But first, nearly all residents of the new 9th District and more than a third of those in the 34th District, which is also a new district, will have to figure out who the candidates on their ballots are.
Most people unaware their district has changed
“Our studies show that most people don’t know they’re in a new district,” said Mark P. Jones, a political scientist at Rice University.

Republicans have made no secret of their intentions in pushing for the new maps. “The underlying goal of this plan is simple: to improve Republican political performance,” state representative Todd Hunter, a Corpus Christi Republican who introduced the map in the House, said in August of 2025. Hunter emphasized that four of the five new districts have a Hispanic majority.

This electoral practice, known as gerrymandering, involves drawing districts to give an advantage to a particular party or group. In November 2025, a federal court ruled 2-1 that Texas’ gerrymandering was racial-based: the map was drawn using voters’ race as the primary criterion, which violates the Constitution. Texas countered that its motive was partisan, not racial, and asked the Supreme Court to block the federal ruling. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the state to use its new maps.

“We thought the 2021 map was a problem, but the 2025 map made it much worse,” said Thomas Saenz, president of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF), which is litigating against both maps. According to Saenz, the new redrawing eliminated effective Latino majorities in several districts. The lawsuit remains open and, he said, will be resolved after the election.
In response to a request for comment from Noticias Telemundo, Eduardo Leal, campaign spokesperson for Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, said the maps “were drawn to comply with the law.”
Same number, new district

The old District 9, in southwest Houston, united Black and Latino voters; Kamala Harris won it by 44 points in 2004 and veteran Democrat Al Green had represented it since 2005. When the new map drew much of that territory into District 18, Green followed suit and in May lost the Democratic primary runoff to Christian Menefee.

The new District 9 retains its number and almost nothing else. Only 3% of its residents lived in the old district: the rest came from the former Districts 29, 36 and 2, according to an analysis by Jones and Michael O. Adams of Texas Southern University. The new boundaries encompass eastern Harris County, including the East End, the Houston Canal corridor and all of rural, predominantly white Liberty County. Had this been the case two years ago, Trump would have won it by 20 points.

On paper, District 9 is a Latino district: 62% of its residents are Hispanic. But only about 50% are eligible to vote due to age and citizenship status, and only 45% are registered voters. In 2024, Latinos accounted for only 37% of TX-9 voters, according to Jones’ and Adams’ analysis.

“Although it has a Latino majority, it’s a district where the majority of voters are white,” Jones said. Districts are drawn using the total population, including minors and noncitizens, and the designers “know that within that Latino district there’s a low percentage who are actually going to turn out to vote,” he explained.

Liberty County, a rural area that accounts for just under a fifth of the district’s voters, tips the scales in favor of Republicans. There, Republican Alex Mealer leads Democrat Leticia Gutierrez by 37 points, while on Harris’ side it’s a virtual tie, according to a University of Houston Hobby School poll co-authored by Jones.

Ryan Taylor, chairman of the Republican Party in Liberty, said that the new district gives its voters a more important role. “It would be a mistake to assume that a voter’s ethnicity determines their political priorities,” he said.
For many voters, confusion

For Jones, the biggest effect of the map is confusion. In Houston, many people no longer know who their representative is, he said, and with the second redistricting in a decade (the first was in 2021, after the 2020 census), “many are going to realize” when they go to vote.

Leticia Gutierrez, the Democratic candidate in District 9, says she’s noticed confusion at her campaign events because some voters believe she’s running against Rep. Sylvia Garcia, also a Democrat. “They’re confusing them, and it’s on purpose,” she said.

Daron Shaw, a professor of government at the University of Texas at Austin, says the strongest argument against redrawing the maps mid-decade is the confusion it creates because voters “don’t really know who their representative is,” and that damages the quality of representation. However, he added, “This isn’t new. Parties that control legislatures will almost always redraw districts in their favor.”
Campos, the voter from District 9, sums it up like this: “It’s not fair that we don’t know who wants to represent us.”
In July, an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Magnolia Park, an East End neighborhood that falls within the new district.

His death shocked the Hispanic community in Texas and has prompted voters with a low propensity to participate to express their desire to vote to send a message to the Trump administration, according to local politicians and analysts.

Gutierrez, District 9’s Democratic candidate, described Salgado Araujo as “a hard-working man who was employing people” and who “was simply going to his job.” Following his death, she said in a video posted to her Facebook account that the new District 9 layout was designed “to silence the East End.”

Noticias Telemundo requested comment from candidate Alex Mealer’s team but had not received a response by the time of publication. The Republican candidate said in July that she trusted the investigations into Salgado’s death would provide “a full account” of what happened and that speculation “is neither helpful nor productive.”
A district with two heads

In South Texas, the map followed a different logic. District 34 lost its portion of Hidalgo County, near McAllen, and gained most of Nueces County, including Corpus Christi, which had belonged to the Republican 27th District. In 2024, with the previous boundaries, Trump won the district by 4.5 points, but the same voters re-elected Democrat Vicente Gonzalez as their representative. With the new boundaries, the district is now 77% Hispanic, and Trump would have won it by 10 points in 2024.
As Jones explains, “it is now a district with two heads,” Brownsville to the south and more Democratic, and Corpus Christi to the north and more Republican.

“They did this to try to get me out of Congress,” Vicente Gonzalez, the Democratic congressman running for re-election in that district, said. “What they didn’t count on is that I’m from Corpus Christi. That’s the community where I was born and raised.” Gonzalez estimates that, with the changes, he lost about 250,000 voters.

With the changes, Hidalgo County was completely removed from District 34, and its eastern part was moved to District 15, according to Richard Gonzalez, chairman of the Democratic Party in that county. He fears that many voters may not know that these changes have already taken place.
“Some may think they are voting for Vicente Gonzalez when in reality they are now voting for Bobby Pulido (Democratic candidate of the 15th),” he stated.

An August poll by Texas Southern University gave Gonzalez a 2-point lead over Republican Eric Flores, within the margin of error. Among Latino voters alone, Gonzalez led 53 to 34; white voters favored Flores 57 to 31.
Noticias Telemundo requested comments from Flores’ team but, at the time of publication, had not received a response.

Flores, a former federal prosecutor in McAllen and former National Guard captain, has the backing of both Trump and Abbott. “South Texas needs a fighter, not an absentee congressman,” he said in May. On immigration, he has shown nuance: in 2025, he said he wants employers to “have the workers they need” through an efficient legal process.

According to Jones, there are no radical candidates competing in this district: The candidates from both parties are centrist Latinos, and ultimately the election will be decided by “the centrist Latino who voted for Trump in 2024, but today has doubts.”
‘We have a lot of power’
Some analysts agree that the new Texas maps were drawn based on the results of the 2024 election, but they disagree on how much that will weigh on the November vote.

“There is no evidence that Hispanics are becoming more Republican,” said Mike Madrid, a Republican political consultant and critic of Trump. His party, he said, “mistakenly believed” after 2024 that it had figured out Latinos. He said that, between that mistake and the political climate, the election is shaping up to be “an extraordinary fiasco” for Republicans.

Jason Villalba, a former Republican legislator and founder of the Texas Hispanic Policy Foundation, called the new map “a blatant political maneuver” and believes the Legislature mistook an economic vote for a realignment. “Republicans are in for a big surprise on election night,” he asserted.

Shaw, the University of Texas professor, estimates that Republicans have gone from having nearly 50% of the Latino vote in 2024 to perhaps 40% in current polls. He calculates that, in the best-case scenario, Republicans will win two or three of the five seats they were seeking.

Meanwhile, Cantú, the medical student, said he wanted to organize workshops so other young people can learn about the changes in their districts and get to know the candidates. “It makes me angry because they don’t give us the correct information,” he said.
For her part, Cantu’s friend Jessica Campos said that Hispanic voters have “a lot of power.”
“The problem is,” she said, “we don’t know it yet.”
An earlier version of this story was first featured in Noticias Telemundo.

title: Man charged with mailing threatening letters with white substance to members of Congress
summary: A man has been charged in Illinois with mailing four letters containing a white granular substance to members of Congress, all of which were sent in envelopes containing his name and home address.
story: WASHINGTON — A man has been charged in Illinois with mailing four letters containing a white granular substance to members of Congress, all of which were sent in envelopes containing his name and home address.

Matthew Unglesbee has been charged with sending threatening letters containing a white granular substance to three members of Congress, along with a handwritten letter that read “HA HA.” A fourth letter with a white granular substance included the note “HAH enjoy the gift.”
Unglesbee is facing two charges: false information and hoaxes, and mailing threatening communications. He will make an initial appearance in court on Monday afternoon.

In an interview with FBI personnel on Sunday, Unglesbee allegedly admitted that he mailed four letters to four members of Congress after hearing about other letters mailed earlier in the month. The FBI is separately investigating letters containing suspicious substances that were sent to members of Congress and elections officials in recent weeks.

Unglesbee admitted that he knew that people would perceive the letters as dangerous, the FBI says. He said in the FBI interview that the granular substance was salt, which he said “kind of looks like” anthrax. He denied involvement with prior mailings.
A search of his residence turned up a fifth unmailed and empty envelope that was addressed to a member of Congress, according to the FBI.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The case began after an anonymous online tipster told the FBI that they overheard Unglesbee talking about mailing a suspicious substance to members of Congress. The tip was received on Oct. 16, and the FBI responded when the letters showed up to the offices of members of Congress three days later.

title: Walter Koenig, actor who played Chekov on original ‘Star Trek’ series, dies at 90
summary: Walter Koenig, the actor who played Chekov on the original “Star Trek” television series, died as one of the final surviving cast members of the beloved show, his representative confirmed on Monday.
story: Walter Koenig, the actor who played Chekov on the original “Star Trek” television series, died as one of the final surviving cast members of the beloved show, his representative confirmed on Monday.
He was 90.
Koenig passed away at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.
“Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world,” McGinnis said.

“Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond Star Trek, his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft.”
With the passing of Koenig, who played trusty Enterprise navigator Pavel Chekov on the timeless science fiction show, that leaves just two surviving marquee cast members from the original series.

Following the deaths of Leonard Nimoy (2015), DeForest Kelley (1999), James Doohan (2005) and Nichelle Nichols (2022), the only two primary cast members still alive today are the 95-year-old William Shatner, who played Capt. James T. Kirk, and George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Koenig was the best man at Takei’s wedding and the Sulu actor fondly remembered his colleague as a “thoughtful man, and a loyal friend” Monday.
“Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades,” Takei said in a statement posted on Instagram.
Koenig’s Sept. 14, 1936, birthday matched with Takei’s wedding anniversary, also Sept. 14, 2008.

“I will always treasure that he and I shared that date,” the 89-year-old Takei added. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”

The original “Star Trek” ran for 79 episodes over the course of three seasons on NBC from 1966 to 1969. Koenig also reprised his role as the Russian crew member in multiple movie versions of the venerable franchise.

Koenig’s Chekov came on board during the second season of Cold War-era “Star Trek,” which aimed to show how characters from multiple races and nationalities could peacefully coincide — albeit in the 23rd century, on a space ship and in the fictional setting of series creator Gene Roddenberry.

The late actor went on to play Chekov in seven “Star Trek” movies: “Star Trek: The Motion Picture” in 1979, “Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan” in 1982, “Star Trek III: The Search for Spock” in 1984, “Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home” in 1986, “Star Trek V: The Final Frontier” in 1989, “Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country” in 1991 and “Star Trek Generations” in 1994.

Koenig got his start in television in the early ‘60s with appearances on shows ranging from “General Hospital” to “I Spy” before landing the role in 1967 that would define the rest of his career. He would go on to work in numerous other projects, including a recurring role in the ‘90s on cult favorite sci fi series “Babylon 5,” but always came back to the world of “Star Trek.”

Koenig never shied away from the Chekov character — doing voice over work in “Star Trek” video games and even making a cameo in 2023 on “Star Trek: Picard” — and always gladly mingled with fans wanting to engage him about the iconic TV series, McGinnis said.

“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen,” according to his agent. “Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.”
Koenig kept working until nearly the very end, winning best actor at this year’s Independent Shorts Awards for “Mr. Fleischmann.”

title: Judge orders DOJ to reinstate former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey, daughter of ex-FBI director
summary: A federal judge ruled Monday that former Assistant United States Attorney Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was “unlawfully terminated” and ordered that she be reinstated.
story: A federal judge ruled Monday that former Assistant United States Attorney Maurene Comey, the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, was “unlawfully terminated” and ordered that she be reinstated.

The Justice Department’s abrupt firing of Comey in July 2025 violated the Constitution’s separation of powers and her Fifth Amendment due process and statutory rights, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman found. The Trump administration’s assertion that it can fire career prosecutors at will would “unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system,” the judge wrote.
He granted Comey back pay effective from the date of her termination through Dec. 20, 2025, when she began a new job.
A spokesperson for the Justice Department said DOJ “disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course.”

In a joint statement, Comey’s attorneys Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron, Deepa Vanamali and Margaret Donovan said that “this decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law.”
They added that the “hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law.”

Comey had worked on a number of high-profile cases in the Southern District of New York, including the prosecutions of disgraced music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs, former Sen. Bob Menendez, D-N.J., and the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his co-conspirator, Ghislaine Maxwell.

Comey filed suit in September 2025, alleging the Trump administration provided “no legitimate explanation” for firing her after almost 10 years of service, and that it had only done so because of President Donald Trump’s “well-known and longstanding vendetta against James Comey, whom he fired as FBI Director in 2017.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Maurene Comey said the only thing she was told about her firing from her boss was that it “came from Washington.”
The Justice Department later said in a court filing that she was removed at the direction of then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.
The judge found Bondi did not follow the law when she fired Comey, depriving Comey of her rights to due process.
“Congress granted the Attorney General power to remove Comey,” the judge wrote, but “Congress imposed limits on that power — limits that, even Defendants concede, were violated in Comey’s case.”
Among DOJ’s arguments were that Bondi had the authority to fire Comey “at will” and for no reason at all, and that Congress does not have the authority to put limits on that authority.

Furman roundly rejected those arguments. DOJ has staked out a “sweeping and unprecedented theory of executive authority,” he wrote, and its position “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.”

The Trump administration has routinely fired career federal prosecutors along with FBI employees, particularly focusing on individuals involved in prior investigations of Trump or with the massive investigation into the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.
Furman seemed to take note of those firings while declaring Comey’s firing unlawful.

“Defendants invented a new and expansive theory of executive power. And they have also utilized that theory to remove other Executive Branch employees who have long held protections from removal,” he wrote, adding the declaration should “serve a useful purpose in clarifying or settling the legal issues involved.”
The administration is also continuing to push forward with a federal criminal case brought against Comey’s father over a photo of seashells that it contends amounted to a threat against Trump.

The seashells case has been delayed until at least early 2027 as a judge weighs whether to dismiss it. James Comey’s team has argued the case is a product of Trump’s retribution campaign rather than a good faith application of federal law and that “dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense” show the seashells photo was not a true threat.

title: House Democrats call on DOJ to name  special counsel in Epstein case
summary: House Democrats call for independent special counsel to investigate evidence of alleged Trump criminal ties to Jeffrey Epstein
story: WASHINGTON — House Judiciary Committee Democrats are calling for an independent special counsel to investigate evidence of President Donald Trump’s alleged criminal ties to Jeffrey Epstein, according to a new report made public Monday.
“The bottom line,” they wrote in the report, “There is more than sufficient evidence to launch a criminal investigation.”

They acknowledged the Justice Department under Trump would be unlikely to appoint a special counsel, — such as Robert Mueller who ran the Russia investigation or Jack Smith, who led the investigation into Trump’s efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
The president has repeatedly denied any knowledge of, or involvement in, Epstein’s criminal activity and said he cut ties well before allegations of sex trafficking by the financier became public.

“None of these allegations are true. This ‘report’ is nothing more than a desperate attempt by crazed Democrats to distract Americans from the surging Republican momentum driven by President Trump’s historic achievements,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. “The President kicked Jeffrey Epstein out of his club at Mar-a-Lago because he was a creep.”

The report comes on the brink of the midterm elections, when Democrats are hoping to seize control of Congress as the president’s approval rating tanks over the economy, affordability and the war with Iran. The report signaled an avenue of focus for lawmakers in January should Democrats win a chamber of Congress.

A bipartisan law signed by Congress last November ordered the release of millions of documents related to the case against Epstein, who died by suicide in jail while awaiting federal sex trafficking and conspiracy charges. Many of America’s wealthy and powerful appear in the files, including Trump, who is mentioned thousands of times.
But only one person was ever convicted, Epstein’s accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell. No one else has been charged in the United States.

Right now, Democratic oversight efforts have been limited because they are in the minority in Congress, unable to compel witness testimony or solicit documents through subpoena without the help of Republicans. While the Republican-led House Oversight Committee has subpoenaed several Epstein associates and Republicans helped to pass the Epstein Transparency Act, they have been largely unwilling to look deeper into Trump’s ties to the late sex offender.

Democrats’ power would change dramatically should the party win the majority back in either chamber. They would be able to issue subpoenas with or without the help of Republicans. In addition to the Epstein probe, Democratic leaders have promised robust investigations into alleged corruption and grift in Trump’s administration and family businesses.

In their report released Monday, Democrats accuse the Justice Department of obstructing investigations into potential Epstein co-conspirators, including, they say, Trump. The report alleges the DOJ worked to cover up the president’s connections to Epstein, and said an independent special counsel is necessary, because Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was once Trump’s personal attorney, was compromised.

“The women who survived Epstein deserve to be heard, Congress must have the complete files required by law, and an independent special counsel must investigate Epstein’s co-conspirators and DOJ’s cover-up and ensure that state and foreign prosecutors have the evidence they need to pursue justice,” Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the panel’s top Democrat, said in a statement.
A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement Monday that the report was “nothing more than a last-ditch effort by House Judiciary Democrats to mislead the public.”

The department complied with the Congressional act, “making public the nearly 3 million investigatory documents which were responsive to the Act. The Department also freely offered members of Congress the opportunity to view the files unredacted. All these files were part of FBI investigations that spanned decades and these claims were investigated by agents at the time.”
The Justice Department spokesperson said DOJ can’t talk about the existence of any ongoing investigations, but noted the only administration to bring federal charges against Epstein was Trump’s.
The Democrats vowed to continue investigating it themselves.

“Given DOJ and FBI’s abdication of their law enforcement duties and prosecutorial ethics, there is little reason to believe this administration will take even this minimal step,” according to the report. “Accordingly, Congress must continue to use its legislative and oversight powers to pursue justice for survivors and bring an end to the Trump Administration’s shameful, bureaucratic, and political cover-up.”

Trump was at one point friends with Epstein. “I’ve known Jeff for 15 years. Terrific guy,” Trump told New York magazine in 2002, before there were any public allegations of wrongdoing by the financier. “He’s a lot of fun to be with,” Trump said then. “It is even said that he likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side.”

Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 in a Florida state court to felony solicitation of prostitution and procuring minors for prostitution, in a heavily-criticized plea deal. He was sentenced to 18 months, though he served about a year before he was released.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
He was arrested in 2019 on a federal sex trafficking conspiracy charge and one count of sex trafficking underage women.

After Epstein’s arrest, Trump, who was president at the time, distanced himself from the disgraced financier. “I was not a fan,” he told reporters at a July 2019 news conference. “I had a falling out with him a long time ago.”
The staff report on Epstein released Monday draws on interviews the staff conducted with witnesses, as well as files released by the Justice Department related to its investigation of Epstein.

title: Anthropic reveals $80 billion loss, huge spending spree ahead of IPO
summary: Artificial intelligence startup Anthropic unveils its first public IPO filing ahead of what is expected to be one of the largest stock debuts in history.
story: Artificial intelligence startup Anthropic on Monday unveiled its public IPO filing ahead of what is expected to be one of the largest stock debuts in history.

That offering, widely expected to come sometime in mid-November, could value the Claude developer at more than $2 trillion. That could surpass the current record holder, Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in an IPO in June that valued the rocket-AI-social-media firm at $2.1 trillion.

The filing did not include a potential share price, the number of shares to be offered or a valuation for the whole company, all of which will be determined after Anthropic holds a “road show” with investors, prospective investors and its bankers.
Monday’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission showed that Anthropic, like other AI firms, is splashing out unprecedented amounts of cash on cloud services to run its AI models.
The company plans to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon for cloud services through April 2036 and another $120 billion with SpaceX through 2029.
Anthropic also said it planned to spend $115 billion with Google and $45 billion with Microsoft, both through 2033, for computing infrastructure.
The filing said that the company recorded revenue growth of “1,368% year over year for the three months ended June 30, 2026.”
The cost of renting servers and chips grew by 300% over the same period.
Anthropic’s net loss for the first six months of 2026 was $80.7 billion. For the entirety of 2025, the company reported a $42 billion net loss.

Anthropic added that it expects its current cash and sales to be sufficient for the next 12 months but warned that future revenue growth depends on a number of important factors, including the cost of infrastructure. As a result, it said, “we may be required to seek additional financing sooner than we currently anticipate.”
The company said it has raised about $141 billion of capital through the end of June and is sitting on $112.4 billion of cash.
The company plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the historic offering, as they did with SpaceX’s record deal.
But already, the offering is coming slightly later than expected as recent market moves give investors pause about the trajectory of the seemingly ever-expanding AI boom.
For Subscribers
Monday’s filing is unlikely to calm those fears.
Alongside its dramatic spending and borrowing figures, Anthropic warned that it “may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”

“While we have experienced significant revenue growth in recent periods, our business is highly capital intensive,” the company said. “Our revenue growth may not be sustainable, and our rate of growth may decrease.”
For Subscribers

Nevertheless, Anthropic told regulators and investors that it plans to keep burning through capital: “We expect our costs will increase over time and our losses will continue as we expect to invest significant resources towards growing our business and operating as a public company.”
On Sunday, a top Wall Street economist warned that the sector had yet to deliver broad gains to the wider economy.

“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” said Torsten Slok, chief economist at investment firm Apollo Global Management.

“Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493,” he wrote Sunday, referring to the companies left in the benchmark S&P 500 after subtracting Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, Apple, Amazon, Nvidia and Tesla. “And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth.”
The Nasdaq 100, which tracks the largest public AI developers, is up 15% this year. That’s more than the broader S&P 500’s 11% gain so far this year.

Market jitters over potential cracks in the AI boom have also caused a number of smaller IPOs to put their plans on hold. Earlier this month, a number of small offerings delayed or canceled their plans to go public, citing “market conditions.”

But still, the largest AI companies continue to raise massive amounts of funding for their projects. On Monday, Meta Platforms announced an up to $95 billion stock offering, while SpaceX said it had secured $40 billion in funding to buy Nvidia graphics processing units, which it called the largest type of fundraising ever.

As part of every stock offering, companies are asked to outline risks and uncertainties facing their businesses. Some of the risk factors outlined by Anthropic included safety, reliable computing infrastructure and its ability to “navigate an evolving, uncertain, and at times divergent global regulatory landscape.”

“Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the filing said.

Some of those potential risks have manifested themselves recently, as the firms have faced intense scrutiny over a swath of incidents in which their models and agents have hacked into government and private websites and services.

The companies, including Anthropic, have said they’re taking steps to bolster security. But those incidents also came as Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei wrote in September that companies should “pace the frontier,” a way of saying that AI models were advancing faster than humans could grasp their capabilities.

Some within the industry conditionally agreed with Amodei, but Washington sharply rebuked the idea. He and President Donald Trump met privately and again at an industry meeting that took place at the White House.

Trump later said he wanted no holds at all placed on the progress the industry is making. Trump and the leaders of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, Nvidia and SpaceX signed what Trump said was a “morally binding” agreement to police AI safety.

“Look, I say, if you’re going to seek regulation, they can put you out of business,” Trump told Time magazine earlier this year. “But my attitude is, we’re winning against the world by a lot, and I want to keep winning.”

title: Police arrest a 15-year-old in shooting near Florida A&M stadium that injured 12
summary: A 15-year-old male has been arrested in connection with a shooting close to Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium over the weekend that injured 12 people, according to police.
story: A 15-year-old male has been arrested in connection with a shooting close to Florida A&M University’s Bragg Memorial Stadium over the weekend that injured 12 people, according to police.

The Tallahassee Police Department said Monday that detectives had arrested the teenager Sunday in connection with the shooting. The teenager is facing 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and possession of a firearm by a delinquent.
“What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” Police Chief Lawrence Revell said.

“While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy,” he added.
The shooting broke out about 8 p.m. Saturday, near Perry and Manatee streets, close to the stadium, where homecoming celebrations included a football game.
The 12 people injured included minors. One individual also sustained an ankle injury while fleeing the gunfire, police said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

After the shooting took place, the university issued a statement on X asking members of its campus community to stay away from the area. It described the shooting as having taken place “near campus,” which it said remained safe.
“Our hearts are with the victims and everyone affected by tonight’s incident on Perry Street,” the university added.

Police said Monday that they were continuing to investigate the incident but that preliminary findings indicated “a physical altercation occurred before shots were fired” and that “the incident stemmed from a dispute between individuals known to one another.”
They added that “none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets.”
Additional arrests are possible, Tallahassee police said, as the investigation continues.

I love using Scrub Daddy (and Scrub Mommy) sponges to clean all of my dishes, but particularly dishes and utensils that food tends to adhere to a lot. When I use these sponges, they do a great job of wiping crusty food residue from utensils, but they’re also effective at cleaning oil and grease from pans, plates and more. You do have to use a lot of water to make them usable and squeezable, but they also last a long time compared to traditional kitchen sponges.
How to clean wooden kitchen utensils

For things like wooden spoons, spatulas and cutting boards, it’s important to make sure that you dry them just as thoroughly as you wash them, according to Robin Murphy, a cleaning expert and chief cleaning officer at home cleaning company Maid Brigade. Make sure to use warm water, dish soap and a sponge or soft brush to clean them thoroughly.

“Wash them after use, rinse well, and dry them with a clean towel,” she says. “Let them air-dry completely before putting them away. If the wood starts looking dry, condition it with a little food-grade mineral oil.”

Additionally, it’s important to use a brush or sponge to clean wooden kitchen utensils to help clean in between crevices and grooves on wooden surfaces, according to Kadi Dulude, cleaning expert and owner of home cleaning company Wizard of Homes. “Use a little bit of mild dish soap and a sponge/brush to remove all food residue, paying attention to get into grooves and joints too,” she says. “Then rinse well and air dry. Don’t put them flat on a wet cloth or anywhere air isn’t circulating, or mold and mildew will grow.”
Here are your step-by-step instructions from the experts:
After using your wooden spoon, spatula, cutting board or other wooden kitchen utensil, immediately rinse it with warm water to get rid of residue. Don’t put it in the dishwasher.

Apply warm water and a small amount of mild dish soap, such as Dawn Platinum Powerwash Dish Spray, to a sponge, soft brush or Scrub Daddy, and use it to gently scrub the surface of your wooden spoon, spatula or cutting board, focusing on the surfaces and ends that touch food.

Rinse them thoroughly with warm water, pat them dry with a paper towel or kitchen towel, and then place them on a drying rack, so that they’re completely exposed to air and therefore dry as fast as possible (don’t place them flat on a kitchen towel, for example).

For old wooden utensils that are dry and faded, both Murphy and Dulude recommend using a food-grade mineral oil meant for conditioning wooden accessories, such as Kate Naturals Mineral Oil for Wood Cutting Boards. When the wooden utensils are completely dry, apply a small amount of the mineral oil to a cloth and rub the oil onto the surface of it. Allow the utensil to dry completely before storing or using it.
Can you put wooden utensils in the dishwasher?

Both Murphy and Dulude recommend not washing wooden kitchen utensils in the dishwasher (even if the label says it’s dishwasher safe) because the process can be very harsh on the surface of the utensils.

“The dishwasher gets too hot and it’s not good for wood to sit in a hot humid environment for too long. It will cause your items to warp or split” says Dulude. “Some utensils may be safe for the dishwasher, but if you really want to prolong their life, handwash them.” Additionally, water expands as it dries which leads to wooden kitchen utensils cracking and splintering, according to Murphy.
How to maintain wooden kitchen utensils

As I mentioned above, Murphy and Dulude recommend using a mineral oil to help maintain wooden kitchen utensils. A food-grade mineral oil helps restore the moisture in wooden spoons, spatulas and cutting boards without giving them an oily feeling or making foods oily. It’s similar to seasoning a cast-iron skillet or using a moisturizing cream on your face to help restore your natural skin barrier.
When should you replace wooden kitchen utensils?

Pay attention to the surface of the wooden utensil and see if it’s damaged or rough. “Once you start seeing deep cracks it’s time to stop using it because food and moisture will get into the cracks which can contaminate [the next] food [you’re preparing],” says Dulude. “If it’s just [a] small imperfection or roughness then there’s hope you can save it by lightly sanding and using food-grade mineral oil.”
What products should you not use on wooden kitchen utensils and why?

You should avoid harsh cleaning products, like pure bleach or abrasive cleaners, like powders or pastes, because they can mess up the surface of the wood, according to Murphy. She also says to avoid using things like vegetable or olive oil because they become rancid over time, which is why food-safe mineral oil is best. This is also a reminder as to why cleaning them thoroughly is important since they probably already come in contact with things like vegetable and olive oil via cooking and food prep.

title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, dies at 46
summary: Eric Bauza, best known for voicing the lovable “Looney Tunes” characters Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died, his family said Monday.
story: Eric Bauza, best known for voicing the lovable “Looney Tunes” characters Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died, his family said Monday.
He was 46.
Bauza’s family issued a brief statement on his official Instagram page stating that he had “passed away suddenly,” without giving further details.
The Emmy Award-winning voice actor was the “modern voice of iconic “Looney Tunes” characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters,” the statement said.
Bauza died Sunday at his residence, according to the Los Angeles County medical examiner’s office, which noted that he had been diagnosed with hypertensive cardiovascular disease.

title: Chrishell Stause Announces Split From G Flip After Over 4 Years Together: ‘I Feel Like a Little Bit of a Failure’
summary: Chrishell Stause has revealed that she and partner G Flip are separating after more than four years together.
story: Chrishell Stause has revealed that she and partner G Flip are separating after more than four years together.
The 45-year-old actor and reality television star shared the news about the breakup in a tearful video uploaded to Instagram Oct. 26.
“I have a pretty humbling update to share with you guys,” Stause began. “G and I are no longer together, and we have agreed to treat this public separation with love and respect for each other.”
She continued, “That’s not hard for me because I am in love with this person, and I don’t have all the information or the reasons.”
The “Selling Sunset” alum said she hopes that as time goes on she will heal and learn from the relationship.
“Everything’s going to be fine. I’m definitely never doing this again,” she said. Stause was previously married to actor Justin Hartley from 2017 to 2021.

She explained that she recorded the video message because fans “deserved a little bit more than a cold written statement” after showing their love and support for the couple for years. She said their fans can still offer support, but they will have to do so separately now.

“I don’t know what else to say, you guys. I feel like a little bit of a failure. There’s nothing you could say about me that would be worse than what I say to myself. So I just have to kind of heal and figure this out,” Stause said as she started to cry.
She further explained how she is currently processing the breakup.

“I’m a lover girl. I swing big. I miss…” she said before correcting herself. “Or maybe you don’t miss. Maybe these are the lives and seasons you’re meant to have with people, and I had an amazing over four years with G.”
Although the relationship is ending in a way she didn’t expect, she added that she will always love her ex and wishes them both happiness.
Stause and G Flip, 33, met at a Halloween party in 2021, the Australian musician revealed to Vogue Australia. “Chrishell got stood up and then we ended up kissing,” they shared.
The actor confirmed their relationship during the Season 5 “Selling Sunset” reunion in May 2022.

“I recently have been spending a lot of time with someone that’s very important to me. Their name is G Flip,” Stause said at the time. “They’re nonbinary, so they go by they/them, and they are an extremely talented musician.”
A year later, they married in a surprise wedding. Stause posted a video on Instagram of them tying the knot. The clip included a montage of their relationship.
“Love doesn’t always go as planned … Sometimes it’s immeasurably better,” she said in the caption, in part.

They continued to have more ceremonies over the past few years. In July 2025, they exchanged vows for a fourth time during their medieval-themed nuptials in Los Angeles. Stause’s representative confirmed to TODAY.com at the time that the ceremony also marked the couple’s third anniversary.

title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Stars Timothy Simons and Justine Lupe Have Opinions on Sasha and Morgan
summary: Justine Lupe and Timothy Simons share their takes on the “Nobody Wants This” Season 3 love triangle between Esther, Sasha and Morgan.
story: Warning: Spoilers ahead for “Nobody Wants This” Season 3.
In its third season, “Nobody Wants This” goes from a love story to a complicated love triangle.
Noah (Adam Brody) and Joanne (Kristen Bell) have solved their main relationship issues. Their siblings, meanwhile, are just stepping into their own mess.

Questioning whether their long marriage is still serving her, Esther (Jackie Tohn) asks Noah’s brother Sasha (Timothy Simons) for a separation. The separation leaves Sasha reeling — and free to acknowledge the undeniable crackle he shares with Joanne’s sister, Morgan (Justine Lupe).
During a trip to New York, Sasha and Morgan finally act on the spark audiences have long sensed between them. (As we said, complicated!)
In an interview with TODAY.com, Simons says he was “excited” for his character to finally cross that boundary with Morgan.

“Story-wise, I think it’s one of those things that’s been there for a while. If you don’t address it, it’ll just end up hanging too long. An audience would be like, ‘Why aren’t you addressing this?’ I feel like they addressed it in a responsible and earned way,” he says.
After spending the night together, Morgan abruptly takes an early flight home to Los Angeles, leaving Sasha stranded and confused in a New York hotel.

Morgan, after initially wrestling with her feelings, tries to win Sasha back over. But it might be too late. By then, Sasha has become more measured. He also sleeps with Esther, muddling matters further.
Lupe, speaking to TODAY.com, thinks Sasha and Morgan’s story would have been different if she hadn’t left him in New York.
“It gave him a moment to get reasonable, for where he’s at and how he can properly take care of himself. If she had not left, he probably would have been swept up,” she says.

Simons says Sasha is at a crossroads between two kinds of love. There’s the “safety and familiarity” of Esther, with whom he shares a daughter and years of history — “but is it the most emotionally healthy relationship for either one of them?”

Simons says there’s a chance Esther and Sasha wouldn’t make the same decisions about their relationships. “They got together pretty young. Maybe they wouldn’t make the choice to be together now,” he says.
Whereas Morgan and Sasha are both “weirdo, kindred spirits that fit the same role in their families.“

As for what’s next? Lupe says she “doesn’t have a strong opinion.”
Simons says he does have an opinion, but he’s keeping it secret (for now).
“I’m not a writer. I’m not a director. It might not be the best thing for the show. That’s out of my hands. But I do have a personal opinion,” he says with a smile.

title: Matthew Perry’s Sister Says This 1 Thing is Always a Sign From Her Late Brother
summary: Matthew Perry’s sister Mia Perry Bowick said she thinks of this one thing as a sign from her late brother, Matthew — it’s a Batman.
story: It’s been three years since Matthew Perry passed away, but his sister, Mia Perry Bowick, says she still feels his presence.
During an appearance on TODAY on Oct. 26, Bowick described Perry as a “constance presence” in her family’s lives. “I do still talk to him,” she said.
Bowick went into more detail while speaking to TODAY.com, saying that she feels Perry connects with her through one sign.
“My favorite sign for Matty is anything I see with Batman on it. I have a Batman tattoo,” she tells TODAY.com, adding that signs from her brother “show up constantly.”

The “Friends” star was found dead on Oct. 28, 2023. His cause of death was later revealed to be the acute effects of ketamine, with contributing factors including drowning, coronary artery disease and the effects of buprenorphine, a medication that’s used to treat opioid use disorder.
Bowick opens up about her late brother’s life and career in three-part Netflix docuseries titled “The One About Matthew Perry,” out  Oct. 27.
While speaking with TODAY.com, she explained that she associates Batman signs with her brother since he was “obsessed” with the character.

“Ever since he was a little boy, it was just always his favorite superhero, and he just was very connected to him. He had all sorts of really incredible paraphernalia around Batman, and he just loved him. It’s just like an automatic association anytime I see the little Batman symbol,” she says.
Bowick, a licensed psychotherapist, said she regularly broaches the topic of the power of signs from loved ones with her own patients.

“I talk about that a lot in my grief practice: how we can choose to decide that these signs mean something so that it can give you that little boost during the day that you might need, versus like, ‘Oh that couldn’t possibly (be a sign).’ It was like, ‘Well it could, and wouldn’t it be nice to believe that (and) maybe choose that?’ And it kind of gives you a little bit like the warm fuzzies,” she says.
Perry left a lasting impact on his family, but he also influenced the lives of many others, as the director Mary Robertson discovered while working on the docuseries.

“I was really struck at some point in the production by the number of people we were interviewing who had an era with Matthew, and that could be one year or two years or 10 years. And they would routinely, time and again, describe this era as the high point of their lives,” she tells TODAY.com.
“I think Matthew’s influence is incredibly deep and incredibly wide,” she adds.

title: The ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Cast Is Torn Between These Matching Tattoo Ideas
summary: A few members of the “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” cast are considering commemorating their roles in the film in a special way.
story: A few members of the “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” cast are considering commemorating their roles in the film in a special way.
Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace and Whitney Peak stopped by Studio 1A on Oct. 26 to discuss the highly anticipated “Hunger Games” prequel and said they’ve toyed with the idea of getting matching tattoos.
“Well, first of all, we did all want to get 12s,” Grace tells TODAY.com.

In the film, Zada and Grace play two of the children selected, or “reaped,” to represent District 12 in the 50th Hunger Games. Because it is a Quarter Quell, the amount of tributes in the game are doubled.

Zada plays 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, a character who later serves as Katniss Everdeen’s mentor in the original “Hunger Games” film. Grace plays Maysilee Donner. District 12’s other tributes are Wyatt Callow, played by Ben Wang, and Louella McCoy, played by Molly McCann.
Peak plays Lenore Dove Baird, a District 12 resident, member of the Covey and Haymitch’s girlfriend.

To remember the film, which opens in theaters Nov. 20, some members of the cast want to get matching tattoos. But getting everyone on board proved to be a bit challenging. At present, only two people are fully on board: Zada and Grace.
“Whitney did never agree, to be fair. Ben agreed,” Zada says.
“Ben did agree. But then he gets a little wishy-washy on us and then he changed his mind,” Grace adds.
Then they had to decide on a design.
“It was supposed to be 12s for all of us, and then Joe and I are still the only two who still want to get tattoos,” Grace says.
“Now it’s little ladybugs, isn’t it?” Peak asks.

The actors thought “it would be sweet” to get a ladybug. In the book, Haymitch and Maysilee eventually become allies, and one of the first obstacles they face together in the arena are mutated ladybugs that dig into their skin.
Now that they’ve narrowed things down to two potential tattoo ideas, Grace and Zada say they have to determine where they’ll get their ink.
“We can’t decide where because Mckenna doesn’t want it on her ankle, and I don’t want it anywhere else,” Zada says.
“I wear too many heels,” Grace quips.
One thing’s for sure, though. Grace has made it clear that their matching tattoos have to be in the same place on their bodies.
“I have three matching tattoos and it always has to be in the same place,” she says.

title: I’m an ‘ACOTAR’ Obsessive. Here’s What to Actually Revisit Before Reading Book 6
summary: A book influencer, a journalist and two podcast co-hosts share how they’re preparing for “A Court of Splintered Harmony.”
story: “Take It From Me” is a TODAY.com series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields. In this story, a book influencer, a journalist and two podcast co-hosts share how they’re preparing for the next book in the “A Court of Thorns and Roses” series.
Warning: Spoilers ahead for Sarah J. Maas’ books.

Buckle in, “A Court of Thorns and Roses” fans: “A Court of Splintered Harmony” hits shelves Oct. 27, reuniting readers with the Night Court for the first new “ACOTAR” novel in five years. You know what this means: It’s officially crunch time.

The last book, 2021’s “A Court of Silver Flames,” wraps up relatively neatly: Nesta learns to weather her trauma while training to become one of the forgotten female warriors, the Valkyrie; Feyre and Rhysand have a baby; and Cassian and Nesta fall in love and accept their mating bond.

The synopsis for “Splintered Harmony” hints at lingering conflicts, both in and outside of the Inner Circle, that have yet to take center stage. And clocking in at 352 pages, it’s just the beginning of the next phase of the story, what author Sarah J. Maas is calling “The Valkyrie Cycle.” This book, as well as the already announced “ACOTAR” 7, “A Court of Forgotten Melody,” will be part of this arc.
Essentially, readers are in for plenty of new content — and with a new villain on the horizon.
For this recap of the most important things to remember headed into the next “ACOTAR” installment, TODAY.com caught up with four experts for their takes:

Sarah Mori, a book influencer who runs a 5,000 person+ Sarah J. Maas book club called Rosebud’s Realm on Discord and has re-read each of Maas’ books at least three times.Ronnie Boswell and Abby Flock, co-hosts of the romantasy podcast “Dragons in the Details,” which dives into fan theories and lore explanations for “ACOTAR,” “Crescent City” and Rebecca Yarros’ “Fourth Wing” series.Garri James, senior managing editor and book club co-host at The Everygirl, who wrote her own bullet point recap of the entire “A Court of Thorns and Roses” series.
Sarah Mori, a book influencer who runs a 5,000 person+ Sarah J. Maas book club called Rosebud’s Realm on Discord and has re-read each of Maas’ books at least three times.

Ronnie Boswell and Abby Flock, co-hosts of the romantasy podcast “Dragons in the Details,” which dives into fan theories and lore explanations for “ACOTAR,” “Crescent City” and Rebecca Yarros’ “Fourth Wing” series.
Garri James, senior managing editor and book club co-host at The Everygirl, who wrote her own bullet point recap of the entire “A Court of Thorns and Roses” series.
Here are the details they say are worth remembering before diving into the next book.
More of Sarah J. Maas
